title: The Diabolical Envy and the Human Mind
english: It is appropriate for anyone who intends to conduct an examination of a certain discourse to take the premises of the discourse into account, in what is now being composed, and especially since the presented book, being most useful, does not have an unapproachable intellect. For within it, the whole discourse concerning the judgments of God is moved by Job, and how nothing of the things happening occurs to men except by the concurrence of God (Job 29:22), and other dogmatic theorems—and even in the preceding discourse, things concerning patience and endurance and the attitudes of the indifferent—I say, goods and possessions and many children and good upbringing—to these are added the manifestation of free will and the teaching of various dogmas, as we see God giving them according to each of the matters, into which these things are. If, therefore, the premise is necessary, it is sufficient.

A change in the value of things appears to be a variation, this being of bodies decaying and increasing, and this being of a change occurring through choice. And as many as occur according to the body, they show neither an unseemly underlying substance nor a praiseworthy one. For no one is acceptable either in the decay of the body or in its increase; for these things are outside of what is up to us. But as many as are done by the one acting while the reasoning is moving volitionally, these show him either rejected or praiseworthy. And this follows those who change from wickedness to virtue or from virtue to wickedness.

So it has happened that a rational being became an apostate from God, 'having made a neck [bowed] before the Lord of all' (Job 29:22). And this is the devil, not having become a devil—for 'God did not make death' (Wisdom 1:13)—but perfect and virtuous—for 'God made all things very good' (Gen 1:31)—who, having fallen from the right state and blessedness, envies those turning toward this; for 'through the envy of the devil, death entered into the world' (Wisdom 2:24). For he reasons as an outcast toward himself that: it is necessary to obstruct the heavenly...

They are a polity, so that those whom I fell from might ascend. For he thinks the progress of men to be a private accusation, because he himself is the 'Morning Star' of the heavens and a star 'rising at dawn' that shines, but because he was preparing those who would be enlightened by the 'Sun of Righteousness' [Mal 4:2], he fell from the heavenly regions. But these, as I see, hasten toward the visible polity, who have more inclination toward wickedness.

For 'carefully the mind of men is set upon evil things' [1 Cor 6:3], which the apostle wishes to demonstrate, saying: 'Shall we judge angels?' [1 Cor 6:3]; meaning that we, living the heavenly life upon earth, judge those who do not guard their own order, just as the Ninevites judge the Jews for not having believed in the Savior, themselves having been persuaded by the preaching of Jonah concerning repentance. But also that which is said concerning the Queen of Sheba [Matt 12:42] is a demonstration of the same mind; for a woman and a queen, standing far off and intending to travel through foreign districts, having surpassed all these things of Solomon's wisdom, she hastened to be obedient, the Jews having the teacher as a pledge and not wishing to be benefited by him, even though Solomon had more. For he was benefited having been instructed by him, but the Savior was shown to be a wonder-worker capable of persuading the most unbelieving ones by the benefit from the words and signs and wonders; for resurrections of the dead, openings of eyes to the blind, cleansings of lepers, and in general a healing of 'every disease and infirmity' [Matt 9:35] was performed by him.

This, then, was the diabolical envy, because men were hastening to lay hold of those things from which he himself fell. Therefore also he does not neglect the influence against the race; for our 'adversary the devil walks like a lion seeking someone to devour' [1 Pet 5:8]. In this way also, having cast a calculation of love of silver into Judah, he made him a traitor to the Savior, just as into a household.
translator_notes: True OET; Pass A ≠ Pass B. Melito skipped; never Cyril Matthew densify.

title: The Adversary's Strategy against Abraham
english: Having entered into his mind as a bird's nest

He did not accept [the excuse] according to the one saying, 'When the evil one turned from me, I did not know' (Job 2:9), which indicates that: many times, when the adversary approached, he did not flee, so as to know him being present through the sinning. For he did not fail to know [the adversary] being present to the extent that the holy man was warring, but thus he did not know [it] as receiving an experience of his evil memories. And he placed a final assault, the one of the request, thinking through this very blow that he might turn virtue aside, which also he did against the patriarch Abraham, if he would allow a friend to receive the book of the covenant.

Having attempted many and often against the holy man and having been defeated in all things, since he hoped to turn away Abraham, who was lying near and beloved, he brings forward the request for the child, which God performs by himself to shame the adversary, desiring to say: 'Take your beloved son whom you have loved' (Gen 22:2), through various words, stirring up the father's natural affection, so that he might make his courage manifest, which he maintained, neither bringing the coming thing to the wife nor to the children, so that it might not become an obstacle to the upright man. But also toward the words of the child he did not flee, [the child] saying: 'Father, behold the fire and the wood; where is the lamb for the offering?' Therefore, believing that even if the child becomes dead, God is able to raise him up, he did not give [him] according to the command, but he would have slaughtered the only-begotten, if God, having accepted the readiness, had not saved the son for him.

For such a scheming intention belongs to the devil, and we are instructed from the Gospel, the Savior saying to his own disciples: 'Behold, Satan has asked you to sift you like wheat' (Luke 22:31). And the book also has the inscription 'following,' since the whole book contains the history concerning him, without any other being brought alongside. And they add 'following' there, as if some were seeking whose the book might be. And some attribute it to the holy Ezra, and others say even when it is written at the end of the book 'following, following,' as if in the archives, since kings being friends of Job, being pleased with the upright man, they deposited the writing concerning him. Let the lover of beauty seek concerning...
translator_notes: True OET; Pass A ≠ Pass B. Melito skipped; never Cyril Matthew densify.

title: The Fellowship and Purity of Job's Children
english: [The text continues], unless he approves these things. But Job is the fifth from Abraham, as this very thing is said at the end of the book.

There was a certain man in the land of Uz, whose name was Job (Job 1:1). And that man was true, blameless, righteous, God-fearing, abstaining from every evil thing. And there came to him seven sons and three daughters, and his cattle were seven thousand sheep, three thousand camels, five hundred yoke of oxen, five hundred female donkeys wandering, and much service, and he had great works upon the earth.

Consequently, the word is about to narrate a virtue surpassing that of the blessed Job, and it remembers the place and the manner of blamelessness and many children and good upbringing and wealth both in flocks and in other things, in order to teach how he did not despise them through over-confidence—for indeed, not possessing them, he did not think highly of them—once all these things were taken away in the trial. And having announced also his pureness of soul, it shows how the devil did not seek a man who was negligent. For it was necessary before the struggle against the opponent to record the greatness of the athlete, to show that, abstaining from every evil thing, he had not been satisfied even unto this, but was also caring for perfection, which is a subversion of those saying that even children and irrational animals abstain from evil things. For this man was both righteous and blameless.

This very thing is also said regarding the first Psalm, where those standing against him are refuted. For they say that 'to be blessed in not walking in the counsel of the ungodly and not sitting in the seat of scoffers' (Psalm 1:1) would also apply to irrational animals and infants. But they are refuted by what is presented; for it is said: 'But his will was in the law of the Lord, and in his law he shall meditate day and night' (Psalm 1:2), which does not apply to infants and irrational animals.

And it is also good that he dwelt in Uz, which is interpreted as 'will'; for the righteous man does nothing without purpose, but his house and city is pure will. 'And that man was noble from the rising of the sun' (Job 1:3). And this is possible regarding the sensible. But if one intended an ascent, it might be said that the righteous man acquires nobility, not from men, but from the light of the 'sun of righteousness' (Malachi 4:2).

"And the sons of him, going along with one another, were making a drink for each day, taking along at the same time also their three sisters to eat and drink with them." The sons of Job, being well-nourished, did not seek social pleasures with others, but among themselves, according to that which is said in the Psalms: "Behold, how good or how pleasant it is for brothers to dwell together in unity" (Psalm 133:1). They were steadfast in virtue and in sensory things, moving "toward one another" and not away; for their gatherings "in the house of their eldest brother" were not only according to time, but perhaps also according to virtue, as they were being educated for benefit by him. And it is also good to take along one's own sisters, which is a clear sign of temperance and grace.

"And as soon as the days of the drinking were completed, Job would rise and cleanse them, rising in the morning and offering about them sacrifices according to their number, and one calf for the sin concerning their souls." According to the one saying: "From the night my spirit cries out to you, O God" (Psalm 43:27), and: "My God, to you I cry out in the morning" (Psalm 5:3), and: "In the morning I will present to you and look upon [you]" (Psalm 5:3), the blessed Job rose in the morning not for some other work, but to present a sacrifice to God on behalf of the children "according to their number," which is to say, individually and in good order; for nothing is poured out in haste. But after this, he also presented the calf on their behalf in his own way, providing for the children's guidance. Thus, after the feasting was completed, he cleansed them, demonstrating both the sensory cleansing and the intellectual cleansings that complete the process.

If the "calf" offered on behalf of all signifies the "Cross" which remained for the sake of the human race as Savior, consider that He is also "fit for eating" in the parable of the Gospel, because of the nourishing nature of the divine teaching. Do not marvel if the calf alludes to the Savior; for Job was not unaware of the coming of the Savior; for concerning Him he said: "he who is about to grasp the great whale" (Job 41:1). For Job said: "perhaps in their mind the sons..."
translator_notes: True OET; Pass A ≠ Pass B. Melito skipped; never Cyril Matthew densify.

title: The Devil's False Presence
english: "They thought my evils toward God." Great purity is shown in this of the children; for not seeing any perceptible sin of theirs, they offered the sacrifice regarding the intellect, considering that human weakness and softness in youth often have a slip. Therefore also the holy Paul said: "I do not even know within myself, but not in this have I been justified" (1 Cor 11:5), and the Psalmist: "From my hidden things cleanse me" (Ps 139:23). Therefore it must be observed, not that they were struck down by such a death because of sins. "Thus Job did all the days of his life" (Job 1:5).

The unbrokenness of the holy one's tone is shown here, as never perhaps and never not the virtue in action. This also David says about himself, singing: "I will bless the Lord at all times" (Ps 34:1). "And as this day happened, and behold the angels came to stand before the Lord, and the devil came with them." The form of the word shows the discourse more narratively regarding the presentation of the angels in the phrase "and as this day happened", following our understanding of the time and the appropriate state of the presentation before the Lord of the angels, providing their own ministry and their own labor toward God. While they were standing, the devil also stood by.

Even if he is manifold and many-sided, he does not escape God. It has been said, as he himself also came with the angels, not merely "to stand before" him, but he himself is also known by the eye of God which oversees all things. And let the hypocrisy of the devil also reveal the explicit truth, "transforming" himself "into an angel of light" (2 Cor 11:14) and these things hiding from the born creatures, but not being able to escape God, the progenitor of all things and the one "through whom all things" [were made] and the Holy Spirit; for the Trinity is of the same essence. Just as it is said concerning the Word as "he is a critic of the thoughts and notions of the heart and there is no creature invisible before him; but all things are naked and laid bare to his eyes" (Heb 4:13), so also concerning the Spirit: "for the Spirit searches all things" (1 Cor 2:10). And concerning the Father it is said among the apostles: "You, Lord, are the knower of hearts" (Ps 139:1). And appropriately, belonging to divinity alone is that which [governs] the thoughts...

To see. For if this were even evident to born beings, they would have distanced themselves from the sinners as if not to help them, but to turn away out of fear of the greatness of evils, lest they themselves be endangered while acting as ambassadors for such. But even if he had grasped the devil's intention from certain proofs, rather, since they also 'stood before the Lord' (Job 1:6) when he came, and the devil was with them with hypocrisy, it was expected that they would bring to God the judgment concerning his standing, which indeed happened.

For God himself says the following to him: 'And the Lord said to the devil: From where have you come?' (Job 1:7) He said this to him so that hearing it, we might understand: 'From where have you come?' These angels, our own, being appointed to perform divine service for me, were performing this, standing before me, acting instead of a [true] standing—for their standing is not local—but you, from where? For you are not my minister. 'From where' then 'have you come?' You would grasp what was said to Adam by God as similar to this: 'Adam, where are you?' (Genesis 3:9). The 'from where have you come?' was a rebuke of the devil's futile movement.

'And the devil answering the Lord said: Having gone around the earth and walking up and down under the heaven, I am present' (Job 1:7). If the devil's intention was to constitute an answer to the question under God, his answer would be seen as being before God. For God, desiring to speak his own will to his born one, implants it in that one's intellect. But the devil, answering the Lord, is said to answer not thus, but as he chooses to answer. And what is his answer, let us see.

'Having gone around,' he says, 'the earth and walking up and down under the heaven, I am present' (Job 1:7). One should not be surprised if, being a subtle spirit, he passed through the aforementioned places. For even God did not rebuke him as a liar. And also the 'having gone around' is good; for he is not encompassing. But he goes around as 'one seeking someone to overthrow,' so that he might drag those who are persuaded by his evil deceptions, and he might seek out those who oppose him, which also happened regarding Job. Therefore, he does not use force, nor does he come upon us by power. For he is appointed to stand against those who are able to resist.
translator_notes: True OET; Pass A ≠ Pass B. Melito skipped; never Cyril Matthew densify.

title: The Rationality of the Devil and Job
english: "Stand firm in the faith," and: "If a spirit of the one exercising authority rises upon you, do not leave your place."
For it is also said that God provides the power, He who will give "and the outcome of being able to lift up."

It should be noted, however, that the earth and the places under heaven are different places; the earth being under heaven, the places under heaven are not necessarily earth. And the devil, rejoicing in the "spiritual things of wickedness" of the demons, encircled those places. These, he says, having come around, he stays beside, which should be understood thus: having come through all these and finding the blessed Job unable to receive anything of ours, he stays beside, which is to say: I wish to show my hidden thing to your unchangeable eye, desiring him to ask it of me.
And the Lord said to him: "Pay attention therefore with your mind concerning my servant Job, for there is no man on the earth blameless, true, God-fearing, turning away from every evil thing."

Thus, the Lord said to the devil in the same way as to those who are stumbling toward error, not withdrawing; if it is what God wills the devil to understand, it enters toward his rebuke most difficultly, because God did not cease reasoning. For it should not be ignored whether the conversation of God toward the devil is just; for nothing is just on the part of the one who has arranged all things, but even this is toward the benefit, so that he may be disgraced by the reproach of the righteous and blameless man.

The Lord has called Job "servant" according to both significations; for his servant was according to what was said by the Psalmist: "I am your servant and the son of your maidservant" (Psalm 89:8), and a son from the service and of the genuine slavery of the Spirit, having been made worthy of grace, and he himself saying according to the wise Paul: "the Spirit itself bears witness with our spirit that we are children of God" (Romans 8:16). For "he who does righteousness"

"He was born of God." It is also an explicit indication of the devil being rational to say: "Pay attention to your mind" (Job 35:10); for to think is proper to a rational being. Not only is this said about the devil here, but also in: "But you said in your mind: I will ascend to heaven" (Job 35:11), which, as it is said, is a demonstration of him being rational himself.

And if thinking happens through him, it must be sought whether repentance also happens. For after thinking comes thinking and repentance. And just as thinking lies within his will, let it not be that repentance also [lies there]. But he who does not grant these things, let him not hide, making God the cause of his evil—for if he does not possess reason and mind. And even if he has been led astray by something, he still participates in the nature of those who are thus, in being rational. For even if men are mortal, we say that their participation is not according to mortality, but according to the rational, which exists common to both the immortal and the mortal.

And thinking is not accessible only to the serious or only to the wicked. Just as the use of sensation is common to both the serious and the wicked—where the serious man, planning well, has not used it like the wicked man looking up to heaven and making himself a god—so also thinking: being found in the serious and the wicked, it has been led astray according to its use. "Pay attention, therefore," he says, "to your mind concerning my servant Job, for there is none on earth like him" (Job 35:10). It is not a vain thing to say: "of those on earth." For there are rational things concerning him and on his behalf that happen regarding the earth. For it is not the same to say: "there is none like him" as to say: "there is none on earth like him." For how did he not exceed all those on earth, with the God of all things testifying to him in: "A blameless man, true, God-fearing, turning away from all evil deeds" (Job 1:1)? And he turns away...
translator_notes: True OET; Pass A ≠ Pass B. Melito skipped; never Cyril Matthew densify.

title: The Hand of God and the Nature of Touch
english: One is said to mainly abstain from wickedness by nature. For praise has its place when one, being able to be base, abstains from wickedness through hatred of it. Not everyone who does not use wickedness is called to abstain from it; for infants, not using such things, no one would say they mainly abstain from wickedness, for the one doing this acts by judgment and word.

But the distinction between wickedness and virtue requires skill. Nor would anyone say a child abstains from intemperance or is prudent, for he has not yet reached the discernment of these things. Having discussed these matters in the previous passages, when we were setting aside the things from the first Psalm, we rebuked [Job] as being God-fearing according to it. For he is truly God-fearing, one honoring a life of reverence, whereas those honoring things not sacred are found impious.

And to the blessed one is added 'true' according to the theory of truth and the lack of hypocrisy in ethics; for one who seeks virtue through opportunism is not true. 'And the devil answered and said against the Lord' (Job 1:9). It is possible to say, regarding 'against the Lord,' that he spoke against the testimony of God being a lover of evil, or that he thought with audacity; for wickedness is shameless. Thus also, what he brings forth from a lover-of-evil mindset brings forth the deficiencies of the virtue of the righteous.

For what does he say? 'Does Job fear God for nothing? Have you not encircled him and his house and all that he possesses on every side? Have you blessed the work of his hands and made his livestock many on the earth?' (Job 1:9-10). It is characteristic of lovers of evil, who loathe virtue, not to consider the beauties of those nearby as genuine, but to say instead: this one is just through an inability to do wrong, this one is prudent through the so-called foolishness, this one does not have wealth and resources because he is unsuited to them, even while considering the gentle hypocrite as such; and in no way does anyone base accept anyone's virtue as genuine.

The devil, being the leader of wickedness, conceiving such things concerning Job, made these things manifest to the one who knows the hidden, saying that Job is just because of external goods. And 'encircled' (Job 1:10) was said to him instead of security, providing emphasis, as if because of these things he is unassailable and has no vulnerability, the multitude of the un...

Since he is considered to have wealth as the cause of his virtue, he was rebuked for not speaking well. For having these things removed, he remained similarly unblemished. In truth, possessing wealth contributes something to virtue for one who uses it well, but wealth itself contributes nothing to it.

The blessed Job showed unshakeable virtue both in poverty and in wealth. 'But send your hand and touch all that he has; surely he will bless you to your face' (Job 2:5). One may call his hand in two different ways: either the punishing and service-oriented power, which the divine Scripture is accustomed to calling 'vessels of wrath,' or the protective and guarding power, as it is said: 'No one is able to snatch from the hand of my Father.' It is also possible to take the Son into a hand that protects and supports those under it, as it is said: 'The Lord's right hand exalted me; the Lord's right hand made strength' (Psalm 37:30).

And as for 'to touch,' let it not mean here to strike instead of bringing affliction; for we commonly have this expressed in Scripture. For 'do not touch my sheep' does not forbid simple contact, but the audacity against the saints to harm them. And 'he who touches you touches the apple of his eye' (Zechariah 2:8) similarly means one who touches for evil. Even if the one through the devil has become an apostate and 'stiff-necked before the Lord of all' (Psalm 78:9), yet he still has some reverence toward the Creator of all things.

For he says: 'Surely he will bless you to your face,' instead of cursing or blaspheming, using this expression so that the harshest words might not be brought against God, as is foretold. 'Then the Lord said to the devil: Behold, all that he has I have given into your hand, but do not touch him' (Job 1:12). The words placed here seem to mean not to fall into trials apart from divine permission. For God says: 'Behold, I have given all into your hand.' But so that it may become clear that He also exercises permission with measure, it is added: 'but do not touch him.' Therefore, circumstances occur neither by fate nor of themselves, but by the permission of God, according to what has already been laid out for the demonstration of Job's virtue, and also for another reason, concerning which in the following [sections]...
translator_notes: True OET; Pass A ≠ Pass B. Melito skipped; never Cyril Matthew densify.

title: Job's Undisturbed Endurance
english: It will be said: 'And the devil went out from the Lord.' This is spoken more literally concerning the devil, because he becomes one who is outside the Lord, even more so than Cain. For concerning him it was said: 'And Cain went out from the presence of the Lord God' (Gen 4:16). And to go out signifies that he has become invisible to God. Therefore, this one will always be found among those on the outside, even if he came in a feigned manner among the attendants of God.

'And it was as this day; the sons of Job and his daughters were drinking wine in the house of their elder brother' (Job 1:18-19). Consequently, he remembers both the day and the gathering of the children, so that their death might also happen in a continuous way at one time, following the fall of the house, having died. In custom, it is often written that many, as they come together into such assemblies, are thought to be drinking, not only drinking but also eating and talking as if in a banquet. And through allegory, examine the placed texts, lest they were 'drinking wine'—that which 'gladdens the heart of man' (Prov 15:15)—from the elder brother who was beginning the divine instruction.

'And behold, an angel came to Job and said to him: The pairs of oxen were plowing and the females were donkeys grazing with them. And the raiders having come, they raided them and killed the children with swords. But I alone, having been saved, have come to announce to you' (Job 1:19-20). It is presented through these things how the raids occurred in a single day: 'the pairs of oxen and the donkeys grazing were plowing.' And the messenger who announces is to be welcomed, just as it is written in the Kingdoms. It is worthy to understand how the things of the announcement, having happened continuously, have a weight in the narrative and an overflowing tendency toward grief; for the plowing of the pairs of oxen being raided works a double sorrow, and added to the loss of the animals is the loss of the nomadic donkeys, which did not provide a brief approach, and from the expected destruction of livelihood and property, an addition of excessive misery, and the slaughter of the children by the raiders was also announced along with the others. Sufficient to...
Therefore, even if it were falsely reported, it would have been immediately disturbed. However, despite the harshness of the occurring calamities, the holy man was not at all disturbed.

It has been said in one of the Psalms concerning a holy man: 'From an evil hearing he shall not be afraid. His heart is prepared to hope upon the Lord.' And even as it was said according to the blessed Paul: 'Who shall separate the faithful from the love of God? Neither tribulation nor distress, nor persecution, nor famine or sword' (Romans 8:35), following this, the most manly Job remained inseparable from the love of the Lord, having withstood so many attacks. For anyone might say that, as far as possible, one should despise the irrational and the work coming from them.

But having heard even concerning the slaughter of the children, to have taken this up manfully demonstrates the manliness of the holy man and his patience. It should be observed, lest the one being saved alone, in order to announce, was being saved for greater temptation. For if Job, having endured the occurring things unshakeably even until the stretching out of his own body, was not so unperturbed by the lesser things while the greater pains were present, then the lesser were not so unheeded.

'While he was still speaking this, another angel came and said to Job: Fire fell from the heaven and burned up the sheep, and the shepherds it devoured likewise. And having been saved, I myself came to announce to you.' The successive announcement of the pains demonstrates the excessive and marvelous manliness of the blessed one. For see the observation, how while the one announcing the former things was 'still speaking,' the second one did not come for their healing, but was announcing for an escalation, announcing harder things, as it is customary for the announcement of pains to overturn the reasoning and to hollow out and thus disturb, as if to make one move outside of the proper state, being drawn toward the various sorrows.

But the holy man was not such a one. But as an unbreakable wall, remaining likewise unshaken against the majority of those attacking who were able to see him, so the holy Job, having 'the foundation' upon 'the rock' of salvation, was not moved when the temptations fell upon it. And it is worthy to behold also the things of the second announcement, how it raises up the distress toward an escalation. 'Fire,' he says, 'fell from the heaven and burned up the sheep and the shepherds it devoured likewise.' For even if the holy man...
translator_notes: True OET; Pass A ≠ Pass B. Melito skipped; never Cyril Matthew densify.

title: The Succession of Calamities and the Second Messenger
english: He accurately understood the doctrines of truth, knowing that the administration of trials did not occur without God, but that what was happening brought him the greatest sorrow because of those being stumbled, as also God was acting against him.

For the simpler people might have reasoned that the ones coming to capture, having taken the livestock and being able to slaughter the children, were doing this not from God, but by the law of enemies coming in disorder and acting out of hatred. When fire was announced as having descended from heaven, there was fear, lest any of the weak should reason that virtue is nothing and that God punishes one possessing it.

But even when this happened, the holy man did not falter, being entirely mindful of God. For even the devil does not have the authority to bring down fire from heaven, but this has happened by divine judgment, so that God, who gave Job the authority, might present him to the devil, to show that the blessed one among men cares for nothing, even if he weaves many schemes.

For indeed God has caused that which is not possible by him to happen, in order to expose the adversary by presenting the greatness of the athlete; Job, bravely enduring, was not facing a small or trivial blow, but the destruction of tens of thousands of sheep, and with the shepherds, it turned out not to be a few.

And the angry one was being guarded again, for which cause we have previously mentioned. 'While he was still speaking this, another angel came and said to Job: The horsemen made three heads for us and encircled the camels and captured them, and they killed the children with the sword. But I alone was escaped and have come to announce it to you.' (Job 1:19).

Perhaps there was a military camp in the land, which fell upon the camels divided into three divisions. For as he says it is well known: 'The horsemen made three heads for us.' It is also possible that a continuous attack of horsemen was occurring then, and was moved by the devilish suggestion, and thus the messenger said it because it was happening out of habit: 'The horsemen made three heads for us.' They did not only take the camels, but also killed the children. Understand, then, how the sequence of trials occurs in a more distressing order. First indeed...

First, five hundred yoke of oxen were taken captive, and five hundred female donkeys were nomads. Then, fire was sent from heaven against seven thousand sheep, making things more severe than the previous suffering. Third, three thousand camels were taken away, and the children were slaughtered just as before; a costly matter and an unbefitting judgment regarding property.

After these things, the death of the children was continuous, as will be made clear in the things to be revealed. For indeed, if previously the death of the children was announced, the things that arrived were astonishing. But when something happened by way of a command, their successive sharpness and the agitation of the mind were more sufficient, which the devil also wickedly did by making a request. And he was despondent, when the holy man's reasoning was broken.

While he was still speaking this, another angel comes, saying to Job: 'While your sons and your daughters were eating and drinking with their elder brother, suddenly a great spirit came from the desert and struck the four corners of the house, and the house fell upon your children and they perished. But I alone was saved and I have come to announce it to you.' (Job 1:18-19).

It is not useless that it says: 'your sons and your daughters eating and drinking,' but it is toward a command of malice, and this chief-evil devil is dealing, so that the announcement of what has happened might become a heavy grief, exceeding the sorrow of the holy man. For if the children had fallen asleep, the one reasoning without being moved by the terrible thing would not have been so distressed. But when he was turning toward a necessary healing of the body, the temptation was brought, and this has a more severe grief.

For it is not doubtful that many were present at such a time, of whom the announcer did not remember, being satisfied with the exceeding loss of the children and following what happened to those present. For such a thing is customary in the Scripture; for when the Savior broke the five loaves, from which he satisfied five thousand men, the evangelist remembers, saying: 'apart from women and children' (Matthew 14:21), mentioning only the preceding numbers. And what also is the 'spirit' that 'came from the'...
translator_notes: True OET; Pass A ≠ Pass B. Melito skipped; never Cyril Matthew densify.

title: Job's Wisdom and the Soul's Departure
english: Having touched the four corners of the house and having struck it down, one should investigate whether it was an excessive storm that thus battered the house and brought it down, or a spirit serving the devil, or the devil himself. For this is a great, evil spirit, having touched the four corners of the house and having brought it down. For either of these is possible if one seeks it, if the reporter was able to know whether this was a spirit serving the devil or the devil himself.

If the spirit thought it to be a storm, this should be said as being like the descent of fire from heaven against the sheep (Job 1:6), and what is said regarding it and fitting to it. For the devil is not able to move the wind. It also applies as an immediate, emphatic indication that one cannot escape the fall when such a thing happens, perhaps found outside the reporter.

“Thus Job arose, tore his clothes, and shaved the hair of his head, and falling to the ground, he worshiped and said: ‘Naked I came from my mother's womb, and naked I shall depart there. The Lord gave, and the Lord took away; blessed be the name of the Lord’” (Job 1:20-21). The divine spirit and that of the devil forestall the maliciousness of evil men. For perhaps one of such people would say that Job was not fond of children, since he did nothing worthy of sympathy. But his feeling and his manliness are shown together, that he received the terrible horror and grief of the death of the children neither unfeelingly nor ungenerously; for through “tearing the clothes and shaving the head”—for the ancients were accustomed to do this at deaths—he shows sympathy and familial love. And the following things bring forth a sign of manliness and surpassing wisdom in advance.

For if he says, 'and having fallen to the ground' (Job 1:21), he did not despair, nor did he leave an unseemly word to a wise man, but he worships the Originator of all, being persuaded that these things happen not outside of divine judgment, and that they happen from the beginning followingly and according to some correct reason.

For he also brings forth after the worship: 'Naked I came out from my mother's womb, naked and I will depart there. The Lord gave, the Lord took away. As it pleased the Lord, so it happened. Blessed be the name of the Lord' (Job 1:21).' For understand, how after courage and prudence is found in the blessed Job, through which divine [teaching] introduces doctrines through the words that are profitable to all the race of humans.

'Naked,' he says, 'I came out from my mother's womb, naked and I will depart there.' Concerning which those deliberating on nothing divine regarding the immortality of the soul ought to be questioned. For where will Job depart naked? Perhaps in the womb of the mother? For from there he went out naked according to what is said. But away with this false thought. It is evident that this was said for the instruction of not letting the soul be scattered, as it seemed to some.

For the blessed Paul also writes something similar, saying: 'For we have brought nothing into the world, and we are able to bring nothing out' (1 Timothy 6:7). For just as the bringing out implies the dead person existing, so the one not having brought in is existing and enters from some place bringing nothing of that kind.

And that doctrine, being unknown to many, he introduces saying: 'The Lord gave, the Lord took away' (Job 1:21), presenting after this, that his possession did not happen to be unjust and having taken its beginning from some unbefitting assistance. 'The Lord makes poor and makes rich' (1 Samuel 2:7), not by any irrational whim, as those introducing fate deliberate, but so that it may be known that the one stretched out in these things, whether he carries them appropriately, along with...
translator_notes: True OET; Pass A ≠ Pass B. Melito skipped; never Cyril Matthew densify.

title: Divine Providence and the Integrity of Job
english: There are other causes, some known to men and some known to God alone as secret, which the blessed one says: 'The Lord gave, and the Lord has taken away; blessed be the name of the Lord' (Job 1:21). The word 'it seemed good' must be heard not simply, but as if the God Himself were judging it so firmly.

Something similar is brought forward in the Acts of the Apostles, as the apostles were writing a letter regarding not circumcising those coming to the godliness, saying: 'It seemed good to the Holy Spirit and to us' (Acts 15:28), not simply, but as a settled decision. It might also be that the word reveals this thing to the opponent, that Job was not handed over because he gave in to the provocation of the devil, but so that glory might be produced for the Lord. And this was what God Himself said to Job: 'I have used you in a different way, so that you might be revealed as righteous' (Job 2:3), and that virtue stands not by means of money nor by means of children.

It is also wonderful that he says such a thing of thanksgiving: 'May the name of the Lord be blessed' (Job 1:21), which is a rebuke against those who complain about such accidents and bring such things forward, which is not even good to say. But the holy one is not such an unwise person, being unbending in his reasoning even when such things happen, becoming a herald of true dogmas and divine things.

The phrase 'so Job tore his clothes' (Job 1:20) is to be taken typologically. It might be possible to say that for this reason he stripped himself, first showing to the one testing him that, if you desire even the remaining things, you have these also; then showing symbolically that just as a combatant departs from an opponent. And the removal of the hairs might be a symbol of considering all excess to be nothing great, but being well-disposed toward the just and wise man, neither being debased in 'reliefs' nor being distressed in 'tribulations,' which the blessed David also sang in presenting: 'I will bless the Lord at all times' (Psalm 34:1).

'In all these things that happened to him, Job did not sin against the Lord, nor did he give unreasonableness to God' (Job 1:22). A great testimony is given by the Holy Spirit to the blessed Job in saying: 'In all these things Job did not sin against the Lord' (Job 1:22). For it is often the case that one does not sin openly, but happens in...

What kind of thoughts cause disturbance, as it is said: 'I was disturbed and I did not speak' (Job 1:21). But the presence of 'before' indicates that no stumble occurred, for he was being watched by God. For 'no one sinned thus' is not the same as 'no one sinned against the Lord,' which shows a purity surpassing even in word, deed, or thought of the holy man who stumbled.

To this end, God used to call those repenting: 'Remove the wickedness from your souls before my eyes' (Prov 28:13), which implies that we must not only refrain from deed, but also from the thought of evil, as seeing God. The Savior also says in the Gospel: 'But when you give alms, do not blow a trumpet as the hypocrites do' (Matt 6:2). And also: 'He who sees in secret will repay you' (Matt 6:4). Just as he who gives alms in this way does not hear the praise of the many, so he who does not sin against the Lord is free from all evil.

It is also good to say: 'And he did not give foolishness to God.' For he who is convinced that what happens is managed by divine providence does not attribute foolishness to the God who governs, unlike the unbelieving who often blame [God] and say: 'This ought not to have happened, or that; this one ought not to have suffered poverty or to be rich or to be sick or to be healthy,' or: 'Why did the young man depart from the life of the elders while they were still in it?'. In short, those saying such things assume the governance is foolish.

But the holy man, even in such circumstances, blesses the Lord, being convinced that the judgment of God is just. 'And it happened as this day, and the angels of the Lord came to stand before the Lord, and the devil came among them. And the Lord said to the devil: From where do you come? Then the devil said before the Lord: Having gone through the earth and walking throughout it' (Job 1:7-8). Having received from God the authority for an initial approach, the devil destroyed all that Job possessed, both his belongings and his children, but he was not able to overturn the resolve and the courage of the holy Job. For he remained through greatness of soul, the same man, according to godliness. And rightly so, for it was being divided: that God sends pleasant things and they are taken away. He attempts a second petition to move against his body.
translator_notes: True OET; Pass A ≠ Pass B. Melito skipped; never Cyril Matthew densify.

title: The Meaning of Akakia and the Devil's Vain Attempt
english: He strives to subject him to unendurable labors. Regarding these same verses, for those who have reached them, what was said to them should be applied to these, so that the same things are not said many times, only adding this: that the diabolical nature is shown to exceed all. It should be said regarding the question, 'Where do you come from?' that the most convicting thing was said by the Lord to the devil, as he had nothing to say of his own with boldness or in a way to cause hesitation, because he had been defeated, which he himself shamefully did not admit.

It should be noted how the devil does not answer in this way now. For then he said, 'Having gone around the earth and walking through under the heaven, I have returned' (Job 1:7), but now, 'Having gone through the heaven and walking through the whole [world].' And he visited, lest as a liar he would not wish to remember that 'he went around the earth,' so that, not even attacking the beginning of Job, he might be thought to do so only from shamelessness. For he knows that nothing is hidden from God. For he also did not say, 'Of those things which you gave me authority over, I have done; I have taken away the existing things of Job and the children they took away.' For it would have been consistent to say this, and, 'The same remained.' But he moves toward a second petition, from which he thinks he will overturn the purpose of the holy man.

And even if the devil hides his own will in having said 'the whole [world]' instead of 'the earth,' let us show from the Scriptures how the earth is often called the whole [world]. For it has been said, 'The whole [world] was filled with the knowledge of the Lord' (Isa 11:9). And Job himself in the following says concerning God, 'He who makes the whole [world] in the highest' (Job 37:7), indicating that God draws a man from the earth through virtue toward heaven. 'And the Lord said to the devil: Pay attention to my servant Job, for there is no man on the earth like him, righteous, God-fearing, blameless, avoiding all evil; and he still holds to innocence' (Job 1:8). And now, 'Pay attention with your mind' (Job 2:3), as was said before, has permission to be used, because after the struggle he was strengthened. For the devil, thinking that Job rejoices in external things as if they were good, was saying, 'Did you not surround the inside and the outside of his house?' But when his attack became in vain, the 'pay attention' is said instead of: 'You have known through the trial' the courage of the 'God-fearing, blameless, innocent, [and...]'

While being kept from all evil. And to these things the Lord brings an accusation: 'yet akakia remains.' Pay attention, then, that He will not 'bless me personally,' as you thought. It should be noted how it is said in the Septuagint: 'abstaining from every evil thing' (Rom 16:9), but now: 'from all evil' (Ps 1:1). From this it is known that 'evil' is used for 'poneros.' Also what is written: 'those who love the Lord, hate evil' (Ps 5:5), instead of 'hate wickedness.'

Akakia signifies different things; for it denotes both the absence of wickedness and goodness of character. When the saint says, 'God judge me, for in my akakia I have walked,' he means akakia as virtue; for one possessing virtue is devoid of wickedness. And in others: 'the guileless and good-natured clung to me,' he speaks of the diverse akakoi—for these are good-natured—and being good-natured is a recognition of virtue. But when it says: 'they deceive the hearts of the akakoi,' and: 'the akakos believes every word,' and again: 'that I might give guile to the akakoi,' it means the pure and unblemished. To whom he also prays that guile might be given, not the guile equal in power to wickedness, but prudence.

Job therefore 'still had akakia' with all words being made upright. 'But you have said that you will destroy his possessions for nothing.' The Lord exposes the vain work of the devil against the saints. For he who acts without cause labors in vain. So even if the devil, hoping to seize the saint, attempted through the destruction of possessions and children—and having recognized the attempt was futile against the saint's courage regarding his possessions—he fought him in vain; for nothing of what he hoped for happened.

'But the devil, having taken up the challenge, said to the Lord: skin for skin. Whatever a man has, he will lay out for his soul. Not indeed, but stretch out your hand and touch his bones and his flesh; he will not indeed bless you personally' (Job 1:9-12; 2:4-5). Considering the three kinds of so-called goods—those external, which are divided into wealth, property, health, and other bodily things, and others which are virtues—he thinks only the undifferentiated goods are such, and he thinks Job has this same mindset, and he shamelessly says to the Lord—that is to say, speaking according to what we understand has been said before—that a man would lay out everything so that he might not suffer something himself.
translator_notes: True OET; Pass A ≠ Pass B. Melito skipped; never Cyril Matthew densify.

title: The Devil's Assault and Job's Desolation
english: the external possession

Regarding the angels, the pattern follows. Of the history, it is this: 'The devil went out from the Lord' (Job 1:7). Having gone out, he does not wait, but immediately performs the work of the temptation, surrounding him with a total-body wound, intending by the blow to dissolve the tone of his virtue. By mentioning the extremes, he shows that he also touched the middle parts.

'And he took a potsherd, that he might scrape the sores' (Job 2:8). The verse signifies the wilderness and his helplessness, because no one was present with him while he was nursing, but also because the wife was absent due to her haste toward work, from which both she and he were perhaps being nourished; for in the following, the woman saying to him, 'And I, a wanderer and a vagabond, receiving place from place and house from house, when will the sun set?' signifies the wilderness. To such an extent was his body dissolved, so as to be reduced to sores. Therefore, with the potsherd, he scraped himself while being sick in soul and unbending.

'And he sat on the ashes outside the city' (Job 2:8). It is probable that in those cities they did not permit one having such a body to live. Therefore, outside the city on the ashes he sat, and he perceives the continuous change, from what prosperity and enjoyment he has changed into what kind of wickedness under the tempter, so as to be a stranger and to sit on the ashes, without a household being with him, nor even a friend or even the wife herself, as was previously stated; for she does not seem to be acting toward him without distinction, as we have placed it.

'And after a long time having passed, his wife said to him: How long will you endure saying this?' (Job 2:9). 'Behold, I wait for a little more time, expecting the hope of my salvation. For behold, your memorial is being blotted out from the earth, sons and daughters, whom I labored for in vain with pains in childbirth. But you yourself sit in the rot of worms, staying awake through the night. And I, a wanderer and a vagabond, receiving place from place and house from house, when will the sun set, so that I may rest from the labors and the pains that now seize me? But say one word to the Lord and end.' The devil, having become weary from so many blows and being unable to cast him down from the loss of his property and of the...
translator_notes: True OET; Pass A ≠ Pass B. Melito skipped; never Cyril Matthew densify.

title: The Blasphemer's Fate and Job's Endurance
english: Children of corruption, besides the immoderate affliction of the body, a third thing he weaves for him of old: the conversation of the wife; perhaps through her he might have deceived Job, just as through Eve he might have deceived Adam. For having passed a long time, such that even he is not able to shake the athlete, the woman brings forward the matter of brevity, perhaps remembering the suffering, to rid him of it, if he should speak a word to the Lord irrationally.

And to see in each word how he is called toward brevity: 'How long will you endure?' (Job 7:25),—submitting to brevity a provision for a great time of his sickness, and then after that: 'Saying: Behold, I wait a little more time, awaiting the hope of my salvation' (Job 7:26)—in a certain way he turns his expectation toward the impossible. For perhaps many times, he having preferred the things of the good hope while she was departing from him, stopped the brevity, which not seeing, having a weak thought, she considered him falsely hoping for brevity. For an irrational soul loves to always consider expectations as uncertain.

But as the repayment she thought was near, the total hopelessness, he says: 'Behold, your memorial has vanished from the earth' (Job 7:10). No son or daughter is left to you to guard the memory of the succession, she says only that: even if they should be healthy, the enjoyment of health is without children, [they] being or being destroyed. And these things indeed if only were present, patience would have had a reason, he says, but toward these things also you yourself 'sit in the rot of worms' (Job 7:5), and I from poverty remain 'from place to place' (Job 1:8).

Through all these words, having sent the arrow of brevity from herself, she brings the end of the most trivial conversation, saying: 'Speak a word to the Lord and end.' To which someone might say: how could the woman have this thought, that if he should speak a word to the Lord, he would end? To which someone will speak differently, either having submitted this to her as an opponent, so that the haste...

May he be satisfied with the word: 'Surely I will bless you to your face' (Job 42:10), or perhaps in those cities the one blaspheming against the Lord died by a ruler or the citizens. For perhaps he knew no one, both the blasphemer and the living. For perhaps this happened then, lest the wickedness be poured out. Perhaps he reckoned that even God would not allow him to live after speaking blasphemous words.

And it also appears through: 'Behold, I will make your remembrance depart from the earth' (Job 7:35), as if: you shall have no hope of ever coming to it for the enjoyment of good things, which he alone considered to be good, being irrational concerning the good according to truth. And being ignorant, he spoke a word otherwise true; for the remembrance of those who despised the heavenly human life is not earthly. For the Scripture confirms this, the Psalmist says: 'The face of the Lord upon those doing evil, to destroy from the earth the remembrance of them' (Psalm 37:10). For when some have sinned and are saying 'God is not in the heart' (Psalm 14:3), God brings hardship upon them, so that after they have been benefited, their remembrance may be destroyed from the earth and 'they may be written in heaven' (Luke 20:37), having been transformed into virtue.

And the things concerning the children, as the woman said, reckoning their salvation alone to be the hope, she claims to have borne them in vain. And she also brings before him her own suffering. 'But he looked and said to her: You have spoken like one of the foolish women. If we accepted the good from the hand of the Lord, shall we not then accept the evil?' His patience of soul is shown in this, in not remaining under such pains and the word brought forward unsuitably by the woman, but also saying: 'You have spoken like one of the foolish women.' And looking intently, he has said this, understanding from her reproaches, the holy man that she had brought these things forward by a diabolical suggestion, and being wise, he knew that the first [woman] having been struck by the devil's suggestion had become the cause of Adam's transgression.
translator_notes: True OET; Pass A ≠ Pass B. Melito skipped; never Cyril Matthew densify.

title: The Friends' Sympathy and Arrival
english: Because of this, He says: 'Just as one of the foolish women you spoke.' Then, having placed a reasoning before her that is appropriate, He brings it: 'If we received the good things from the hand of the Lord, shall we not endure the bad?' For the same understanding is toward the pleasant things of the indifferent, not to be overcome, and toward the burdensome, not to be cast down.

For he who is expert regarding things knows that the things called good are not such by their own nature, but follow the opinion of the user; just as also the bad—the harmful, I say—are not bad in themselves, but the use occurring in them is what they are. For many, after wealth, both the foolish and the excellent appeared, like Abraham and those like him, and Pharaoh and those near him. When much affliction came again, some yielded, but some remained steadfast in their reasoning, of whom are the blessed Job and Lazarus, as having received these things from a physician, through incisions and cauterizations, for the sake of salvation.

"In all these things that happened to him, Job did not sin with his lips against the Lord" (Job 1:22). This is said a second time; first, when the first affliction [came], and second, now. And then it was said: "In all these things that happened to him, Job did not sin against the Lord" (Job 2:10), but now: "In all these things that happened to him, Job did not sin with his lips against the Lord" (Job 2:10).

Some indeed think there is no difference between saying "not to have sinned with the lips" and "not to have sinned before the Lord," but others perceive them thus: that regarding the removal of what was present and the death of the children, it was said once, "Job did not sin against the Lord," neither in word nor in thought; but here, the "with the lips" lies as an addition, saying, as perhaps some slight variation occurred—for this is lesser—but rather the movement of human weakness, being compelled by the great pain of the whole body.

The written spirit therefore says, in order to show the endurance of the pain and his courage, that even though his courage was being compelled even to an inaudible thought, he was not shaken so as to do anything from faint-heartedness or smallness of mind, or to speak. Something like this also the [author]...

Job says, 'I was greatly disturbed and did not speak,' indicating that something had happened to him that caused such a disturbance that, even having stilled the movement of his mind, he did not speak. This is in accord with what Paul writes to the Corinthians: 'I do not want you to be ignorant, brothers, concerning the affliction that has happened to us in Asia, that we were burdened beyond measure, beyond strength, so that we despaired even of life. But we have received in ourselves the sentence of death, so that we might not be trusting in ourselves, but in God who raises the dead' (2 Cor 1:8).

When his three friends heard of all the evils that had come upon him, each one came to him from his own country: Eliphaz the Temanite king, Bildad the Shuhite tyrant, and Zophar the Naamathite king (Job 2:11-13). It is most surprising if these things happen to men of great reputation. Therefore, since Job was among the most glorious because of wealth and virtue, the friends, having heard of the severity of the things that had happened, came not from one place, but each from his own country, moved by sympathy, and since these were kings, they did not overstep the man undergoing such a change.

As for 'tyrant,' he says either as a parallel to king—since the name was not well known in that time—or to denote a difference in rank from a king. This is also in Proverbs: 'Through me kings reign, and tyrants decree justice' (Prov 8:15). And these who came to him were led by no other cause. The statement is useful for sympathy, so that we might not, because of the changes that fall upon us, abandon the things of love and brotherly affection.

'And they came to him unanimously to comfort and visit him' (Job 42:11). They had come to do both, since it happened that they suffered both; for he was deprived of property and children, and his whole body was held by the wound. They came to him 'unanimously,' either with much readiness or because, having their houses plundered, they had agreed together to come to him for the purpose of comforting; for the evils had not ceased but were already active. 'And seeing him from afar, they did not recognize him, and having cried out with a loud voice, they wept, each one casting down his...'
translator_notes: True OET; Pass A ≠ Pass B. Melito skipped; never Cyril Matthew densify.

title: Job's Fortitude and the Sympathy of His Friends
english: Their own clothing and having covered themselves with dust. They sat with him seven days and seven nights (Job 2:13). In this, two things are taught by what has been set forth: the courage of the blessed one—while others were discouraged due to the immeasurable nature of what had happened to him—and the sympathy of the friends, who not only arrived, but having seen, did not recognize him because of his sickness, which had also altered his facial features; and having cried out with a great voice, they wept, each tearing his own clothing and scattering dust, which altogether, as it is said, demonstrates both the courage of the holy one and the sympathy of these.

For he remained unbending, which anyone would have marveled at, and through these, Job, not being provoked to anger for a short time because of the suffering overwhelming the others, which is what usually happens to men. And it is sympathetic that they should participate with him seven days and seven nights. Therefore, one should not be stingy with patience toward the weak and helpless ones who are being led by such things.

"And none of them spoke. For they saw that the wound was terrible and exceedingly great" (Job 2:13). Those who had come for consolation were silenced by the magnitude of what had happened. And it is fitting that they previously used sympathy; for he especially loves to endure in those being comforted. For there was nothing useful to them even for healing, the suffering exceeding the help of medical treatment. And it is likely that, having a certain opinion of him as a wise man, they chose a respectful silence, not daring to bring forward a word before him.

"After this Job opened his mouth and cursed his day, saying:" (Job 3:1). The wise man is not a babbler, nor does he bring forth by his tongue what is not possible to become. He curses not the day, which is a chronological interval, but the things happening in it. For by custom, in the Scripture, the things happening are called the day. This the Psalmist teaches, saying: "In a evil day the Lord will deliver him" (Psalm 91:3), not calling the evil day a chronological interval, but the evil things happening in them; and what is said by Paul: "for the days are evil" (Ephesians 5:16), refers to the mind. Thus, one might say the day is good for some because of what happens, and bad for others. For to the peoples of Israel, unexpectedly...
those who love literalism
translator_notes: True OET; Pass A ≠ Pass B. Melito skipped; never Cyril Matthew densify.

title: The Darkness of Evil's Path
english: Having come to pass—and what is established is that which is about to be made, and not everything is manifest under the sun—he who speaks and says: 'Behold, this is new, it has already happened in the ages coming before us.'

But the testimony of both through personal evil and through the benefit of others for life, to be introduced and to be joined to the bodies, is heard by Jeremiah: 'Before I formed you in the womb I knew you, and before you came forth from the mother I appointed you a prophet to the nations' (Jeremiah 1:5); and Jacob and Esau, concerning whom God says: 'I loved Jacob, but I hated Esau' (Romans 9:13), even while they were in the womb; and John in his mother's womb 'leaping and rejoicing' (Luke 1:44).

For these things do not show the souls to be contemporary with the bodies; for he who rejoices in the mother's womb, partaking of the Holy Spirit from his mother's womb, and one being hated before being born and another being loved, these things do not happen without cause.

Furthermore, it is not only through one's own faults, but also to be joined to the body through the benefit of others, and it is more laborious; for just as it is not fitting to praise the cause of the war because of those conquering in war, which is a pretext causing grief to many, so it is not fitting to praise those succeeding, but rather to be convinced that even among themselves some, having been tested, have reached ultimate evil, and they have become causes of labors because of the benefit of others.
Therefore, the evils happening for this cause, Job says they are a painful and worthy-of-curse day: 'Let the day perish in which I was born' (Job 3:3). And he says this on behalf of all the race.

For the saint knew that much trouble was happening to those seeing what happened to him, knowing that he suffers unworthily, raising the word to every cause, saying only: 'If not because of the fall of many, a character of manliness was not needed.' Just as the affectionate physician will appropriately curse the disorder after having fallen from many's lawlessness, so the blessed one, healing, because these things do not happen arbitrarily, but according to a certain rhythm and a following intended so that the fallen might be benefited, curses the day of the fall of men, sharing the word.

He expresses himself more narratively with words, so that the form of the discourse might be evident. He says, therefore, that the cause might cease and no longer exist, she who worked the entrance to life.

Furthermore, since childbirth also happens in the night, he also takes the name of the night: 'may that night be darkness,' so that it might be said: that those walking might no longer find the way of the generation of evil, being hindered, just as one says concerning those falling into disorder: that the way of the lawless might no longer be prosperous. 'And let the Lord not seek her from above.' For it was proper for the holy man to pray that virtue might drive the rational things forward and that they might no longer suffer a turning toward a worse state—not the same one—according to those being brought in by reincarnation. 'Nor should light come into it.' The impulse toward the worse might be prevented for the speechless ones who remain, so that according to what has been said, 'the light of the ungodly shall be extinguished' (Ps 108:2). 'And let darkness and the shadow of death take her,' so that this concept might darken those drifting into evil errors, hindering their impulse toward the evil by making them think that the attempt is deadly. Similar to this is what is said by the prophet: 'I will build up its paths with stumbling blocks, and its path shall not be found' (Job 5:13; Prov 1:12). For evil is greatly hindered both by fear and by ignorance. For someone will come to hold a hateful attitude toward it. 'Let a gloom fall upon it, let that day and night be cursed, and let darkness carry it away.' These things are not to be considered curses, but prayers for the cessation of the occurrence of evils. For according to what has been previously explained, it is right to pray that the cause of the fall and the way of this be unknown, 'so that there may not be prosperity in an evil man.' For the desire for virtue works to make the path toward evil more unknown, while it, being rebuked, brings about a complete forgetfulness of its activity; for this would be 'to carry it away into darkness.' It itself—I say evil itself—is also worthy of a curse, preparing those who act for the things worthy of a curse. 'Let it not be in the days of the year, nor be numbered in the days of the months, but let that night be pain.' In number and in memory, the holy man does not want the day of the fall to become painful because of...
translator_notes: True OET; Pass A ≠ Pass B. Melito skipped; never Cyril Matthew densify.

title: The Economy of God and the Defeat of the Devil
english: Because of that dark cause and the night, which is called excessive and dim, so that some correction might arise from repentance... [he prays] that the one who has come into repentance be made as if enclosed in that year, about which the Psalmist says: 'He will bless the crown of the year with your goodness' (Ps 65:11), and to sing, progressing: 'You will teach me in your counsel in your power' (Ps 25:5). 'And let neither joy nor gladness come upon it.'

Being a fellow-laborer, the saint prays that no one should fall and be delighted or find pleasure in this. For often, seeing someone hastening toward evil deeds, we pray, saying: 'May he not happen to be the one striving.' With this same mind, the saint, while praying, sings, not cursing: 'Let the deceitful lips that speak lawlessness against the righteous with pride be made silent, and let them be brought to nothing' (Job 5:1). And for the deceitful lips to become silent, what would it be other than to cease speaking unjustly, once the speaker recognizes how improper such a thing is?

And he, therefore, prays that no one might be so perverted as to think that it is a matter of indifference or a source of joy to fall into the state that leads to human weakness. The Savior himself says: 'It would have been good for him if that man had not been born' (Matt 26:24), and in Ecclesiastes it is shown: 'Better [is the one] than these two, who has not yet become' (Eccl 4:3). But for the one not yet born, since the birth is clearly shown to be a good thing if it happens, it does not happen without foundation. 'But he will curse it, the one who curses that day, he who is about to grasp the great worm' (Job 5:1).

This is the prayer for the loosening of the cause of what happens, being evils for those who have come upon the path of birth through themselves, and pains for those through others. He prays, therefore, that the fall might be a curse worthy of the actual cause of the human accident, so that those being born in it, recognizing that it is full of curses, might flee from it as...

It is not a different energy of the conquering God, but according to the economy, to join with the one who conquers. For he did not say, 'but the conqueror will destroy that day' and add 'the creator' or 'the teacher'—nor does he follow with these, but 'he who is about to seize the great sea monster'.

Since the devil has been called the cause of the fall of men, he brings a prayer for this, in order that it might be loosed, following the prophecy, as 'the devil, who has the power of death, shall be destroyed' (Hebrews 2:14); for this was foretold to the purity of the soul moved by the Holy Spirit, as also authority will be given to the saints 'to tread upon serpents and scorpions and over all the power of the enemy' (Luke 10:19), so that others, rising up from these, might be delivered from the clinging sin as they hear of progressing in virtue: 'he shall tread upon the shield and the basilisk and shall trample the lion and the dragon' (Psalm 91:13), who is the devil. For it is said concerning him: 'our adversary the devil, as a lion, walks seeking someone to devour' (1 Peter 5:8), and again: 'having crushed the heads of the dragon' (Revelation 12:5).

And well is 'he who is about to' said, signifying that according to the incarnation. For it was not fitting to destroy the devil by naked divinity, but through this temple of the Word having come to be, who was born from the seed of the one deceived and harmed by the devil. For it was a boast for him to have existed having seized him by naked divinity.

But the various names of the devil signify his various energies, not his essence. For devil, and adversary, and evil, and lion, and dragon, and serpent, and sea monster, are called because of the manner of his evil working in different ways, which is a subversion of the Manichaean dogma. 'Let the stars of that night be darkened and not remain, and not come into light, and not see the Morning Star rising' (Isaiah 14:12). The things having happened on the fourth day...
translator_notes: True OET; Pass A ≠ Pass B. Melito skipped; never Cyril Matthew densify.

title: The Divine Economy and the Suffering of the Just
english: contrary to his courage

What is, is the absolute good to exist. For it is blessed to be outside of this life. To those who know, Jesus says: 'You are no longer of this world, but I have chosen you' (John 15:19). Therefore, it is better not to have even begun the path of such a way, even if it happens through divine economy. For it is good if no one in health needs a physician. Thus, not being in the same state follows, which also follows as something laborious and unpleasant, as it brings about: 'For he would have removed toil from my eyes' (Job 5:7). This indicates not only the one suffering and the toil surrounding him, but also that he saw many being led astray; for the eye of the righteous is weighed down by works being performed by the wicked. And the toil that encroaches upon life is not small. In injustice, all these things exist... [text garbled/unclear]... which would not happen if evil were not being done.

But even Habakkuk allows such a voice, saying: 'Why have you shown me troubles and pains, to make me see violence and unrighteousness?' (Habakkuk 1:2-3). 'Why did I not end in the womb, come out from the stomach and not immediately perish? Why did my knees meet, why did I suck breasts?' He avoids the economy intended for the benefit of others, as it seems, according to Jonah, to demand the teaching of God's judgments, which is a private matter of the righteous, not being completely ignorant, but so that others may learn this kind of speech being personified. For Jeremiah approaches thus: 'You are righteous, Lord, but I will speak judgments to you' (Jeremiah 12:1), which is indicative of knowing what happens through these, concerning which he asks: 'Why does the way of the ungodly prosper?' (Jeremiah 12:1).

The judgment of God in reality receives much variety: the unrighteous being prospered, and the righteous being distressed and partaking of filth, as Jeremiah himself, being holy and having been sanctified from the womb, suffered so many things as to be cast into a pit of mire. But also Lazarus and the rich man—the one suffering evil, the other living with much ease—bring forth the precision of God's secret judgments (Luke 16:19-31). And this 'prospering' is called so as toward the glory of the many. Therefore, the saint is not vain-speaking, but asks so that it brings about the others learning such things. This also exists in what is said in one of the Psalms: 'How good to the...'
translator_notes: True OET; Pass A ≠ Pass B. Melito skipped; never Cyril Matthew densify.

title: The Spiritual Warfare and the Choice of Company
english: God is with the upright in heart. As for me, my feet were shaken a little, and my steps were poured out a little, because I sought peace among the lawless, seeing sinners (Job 13:15). For it does not waver, it is clear; for he says, 'How good God is to Israel' (Job 10:18). He thinks these things as being understood by those having a straight heart.

He posits himself as being shaken while being firm, and receiving the countenance of those being displeased, so that after the words of doubt, the words of teaching might be brought forward. And Job, indeed, inquiring of God, wants to learn—for this he brings forward the countenance—the cause of such a struggle. For indeed, regarding the cause of the way in the body, he says as if receiving it: for indeed... having fallen into so much evil, as if they had come to entreat for the fellowship of the body and the helpers of the providential economy, so as to say the things set forth.

'Why then did I not finish in the womb?' (Job 10:12). For the saints, in reverence, entreat that they not grasp the benefit of the weaker ones. Because of this, he also says the following: 'And from the stomach I came out and was not immediately lost' (Job 10:18); likewise also: 'Why did my knees meet [me]? Why did I suck breasts?' (Job 10:9). For the holy one willed that disease should not happen to the rational ones, so that a sequence might not occur for the pure to come through them in a medicinal manner.

And also good is: 'Why did my knees meet [me]?', which indicates a journey. For with others, because of their own faults, life followed here, but with the saints, they met not as those responsible, but as those executing an economy. 'Now, having slept, I have rested, but having awoken, I have not ceased with kings and counselors of the earth' (Job 3:13, 29:25).

For if, he says, such a sequence and order had not occurred as that which led me to this state through those needing treatment—that is, if I had happened to finish in the womb, not coming out from the stomach and being immediately cut off, and not having met knees nor sucked breasts—it would be, if not through the providential economy administered through us, 'now having slept, I have rested', which is: having ceased my course in that life of the divine and heavenly rational ones. The kings and counselors tyrannize the earth of the gentle, concerning whom it has been said: 'Blessed are the gentle, for...'

"They shall inherit the earth" (Psalm 37:11), taking for ourselves kings in high positions and counselors of a lower rank, over whom the kings rule. Such an analogy is contained in the parable in the Gospels: "become more than ten cities or five." "who were proud upon swords." The saint, not being a lover of war, did not want to have his social intercourse with such kings readily available, who, being ready to fight, consider such social intercourses to be good; but knowing "that our struggle is not against blood and flesh" (Ephesians 6:12) according to the apostle, "but against principalities, against powers, against the rulers of the darkness of this [world], against the spiritual forces of wickedness," against whom those living well fight, having armed themselves with the salvation "panoply," he wanted to have his social intercourse without being provoked by human generation. But one of those peaceful ones was the one seen by Jesus, son of Nun, as a commander of the Lord, to whom he said: "Are you of ours or of the adversaries?".

Being discerning, the saint knows and does not readily recognize that even the adversary often "is transformed into an angel of light" (2 Corinthians 11:14). These, however, are also men, not preferring arrogance, but rejoicing in the victory over the adversaries and "rejoicing in God" (2 Corinthians 6:10). "Or with rulers, of whom there is much gold, who filled their houses with silver" (1 Timothy 6:17). Having the same mind and what has now been set forth, let us receive it familiarly with the person of the saint. For not being a lover of silver or a flatterer, it did not seem right for him to spend time with the rich, he who bravely brought about the loss of all possessions and wealth and did not accept riches, being without following friends and having a free intention and an unshakable word; how would he want to have his social intercourse with such rulers and kings, who happened to be adorned with wealth? To some, appearing as a good wealth, the wonderful Paul writes: "You have already become rich; you have reigned without us; and would that you had reigned, so that we might also reign with you" (2 Corinthians 6:10). For they have possessed much gold, which indicates a pure mind, pure ones, approaching clearly with the light of knowledge. These themselves also, by the analogy of nature, not by the spoken [word]...
