translator_notes: True OET; Pass A ≠ Pass B. Melito skipped; never Cyril Matthew densify.

title: The Meaning of Eternity and the Eternal Servant
english: By the word, they filled their own houses, having their own minds adorned by participation in the word of surpassing purity, not possessing any such state which has become Job's for the sake of the divine economy; for because of conversation and interaction with men, such a mind does not have its likeness unblemished, which would have been wiped away if it were not for sin, but because something else had happened, which occurred for the sake of the benefit of others. 'Either as a fetus proceeding from a mother's womb, or as infants, who did not see light.'

To the words 'and I suckled breasts,' this is given through the middle of the verses spoken from 'now having slept I am at rest' until 'who filled their houses with silver.' Let the same thought be applied to the previously spoken things; for just as it happened to come into existence involuntarily, so it happened for him to be in the state of a fetus, so that he might not participate in more of this kind of distraction and friction according to generation, or even if he had become an infant, to turn back again, so that he might not be born in the state of age after the infantile state.

For in truth, such a thing would not be outside of perplexity and seeking, regarding those not reaching unto life, and those dying immediately after birth, which the philosopher will investigate not as if these things happen by chance, but as being the just and good of God, the God of all things, governing all things by word and order and measure and weight. The saint himself knows the judgment and does not say this without anxiety, but praises the better state and being persuaded that this is to be preferred. 'There the impious burned a fire of wrath, there the wicked rested from the body, but the eternal ones were of one mind.'

The whole verse of the divine thought being tested by Job is a teaching upon the difference of human generation. For having understood regarding it being better for him not to approach the human way or to be born, or having been born to be immediately freed from this, he proceeds and teaches a certain cause, as if this thing was being studied not a little by the opposing powers. Since the word showed how the souls encountered various errors of generation, and the devil and those with him are lovers of sin...

Just as it stirs those given to it into wickedness, this very thing interprets by saying, 'There the ungodly burned up a fury of wrath' (Ps 58:6). By saying 'there,' he refers to the other world from this one, as in: 'Naked I came from my mother's womb, naked I will depart there' (Job 1:21).

However, even if such a thing is a mere paper against evil powers, God forewarns through His economy and has given laws to each to prevent sinning, so that while passing through this [life], one might think heavenly things and desire a similar life there, so that having worn out the body, one might have a rest as one who has become a combatant against the habit of wickedness. For this is what is meant by: 'There the combatants rested from the body' (Job 42:6).

For the saints, having been pleased, through many tribulations on earth—of which they become combatants in body and not in mind—have a rest with the angels, having attained it eternally. And if those are eternal, and their rest is communal, it is evident that the souls too are eternal; for they are immortal and, having despised the temporal, possess the eternal.

It should be noted that 'eternal' is spoken of in several ways; it also signifies the without-beginning and the without-end, as in: 'God is eternal.' For God is called eternal because His existence has neither beginning nor end. And something else is eternal, as it is said: 'The things not seen are eternal' (1 Cor 15:51). For these are not eternal as God is, but because they remain always without falling away. And differently is the eternal, when it is measured against the present, as it is said: 'The sons of this age are wiser in their own generation' (1 Cor 3:19). And the time extending the life of a man is also called an age.

Regarding the Hebrew who was unwilling to be set free in the seventh year, it is said: 'He shall be a servant for an age' (Ex 21:6). For no human being remains a servant at all through death. According to this, Paul also writes: 'If meat makes my brother stumble, I will never eat meat for an age' (Rom 14:21), instead of 'through life.' 'They did not hear the voice of a tax-collector.' For this age is filled with tribute, in which one has come here for the sake of the economy. For there are many who, having come under the yoke of sin, [pay] taxes and dues to the adversary...
translator_notes: True OET; Pass A ≠ Pass B. Melito skipped; never Cyril Matthew densify.

title: The Heat of Sin and the Shade of Virtue
english: They provide. Regarding Jerusalem having become liable to such tributes, the prophet Jeremiah lamented, saying concerning her: 'Having begun in cities, she has come into tribute' (Jeremiah 46:10). This is a gathering of debtors of souls, or she subjected her own liberty to the most brutal tyrant.

These are holy, even showing that what is in the Gospel regarding kings is not to be subordinate. These, therefore, the ones released from the present [affairs], either because they have not been tested or even after testing being superior to them, one side is outside the tribute of strangers, not those making the trial... 'the small and the great is there, and the servant having become familiar with the lord and having attained a shadow.' The impersonal nature of the one ruling in these matters is shown. For not in another way does one lord and another slave or poor man enter into life.

For in [the phrase] 'a certain king or tyrant,' Wisdom does not exclude another 'beginning of generation'; for 'one' is the 'entrance into life for all, and an equal exit,' even if there was a difference according to movement. These were not born differently. But also the servant serving the lord, even if he is not lord but a slave of the lord throughout the whole way, attains a shadow, so that from this shadow, having a symbolic meaning, he may be raised up from the laws that were given and here unto the heavenly citizenship.

It is to be expected also differently; in this present life, a difference has been established between the small and the great and the slave, bringing greed into variety. But in the coming age, Paul says, 'there is neither male' 'nor female, there is neither slave nor free' (Galatians 3:28). Similarly he would say, as neither rich nor poor, but the demonstration of works, by which the one in this living will be considered great and free there, though small or a slave. For he says, 'I saw' 'slaves on horses and' (Revelation 6:5)...

Even what is supposed to be great is found there in punishment. Perhaps it is also possible that since the great one is great from each person according to virtue, the small one will likewise be found there in the same way.

According to this thought and what is carried in Ecclesiastes, it is understood thusly: 'wherever the wood falls, there it remains' (Eccl 9:3), saying wood for the man, who if he has fallen in punishment—that is, if he has reached the end of this life being in sins—thus 'he shall be there.' But if also in virtue, similarly: 'for all must appear before the judgment seat of Christ, so that each may be brought according to what he did through the body' (2 Cor 5:10).

And the servant who serves God intellectually is there, obtaining shade and rest, having escaped the heat of life: 'a wise son was saved from the heat' (Prov 10:1), not being consumed by the heat, according to those in the parable who did not receive the seed into depth and fell by the flame of sin. This promise is said to David in the Psalms: 'the sun shall not strike you by day, nor the moon by night' (Ps 121:6), which according to the literal sense we do not find. For he himself, being righteous, was labored upon by the heat of the sensible, but was unlabored upon by the heat of sin.

For it is common for those falling from without to perceive the righteous and the unrighteous, but it is the property of the diligent to flee from the heat of evil. 'Why then is light given to those in bitterness, and life to souls in pain? Who are partakers of death and do not find treasures by digging, but become content if they happen upon them' (Job 26:10).

The hidden and not manifest to all, the judgment of providence, the holy teacher examines for the sake of those hearing, so that first they may not be displeased with the things happening, and later, knowing that it comes from God, they may not consider the things happening to be either accidental or caused by fate. For there are various things following men...
translator_notes: True OET; Pass A ≠ Pass B. Melito skipped; never Cyril Matthew densify.

title: Rest for the Saints
english: Regarding various sufferings, such as being in poverty, or passing from wealth into poverty in different ways, or being in various crises and others in some evil, and not only experiencing such bad things but also important ones, examining the judgment, he asks saying: 'For why is light given to those in bitterness?' (Job 36:30). For if he knows, but indeed wishes us to be enduring, he instructs, as it is fitting to receive the teaching of these things from God. And regarding those being embittered because of the injustices of men, he says: 'For why is light given to those in bitterness?' (Job 36:30). Such a thing even Jeremiah, alluding to it, said: 'I sat alone, because I was filled with bitterness' (Jeremiah 9:21). And he fell into bitterness because he saw the irregularities and injustices concerning men. And these same ones also grieve.

Or did not the blessed Paul have pain, saying: 'Great sorrow is mine, and unceasing pain to my heart. For I wish that I myself might be an anathema for my brothers, my kinsmen according to the flesh' (Romans 9:3), who happened to be outside of it because of 'turning away from the truth' (Romans 2:8)? And he also shares in death, saying: 'It is better to depart and be with Christ' (Philippians 1:23), just as 'digging up a treasure' (2 Cor 4:7 allusion) is the desire for this, as one of the saints says: 'Woe, that my sojourning has been made long' (Hebrews 11:13), and writing about Paul concerning similar things: 'For they do not have here a staying city, but they seek the one that is to come' (Hebrews 11:16). Therefore, not even being lovers of life are they ready to die, as the blessed Paul says: 'Daily I die' (1 Corinthians 15:31). For because of this readiness he wrote thus. For a lover of life would not say this. For the saints know that if they come out of this life, they will receive the divine rewards.

Therefore, just as they are 'digging up a treasure' (2 Cor 4:7 allusion), it happens even if the digging is done with toil. Just as also the saints themselves through much toil look forward to entering the kingdom—but hope deafens the toil—so also those contending in the struggle suffer much, looking toward the crown. It is also fitting for these same saints the following half-verse, if he says: 'But they became circumspect, if they should encounter [it].' No one of the bad ones, even if he is in crisis and because of this desires to depart from life, per...

One becomes rich after departing. For if the afflictions of those here have ceased, but instead they receive the blows that have become established, and even as they withdraw they possess the impulses, or passions, or wildness, or other sufferings of the soul, which have been sent to them here having been strengthened. Because of the following blows, they are not without joy.

Therefore, let this also be understood concerning the saints: either they are not without joy, being sent by angels and encountering the bosom of Abraham and exchanging this [life] for the kingdom, despite the circumstances for which they suffered externally and for the sake of virtue they endured pains; and even the blessed David, looking toward those things and though being king, considering life to be like a prison, sang to God: 'Bring my soul out of the prison' (Ps 142:7). For he was not being guarded in a sensible prison. There is also the thought from what is approaching, as he desired the deliverance from here; for he says: 'The righteous shall wait for me, until I am repaid' (Ps 116:15). And this is equivalent to: 'so that we may not be perfected apart from ourselves.' Of these are the true masculine sacrifices, and those of the promises.

If this is so, how are the saints not without joy, encountering the end of this life, after which the kingdom of heaven shall receive it? 'Death is a rest to a man; for God has shut up [the door] against him' (Wis 1:15; Ps 108:7). If anyone wished to take this according to what is at hand, he might say, that for those in circumstance and in pains death is a rest, since 'God has shut up [the door] against him' (Ps 108:7), dismissing the circumstances. But he who follows with the first thought will have nothing to complain about, saying, as if not all those who end in rest become [so] by receiving the bad blows.

And this should also be noted, that he did not say: 'death to a man,' but 'to a man of valor'; for he who has courage and is in virtue is unshakeable toward death, having himself most ready for it and singing: 'My heart is ready, O God, my heart is ready' (Ps 57:7). And this same shall have rest, receiving the promises directed toward him. And moreover, he shall have rest while suffering, because that which 'God has shut up against him' (Ps 108:7) through the common decree of that which is said concerning Adam, 'Dust you are and to dust you shall return' (Gen 3:19), is released by 'departing' from him 'pain and sorrow and sighing' (Rom 8:22) because of having heard: 'Enter...'
translator_notes: True OET; Pass A ≠ Pass B. Melito skipped; never Cyril Matthew densify.

title: Watchfulness and the Providential Care of the Saints
english: "...to the joy of your lord." "For before my food a sigh comes to me, and I weep, being seized by fear. For the fear which I cared for has come to me, and which I was afraid would meet me." Fear does not always signify the passionate, nor the refined and perfect, but also a middle kind, concerning which neither the passionate nor the refined occurs, but as one might say, one of these things happening either for the benefit of others or because of a fall.

For if the blessed Paul says: 'I fear, lest as the serpent deceived Eve' (2 Cor 11:3), he does not have the fear passionately, nor is the perfect and pure signified in this, even if the wise Paul had it, but rather a care for the salvation of others. It has been said concerning the perfect: 'The fear of the Lord surpassed all things' (Ps 112:7), but concerning the passionate, in order that it may not be carried along, the saying says: 'Do not fear their fear' (Matt 10:28), and: 'Do not fear those who kill the body' (Matt 10:28), and: 'There they feared a fear, which was not fear' (Job 3:25). And all these things are seen because of the saying: 'And I weep, being seized by fear.'

Let us see from the beginning the things set forth: 'For before my food a sigh comes to me' (Job 10:1), which is instructive, that others, having lived a life of luxury, and finding only pleasure and enjoyment and caring for nothing else through their works, cry out to themselves: 'Let us eat and drink; for tomorrow we die' (Eccl 2:2); but the holy man, also according to the blessed Paul saying: 'Who is weak and does not faint? Who is scandalized and am I not burned?' (1 Cor 10:12), approaches sensory food not without a sigh because of human weakness and not for the sake of pleasure, but understanding the pure and incorporeal life and that table which the Savior promised to his own disciples, saying: 'That you may eat and drink at my table in the kingdom' (Luke 22:30) of the heavens, sighs; even while receiving this, he sings in his mind: 'My soul longs and even faints for the courts of the Lord' (Ps 42:2).

And since the holy man, even if he be perfect, knows that it is possible for a man to fall into a lapse as long as he is in life, he leads into: 'And I weep, being seized by fear.' And because the mind is strengthened, the weeping in the pains is according to the saying: 'I shall wash my bed every night, with my tears my couch' (Ps 6:6).

"...to find for me." The saints do this, not by neglecting themselves, but being awakened by prudence, so that through these things they may call upon God for help, just as the blessed David says when calling a congregation like himself: 'Come, let us worship and bow down, and weep before the Lord who made us' (Ps 95:6). For great is the good of the care that comes through vigilance, which the Lord says he desires the disciples to have: 'Watch, for you do not know at what hour the thief comes' (Matt 24:42).

Nor are the saints any less anxious because of approaching temptations, not giving themselves over to negligence, but preparing themselves for these, fearing lest they, having preached to others, themselves become unproven. And they do not avoid the stumbles. They are not without reason ready for preparation. For this reason, the blessed one himself always remains, holding back the uprisings from the devil. He wished not to be in circumstances, since human weakness, as far as it reaches its measure, cannot bear the immeasurability of labors, unless a brave calculation overcomes the weakness. For this reason he says: 'For the fear I thought [was not there] came upon me, and which I thought would meet me' (Job 5:7).

And he did not say these things by being overwhelmed, but according to the understanding assigned to him. For he had fear, lest he be delayed in his life and be tested by tribulations and circumstances, from which it happens to trip many. Even if they were invincible, they do not want to be drawn into temptations, so that neither the adversary may have more torment through them, nor may he cause them to trip the human weakness as we said; just as a pilot steering the ship straight does not want to be tested by a storm, lest he also fall by a stumble. Because they do not avoid circumstances through cowardice, one of them is heard saying regarding their common [faith]: 'Our God is a refuge and strength, a help in the tribulations found by us exceedingly. Therefore we shall not be afraid when the earth is shaken and mountains are moved in the hearts of seas' (Ps 46:1-2). In agreement with these, the apostle says: 'Who shall separate us from the love of Christ Jesus? Tribulation or distress or persecution or famine' (Rom 8:35) and the...
translator_notes: True OET; Pass A ≠ Pass B. Melito skipped; never Cyril Matthew densify.

title: The Principles of Teaching and the Nature of Trials
english: Sixth. Regarding the fact that these things do not occur without sweat, he brings forward: 'but in all these we prevail through him who loved us' (Rom 8:37), which is an example through the agonistic struggle, with which victory occurs.

And well also is 'he met me'; for as to an athlete, the trials met him. For the devil does not fight those who happen by chance, as also the Savior shows, saying to the disciples: 'Behold, Satan has asked you to sift you like wheat' (Luke 22:31). He met also with this one having himself most ready for the fight, as the matter showed and the following shows: 'I have neither found peace nor rest nor ceased, and anger came upon me.' His preparation toward the opponent is shown from these.

For being watchful and having hope and the gift of the Spirit, he stood toward the adversary, knowing this; and Paul [says] that 'the struggle of the saints is not against blood and flesh, but against principalities, against powers, against the rulers of the darkness of this world, against the spiritual forces of wickedness' (Eph 6:12), and against the devil himself, the arch-evil, who 'prowls like a lion, seeking someone to swallow up' (1 Pet 5:8).

However, even so, despite his being watchful, the devil did not neglect him, in order to make an excuse, so that he might bring upon him what he brought upon him, which he calls anger because of the hardships, knowing that they were not brought upon him because of malice. For he says: 'I know that I shall appear righteous.' And in another way he knows to call the hardships anger. For he says: 'You sent out your anger and consumed them like a reed' (Ps 127:4).

But if we hear of the anger of God, we do not consider this to be His passion according to human reasoning. For such a passion is not in the nature of things to be sent out, nesting in the soul. But the said anger of God is sent out; for he says: 'You sent out your anger', which is the hardships. For these things also are sent. And this one, therefore, calls these things anger, which happened to him.

Thus, having composed such a narrative, in which there is instruction concerning the judgments of God and divine mysteries, which we have laid out as much as possible, this saint is manifest not as one having become passion-driven because of what happened, but also having within those things a longing and love for divine contemplation and a heavenly one. 'Eliphaz the Temanite, having taken up the speech, says: Has not much been spoken to you in toil? And who will esteem the strength of your words? For if you have spoken much...'

You, whom [He] once encouraged with words when hands were weak and caused the weak to rise up, and to whom [He] provided courage when knees were failing, now fear has come upon you and seized you, but you have hurried [to abandon Him]. All teaching and distinction have principles, of which, possessing them well, everything proceeds according to the word. But when the principles are not well, many errors follow.

Let the example of heresies be given; for if someone posits the father of the Son to be ungodly beforehand, many falsehoods follow this false beginning; for he will suppose the Son to be a created thing, not eternal, since it is not possible for him to be eternal if the [Father] pre-exists [as ungodly]. And if the Father pre-exists according to their false hypothesis, the Son would not be eternal. And it follows that he is a creature and a work, with which follows that he is changeable and altered. With this being so, there will not be God in essence. Therefore, if ever you encounter false dogmas, seek their beginning; for this being overturned, everything collapses.

Let a second example of the same kind be set forth. There are some who introduce an opinion, thinking that they have made the Savior appear to be such. It must be sought for whose sake he arrived, and it is clear, that it is for the sake of the salvation of men. And if he will appear to be [such], and if teaching will appear to have become [such], then the cross and the ascension will also appear to be such, following which it will appear that salvation, and not truth, has come to be. This follows the absurd beginning.

And regarding the words set forth by Eliphaz, there is something like this. There are two irreconcilable principles concerning the things coming upon men: one is for the correction of sins, the other is for the showing of courage and testing of those being afflicted, which is what the saying having this character means: 'Blessed is the man who endures temptation, because having been tested, he shall receive the crown of life, which He promised to those who love Him' (James 1:12). And again: 'Consider it all joy, my brothers, when you fall into various trials, because the testing of affliction works patience, and patience, testing, and testing, hope' (James 1:2-4). And there are also testimonies to receive of the other kind from the Holy Scriptures. For it has been said: 'I will confess my sin to the Lord, that I have sinned against Him' (Psalm 32:5). For he says that the induction occurs through sin. Therefore, the things that are heavy are common and...
translator_notes: True OET; Pass A ≠ Pass B. Melito skipped; never Cyril Matthew densify.

title: The Strength of Words and the Error of the Friends
english: scourges

Because he brings tribulations toward the things accomplished. Because of this, they spoke their own assumptions contrary to Job (Job 4:4). Therefore also God granted them forgiveness and, on account of ignorance, caused them to bring a sacrifice. For he did not do this with an evil intention, but as justifying providence; this is what they were saying, even if they lacked precision.

From this very confusion, the first [friend] brings forward the words, beginning by asserting: 'Not many times has it been spoken to you in toil' (Job 4:4), which indicates that: you yourself also many times used words toward those fallen into tribulations, so that we might hear actively what has happened to you. It can also be said passively, so that the saying might be: 'Having now first been in toils, did you have the one speaking to you the things of consolation?' instead of not receiving. For Job was not only then in distress. For it is likely that he was among the afflicted for a greater period of time.

Furthermore, regarding the things said to Job, he brings forward the thought differently, as if having heard his words from one who is brief, saying: 'But who will estimate the strength of words?' (Job 6:30). He himself brought consolation to many, but no one is able to bear your words, which are filled with brevity. And he was saying these things, not knowing the magnitude of the things spoken by him.

And he accepts a comparison from him, saying: 'For if you have encouraged many' (Job 6:30), and the following, indicating that: what you provided to others for exhortation, you are not reminding those placed by sorrow in a way of a warrior—'you were diligent'—instead of being troubled; and doing many things for help and consolation to those being afflicted, as if stretching out a right hand to them, according to that said in Isaiah to the leaders: 'Call upon the hand' (Isaiah 58:9), the words signify sympathy and compassion. 'And to those whose knees are failing, you have provided courage,' providing strength to men persuaded by weakness through the diligence toward them.
translator_notes: True OET; Pass A ≠ Pass B. Melito skipped; never Cyril Matthew densify.

title: The Misunderstanding of Job's Friends
english: Regarding the lifting up, those with paralyzed knees are 'those bowing to Baal' (Job 1:5), proclaiming another god, the one serving through sin. 'Now trouble has come upon you and has struck you' (Job 4:7), signifying a severe onset of the situation.

Following what was said there, one should understand that a more severe tribulation than the situation existed: an onslaught brought on by friends through their words. For since the comforter was not [present], the matter was even more terrible, and the words being heavy, they provided no small amount of discouragement.

'Is not your fear in folly, and your hope and the wickedness of your way?' (Job 4:7-8). The inspired Spirit testified to Job that he did not give folly to God, but this [accuser] having a different impression concerning what had happened to him and calculating that he suffers because of sins, thinking that he had spoken in a moment what he uttered, says: 'Is not your fear in folly'—thinking himself righteous—'and your hope and the wickedness of your way' (Job 4:8). For folly, he says, is also the hoping that one will appear righteous. For such things are not brought upon the righteous. And this very way is called a way of wickedness, because Eliphaz thought throughout that the blessed one suffers because of sin. Thus he also attributed folly to him.

'Remember then, who being pure perished, or where have the true whole-rooted ones perished? In the manner in which I saw those plowing the uneven ground, but those sowing them shall reap thorns for themselves. They shall perish by the command of the Lord, and shall be destroyed by the spirit of His wrath' (Job 18:5-7; 27:18). Still holding the same mindset, that Job has received experience of the circumstances through sin, he says these things to him, thinking that no human being, being pure in life, fell into tribulations and 'perished whole-rooted' (Job 18:5), alluding to the loss of children and goods and possessions. For this 'perished' means this to him.

He compares the wicked ones, these, and assuming that they fall into injuries—saying something true like 'those sowing injustice reap thorns' (Job 4:8)—he is seen to propose retribution, which he says is sent from God, and regarding this, being rightly disposed, he says: 'They shall perish by the command of the Lord, and shall be destroyed by the spirit of His wrath' (Job 27:18). Something similar is said by the blessed Paul: 'Who will render to each...'

Regarding his works: 'the strength of a lion, the voice of a lioness, and the roaring of dragons was extinguished. The ant-lion perished because it had no food, and the cubs of lions left one another' (Job 28:7-8). 'If any true word has happened in your words, none of these evils would have encountered you' (Job 22:28).

Even if Job's friends, of whom he was one, were pierced [by error] because they were divided regarding him as one having fallen into afflictions through sins, they nevertheless possess human understanding, which is not impenetrable. Therefore, we do not yield to them in their words, even those spoken from understanding, because they remained divided, as if they were unable to grasp the whole truth concerning the mind and the end revealed from now on; 'for if,' he says, 'any true word has happened in your words, none of these evils would have encountered you' (Job 22:28), which, as we said, was not spoken naturally or coherently by him.

For he thought this alone to be the cause of afflictions, saying it is through sin. But he does not coherently explain the changes concerning men: 'the strength of a lion, the voice of a lioness, and the roaring of dragons was extinguished.' For he says he sees these as a figure of speech, having suffered a change of many who are arrogant and think greatly of human things, such as Nebuchadnezzar, who came from kingship to the lowest private person.

But also what was said to the rich man: 'I will pull down my barns and build greater ones'—'Fool, this very night they take your soul from you' (Luke 12:20)—this is a demonstration of that mindset. 'Lion,' indeed, is how he has been seized by boldness, and 'pride' as if 'having trusted in himself.' Which the blessed Paul also understands concerning Nero, saying: 'In my first defense no one stood by me, but the Lord stood by me and rescued me from the mouth of a lion' (2 Timothy 4:17).

But also Jeremiah, saying: 'A wandering sheep Israel, lions have driven him away' (Jeremiah 50:6), explains further who the lions are, saying: 'The first devoured him, the king of Assyria' (Jeremiah 49:3), and the following. But also: 'God crushed the millstones of the lions' signifies the defeat of arrogant and bold men. And the 'lioness' is accepted instead of a profligate manner, which has such a nature. For when she needs food, she does not cry out, lest the beasts who owe food to her should flee.
translator_notes: True OET; Pass A ≠ Pass B. Melito skipped; never Cyril Matthew densify.

title: The Terror of Divine Judgment
english: Whether it becomes. But even if the male is of this nature, but from the dominant one and towards his royal and arrogant one he remembered. And he has made a memory of the 'dragons', alluding to serpent-like men, as they themselves are subject to change and concerning them change is happening. But these are deceitful and working deception, according to that which is said: 'But I fear lest, as the serpent deceived Eve through his craftiness, he corrupt your minds' (2 Cor 11:3). And he seems like a 'myrmecoleon' to a boasting and forward man, who because of the unstable and unweighed thing falls down. It is said that this is born from a lion with an ant having come together, not by the life-giving nature, but by another, which indeed has the size of a lion, and so it is called. And the historians say that because the father is flesh-eating and because the mother is poison-producing, he perishes, being unable because of the birth from both to use a single food. As to how it is, let the one encountering it judge.

And those receiving this devil are likely saying, that to the saints the ant is [present] through weakness, but to those sinning the lion, because he 'has given him a place'. 'And the packs of lions left one another', which he said alluding to the lawless and wild men. For indeed the packs, until they are under the mother, are together, but when they become men, they tear one another apart. So also the crafty and wild man, until he has some benefit—I say human—from the one accompanying him, he hides his malice, but having been filled with the one striving, he cares little for the benefactor.

And it is necessary to understand the 'true' 'word' that proceeds from intention as being without falsehood; for there is also a word in the soul. And this must be said, that it is not fitting to regard the weighty or worthy of understanding words of every person in the Scripture. For in the Gospels, indeed the foolishness of the Jews, but even Nicodemus used words not wisely; for when the Savior said, 'It is necessary for you to be born from above' (Luke 3:23), he said, 'Can not a man, being an old man, be born or enter a second time into the womb of a mother?' (John 3:4). Thus it is not necessary to always require understanding from every person in the Scripture. 'Whether he will not receive my ear's outcry from him...

But with fear and a nocturnal sound, a fear fell upon men; and a shudder met me, and trembling, and it greatly shook my bones, and a spirit came upon my face, and my hairs and flesh shuddered. I stood up and did not recognize it; I saw, and there was no form before my eyes, but rather a wind, and I heard a voice (Job 4:12-14).

Since he used words more abundantly, the first things are to be thought of as exhortatory, then as cleansing, as Job having hurried because of the things that happened to him and because he suffered through sin—for this Eliphaz posited from the beginning—and in addition, that human matters, even if they are prosperous, receive much change. Considering that it is possible the listener might not pay attention to what is said by him, for the sake of a confirmation, he brings forward the things set forth, saying: 'Whether my ear will be opened by him?' saying only this: let no one of those listening think that I am found to be unwise. For my ear of understanding receives wonders from him, him speaking of God. For this is significant of authority, as in: 'He himself speaking, I am present,' and in: 'He himself was wise against them, and his law shall by no means be set aside,' making it clear that it is of God. For indeed, if human understanding is imposed upon that which is from God, it is filled with fear according to the saying: 'I understood your works and was terrified' (Psalm 119:46). And to the same thing, 'sound' is followed by 'nocturnal,' which is much ambiguity, from which it happens to shudder and be afraid for one who has begun to perceive something of God's judgments. Not only that, but also 'the bones' of such a thing are disturbed, which is the power of the soul. For every human reasoning fails before the precise understanding of divine things. This is the same thing Habakkuk, having perceived, says: 'From the voice of prayer, trembling entered into my bones' (Habakkuk 3:16). Therefore, when one, desiring to ascend according to the intellectual faculty, encounters the fearsome divine works as previously stated, there comes a certain type of non-precise understanding, which is indicated by: 'and a spirit came upon my face.' Next also is: 'and my hairs and flesh shuddered.' For a man does not endure a great disturbance if he should dare to impose himself upon the judgment and wonders of God. 'I stood up, and there was no form before my eyes,' so that it may be as the saying goes.
translator_notes: True OET; Pass A ≠ Pass B. Melito skipped; never Cyril Matthew densify.

title: The Imperfection of Human Righteousness
english: For if a man wishes to rouse himself toward comprehension, the precision of the spoken word flees from him. This is similar to the saying: 'A deep depth, who will find it?' 'But I heard a wind and a voice.' For one using understanding receives certain wonderful things and echoes of the administration from God.

And he cannot grasp it entirely, and most certainly not; for if Paul, speaking in Christ, says: 'O the depth of the riches and the wisdom and the knowledge of God! How unsearchable are his judgments and untraceable his ways' (Rom 11:33), how much more will the one imposing human reasonings be at a loss toward comprehension? 'For what? Will a mortal be clean before the Lord or blameless because of his works?' (Job 4:7). We assume they have human understanding, and in those who preceded Job's friends. For it is not a small sign of understanding to leave lands behind, being kings, and to come because of sympathy for Job, even while they say as if they have not departed from sins.

However, though they use human reasonings, they are indeed certain. For as has been said before, setting one cause for the inductions, they think that Job also suffered because of sin, proceeding to this from a plausible word, understanding the weak nature of human intellect. Therefore also Eliphaz says regarding the things before him: 'For what? Will a mortal be clean before the Lord or blameless because of his works?' (Job 4:7). This, indeed, would be plausible if he were examining according to his own concept, and it holds the rebuke. For if the one falling into bitter afflictions is so because of sin, no one has been clean, no one has existed apart from bitter things.

But these things this man says, while divine discipline teaches, how even wicked men, being in all things in sins, led their lives without restraint. Of whom the rich man who with Lazarus was rejoicing every day, clothing himself brilliantly in fine linen and purple, remained in most pleasant living until his last breath, while the righteous Lazarus was testified to not having had rest there. But also the one who heard: 'Fool, this night they take the soul from you. But what you have prepared, to whom will it be?' (Luke 16:20) is written to have not been left without sharing. And this the divine word teaches, even if he also said this humanly, that

A pure person is not entirely contrary to the Lord. This is shown by the saying, 'his stars are not pure before Him' (Job 9:3), and by the Psalms: 'No living thing shall be justified before You' (Ps 143:4). For he did not say, 'no one is justified,' but rather, 'before You.' For you will find that all are lacking when they are toward God, and they do not possess [righteousness] in excess.

For Moses, even though he says he is 'instructed in all the wisdom of the Egyptians,' says: 'I am not able to speak before the yesterday and before the third and from when You began to speak to your servant' (Ex 4:10). For in the presence of the [divine] weight, he seems to be lesser. Or he says something else: 'But I am another kind of man.' But even Abraham, the 'friend of God,' having been humbled, says: 'Since I have begun to speak to my Lord, I am dust and ashes' (Gen 18:27). He does not utterly dishonor himself, but [speaks thus] from when he began to speak to God.

And 'mortal' and 'man,' if said by Eliphaz from a parallel [passage], we, applying a more precise word to the discourse, say that 'mortal' is such as is subject to a woman. For 'man' is not said of every human. 'If he does not believe according to his children, but regarding his angels he thought somewhat crookedly, he struck those dwelling in clay houses, from which we ourselves are from the same clay, in the manner of chaff. And from morning until evening they are no longer.'

He wants to lead the proof from the greater thing and make it certain that every man is under sin, saying that even the children of God are not believed by Him, which is to say: they are not as if they were unshakeable. 'But regarding his angels he thought somewhat crookedly' [of] those having sinned. And if this [is so], much more according to those dwelling in clay houses. Since they have happened to be from the same clay, He will not spare those sinning, sending the punishments to them in the manner of chaff, who also will not endure His judgment many times from morning until evening.

But indeed this is the most complete understanding of the things said; for if anyone were to seek whence this man has this impression concerning the departed angels, through whom he says God thought somewhat crookedly, it would be said to this: that while being a sensible man, he knew that the angels are not naturally good, but are liable to change. And it is not incongruous for him even from the demonized...
translator_notes: True OET; Pass A ≠ Pass B. Melito skipped; never Cyril Matthew densify.

title: The Nature of Divine Providential Correction
english: To understand this concerning men, about whom the divine teaching says: 'And he has kept those angels who did not observe their own rank in darkness.' And he says that men dwell in houses of clay instead of the material things, saying more simply that men were composed of the same clay. For not even the soul is of clay; for the body has been said to be clay.

'He struck them in the manner of a threshing floor.' This indicates the punishments sent against them as being insignificant. This is shown in Wisdom 11. But also the prophet says: 'The ruler asks, and the judge spoke peaceful words; it is the incense of his soul. And I will bring out their good things like a grain being threshed and walking according to a rule in a day of scrutiny' (Job 36:1-3), which is indicated by the continuous and sudden nature of the punishments and that which is sifted. For this indicates a rule. For if not 'he brings wrath day by day,' but 'he gives to each according to his works,' he makes this a rule instead of mixing it with goodness.

'Because they were not able to help themselves, they perished. For he breathed into them and they were dried up; they perished because they did not have wisdom.' Holding to the same principle, according to which she thinks that events happen through sin, and she says these things also. Since they were not able to help themselves through virtue after recognizing the evils, the afflictions followed them. And this she places under understanding: being unable to repel the severity of what came upon them through weakness, they perished, demonstrating the insignificance of human power.

This indeed and what follows seems to signify: 'For he breathed into them and they were dried up.' For it indicates that an overwhelming onslaught was not necessary against them, but only the breathing, which sufficed for their destruction, which he called loss. And from the same failing intellect follows: 'They perished because they did not have wisdom,' unaware that many wise men are afflicted...

They cast about. 'And call out, if anyone will obey you, or if you see any of the holy angels.' It seems as if he is providing an exhortation leading the holy one toward repentance, so that having come for the purpose of entreaty, he might happen to find one who assists and listens. And he also presents the phrase, 'or if you see any of the holy angels,' as being aware that they are not holy angels. For if he did not know this, the addition would be superfluous; it is as if he is distinguishing a holy [one] from a non-such. But those who say [he is mocking] claim that he says this ironically.

Regarding the beginning, he speaks again of the error, saying that through sin [10-15] so that he may know [15-20], 'for anger refutes the fool, and jealousy strikes the fallen one to death' (Proverbs 24:22). Thus it is to be read. [The text is heavily corrupted/gapped here] such as those who are displeasing to the providence of God. Why then do I myself fall into such calamities [8-12] and [lose] honor [6-10] according to what is said: 'Do not rejoice when your enemies rejoice, nor let your heart be glad when they stumble' (Proverbs 24:17), or 'jealousy [of] those who do lawlessness' (Proverbs 27:4). Jealousy is like it. And a second retribution [2-6] is [added] to the first [5-10], even if in irony. The phrase 'And call out, if anyone will obey you' will seem to have been spoken naturally, as if no one obeyed. [The text is gapped] as has been said.

'But I have seen fools casting seed, but immediately their harvest was ruined.' [The text is gapped] the mind under the roots... [the text is heavily corrupted/gapped here]... a many-rooted [thing] holds... and he speaks of human [things] happening, for immediately their harvest was ruined. To a great extent... [the text is gapped]... and the rich to be changed into poverty many times. But [it is not] to be praised for what is surrounding [it], but rather for the... [the text is gapped]... of this living... the [nature] of such arrogance, for the divine letter [is]...
translator_notes: True OET; Pass A ≠ Pass B. Melito skipped; never Cyril Matthew densify.

title: The Transfer of Wealth and the Inevitability of Suffering
english: He presents the thought in the Psalms, as it is said: 'I saw the impious one being exalted and puffed up like the cedars of Lebanon; and they passed by and behold, he was not, and I sought him and the place of him was not found' (Ps 73:9). For evil, not subsisting... I say, is unless in the choice of the one acting. If indeed that choice, being made, ceases, evil no longer has its composition; therefore his existence is in his choosing.

'Crush the arm of the sinner and the wicked, his sin shall be sought; and it shall not be found through itself' (Job 5:8). For because it is unsubstantial, it is not found; for evil is not an essence, but has being having been produced in choice. Again, when the wandering and the evil cease.

But concerning evil in general it has been said: 'And injustice lied about itself.' Just as we often say that the earth and its inhabitants and the good are being deceived by poverty, so also evil is said to lie about itself, no longer being [present], when 'all pain, distress, and sighing flees away' (Ps 102:3). And the diet of the punishment being carried out is made thin.

'Would their children be far from salvation. But they were punished at the doors of Hyssop and there shall be no one being taken out' (Ps 106:10). He prays that some discipline may come to the boastful, so that pleasant and human good things may turn away from them, which he called 'salvation'; for such a labor will happen to them. He says, 'they were punished,' meaning they were treated with contempt, being humbled by lesser ones, with no one being a helper.

For humiliation is profitable to the proud, first, so that through such a thing an immoderate evil may be generated, and second, so that they may be disciplined again. And 'they were punished' is derived from 'kolos', which is 'kolobos'; for a small pig is called 'kolobron'. 'For what those gathered, the righteous shall be given' (Matt 13:43). Even if saying this humanly, he would provide a good account, claiming that just as the impious gather, the righteous eat, unless something paradoxical seems to be happening; for not at all is it found to be so. And in the Divine Proverbs it is said: 'Wealth of the impious is stored up for the righteous' (Prov 13:22), which...

Yet we do not necessarily accept this for the sake of history. Since it has been said proverbially, it follows that the Jews are said to be rich, having both law and prophet, though they did not use them properly. This wealth was transferred to the nations. For the vine 'shall be removed' and 'shall be given to a nation that produces its fruits' (Matt 21:43). 'And they themselves shall not be set apart from evils; their strength shall be siphoned off.' He says that not only do the ungodly grasp at wealth, but they shall never be set apart from evils. And their power itself shall be completely emptied, from the transfer of that which is being siphoned until nothing even liquid remains; consider these things, if he speaks them in a proverbial way.

Know, however, that these things will not necessarily happen to the wicked; for many have received the end of this life in clarity of mind. If, moreover, he speaks these things having an apprehension of the coming age and of punishment, consider this also. But what the holy man says regarding those who prosper unjustly, advising the one who pays attention: 'Do not fear when a man prospers, for he will not take all things with him in dying, nor will the glory of his wealth grasp him.' Throughout his whole word, he speaks of these heavy evils: poverty, sickness, infamy, and dishonor.

'For toil shall not come forth from the earth, nor shall labor spring up from the mountains, but man is born of toil, and young vultures fly the heights' (Job 5:7; 38:7). The curses which he brought upon the ungodly, or which he wished to show must fall upon them, he says he did reasonably; for it is the lot of men to fall into tribulations and not to be without suffering (Job 5:7). And the word may also be exhortatory, as it is the custom to say to the many: 'You have not suffered anything outside of human nature; for indeed we have life in toil.' And the very being born of us happens in toil and ill-suffering, among the myriads of those existing and those being born in hardship.

If you are able to interject the word concerning the one born blind into this, consider it. For concerning him, 'the disciples of Jesus asked him: Did this man sin or his parents, that he was born blind?' (John 9:2). 'But young vultures fly the heights' is similar to saying that a person without soul does not fly in evil. And young vultures, he says, in the heights...
translator_notes: True OET; Pass A ≠ Pass B. Melito skipped; never Cyril Matthew densify.

title: Divine Providence and the Reversal of Fortune
english: They fly, instead of saying: they are unceasing—for he does not live in wickedness—so that what he says is such a thing: the soulless and the irrational—for it seems to signify the irrational through the young ones of the vultures—he does not accept a trial of retribution, a man wandering away because of such sins, which he says, following his own principle. 'Not indeed, but I will pray to the Lord, and I will call upon the Lord, the Master of all' (Job 1:21). Having accused the foolish and having said the following about them, he says, 'I do not rejoice as they do, but as one perceiving providence and knowing the Master of all, the God, I call upon Him, considering this to be proper.' Understand, then, that he does not have these whims as if he were wishing to send these things out against a righteous man himself.

'The one doing great and unsearchable things, glorious and wonderful, of which there is no number. The one giving rain upon the earth, sending water upon the heaven below' (Job 9:10). He confesses God to be a provider of all things and a creator. And he does not have these whims as a wise man regarding human things. He also has a whim concerning the invisible and the visible, saying concerning the unsearchable and the great and the glorious, of rain and of water, which if he distinguishes water from the rain, would be the things from springs and snowdrifts and rivers. And you also have these concepts most intelligently in many of the Scriptures, and not least even in Paul writing: 'In Christ were created the visible and the invisible, the earthly and the heavenly' (Colossians 1:16).

And this also must be considered, that from what happened to the holy Job, as a man having been led into fear, he marvels at the works of providence. And the 'there is no number' must be understood as [referring to] a man; for God knows all things. And it is not even wonderful where Solomon also says: 'God has given me the knowledge of things that exist, to know the true constitution of the world and the energy of the elements, the beginning and the middle and the end of time, the changes of the seasons' (1 Kings 3:9) and the following. For even things that are not countable by nature are uncountable to God, concerning which it is said: 'the multitude of the number of stars' (Psalm 147:4), and: 'but even the hairs of your head are all numbered' (Matthew 10:30), which is also given to the worthy to know for the sake of what is profitable, as it was said concerning Solomon: 'the one making the lowly into height and raising up the lost ones' (1 Samuel 2:8).

He ascends also to the providence according to men, and this, while remaining in discussion concerning God of all things, is that He Himself from on high makes the poor rich from the needy, from the submissive makes rulers, from the sick makes rulers healthy, and also the reverse. It is evident that these things, both being actually so and being seen and understood, exist for benefit, according to that which was said by the Holy [Spirit]: 'The Lord establishes kings and removes them' (Psalm 75:10), and 'Through me kings reign' (Psalm 74:10), and 'He raises the poor from the dust and lifts the needy from the ash heap' (Psalm 113:7).

And the precursor of the exaltation from God is our lowliness: 'For whoever humbles himself will be exalted, and whoever exalts himself will be humbled' (Luke 14:11), and again: 'God opposes the proud, but gives grace to the humble' (James 4:6). And regarding 'those having perished' to be 'raised up,' he speaks of those standing in crises and having been tested by change, the afflictions ceasing and the things of rest opposing them, which also happened to the blessed Job, remaining steadfast in the visible works of the soul. But if you take 'the one having perished' instead of 'the one having sinned,' then God 'raises these up' as a 'place of repentance' by providing teaching. But the blessed Job did not suffer such a loss, so that he might need such a resurrection. 'They devise many schemes, and their hands shall not do what is true' (Job 5:13).

Through all things concerning God, according to the way possible for himself, he explains with human understandings, moving not unfeasibly in many matters. Having explained concerning the providence of God and that through it dishonors and honors come about, and that certain humble things do not happen without Him, he moves to show that even if men use a great variety of wisdom, it is God's to provide the end. For indeed, 'the devising of many schemes' signifies to him that even if they should counsel and think themselves clever men, God erases these things, doing toward the benefit of each one. Often many men, having hoped, did not a little fail, and they received what was not expected, God governing, not man managing. Nor do such people have anything true in their own actions, those who, casting themselves upon themselves, thought to be self-sufficient in all things through their own counsels. And it is necessary...
translator_notes: True OET; Pass A ≠ Pass B. Melito skipped; never Cyril Matthew densify.

title: Spiritual Blindness and Symbolic Afflictions
english: To know that in the divine scripture the name of cunning is placed not only in a reproachful sense but also in a praiseworthy one. For when it is said regarding wisdom, 'that I might give cunning to the guileless' (Ps 55:23), it is clear, as it speaks of prudence and a praiseworthy deed; for such a thing is given by wisdom. And again: 'the cunning one was averted from coming evils' (Jon 3:4), which indicates a sensible action, which is accomplished toward him in the manner of repentance when the onset of evils is proven, as the Ninevites did, fleeing the threat; for the wrath is dispersed by this repentance. That cunning is also placed reproachfully is shown in: 'I fear lest, as the serpent deceived Eve in his cunning, your thoughts might be made frivolous' (2 Cor 11:3). And we have the 'hands' signifying actions in the scripture, as this one also seems to have understood. For when it says: 'thorns grow in the hand of the drinker' (Prov 26:5), we do not take the part of the body to mean—for thorns do not grow upon that—but rather the actions, according to which one sins. Therefore, 'their hands shall not do' is true, since God is not willing to fulfill the outcomes of their counsels. 'He who seizes the wise in their prudence, and turns aside the counsel of the many-scheming' (Ps 58:12). That is, he seizes the devices of the wise by his own prudence, or by the prudence of those who shared from him, as Elisha seized the sophistry of Gehazi, whom he caught scheming, saying: 'Your servant has not gone right or left' (2 Kings 6:17). To whom, having understood his movement, he said: 'Was not my heart with you?' (1 Kings 20:42). He also turns aside the counsel of the many-scheming ones, like that of Ahithophel, having prayed the blessed David and saying: 'Turn away the counsel of Ahithophel' (2 Sam 15:31). Not only this, but he also turned aside the counsel of the 'lawless elders' and of Egypt, who had deliberated against prudence, thus as regarding Susanna, because of their many-scheming, saying: 'Squeeze me from every side,' and Joseph, in his youth, with prudence and movement, escaping the devices of the lawless woman of Egypt. 'Darkness shall meet them by day, and the noonday, having felt it, shall be like night; and they shall perish in war' (Dan 2:22). He says that as many as attempt beyond their own power as they think...

What they grasp without the inspiration of God, they find nothing, being overtaken by darkness and groping as if they were handling things in the night, being unable at all to perceive anything with precision. For just as a film lying over the eyes prevents the power of sight, so a passion of this kind acts upon the mind, causing it to fail to see even in bright and manifest things. Furthermore, their being stretched out signifies that ignorance is occurring, for they fail to see even at midday.

You might say that even one who believes in the evangelical message might still be called out in sins, being unable to see despite the presence of a great light; for in what he believes, light appears to him, but in what he does not use toward what is necessary with that light, he is blinded. This happened symbolically to the Egyptians; for they spent three whole days and three nights in darkness. And that they suffered this because of their own cause, it was not simply that the day was obscure to all, but to them alone, while the Israelites suffered nothing of the sort.

But also the men according to Sodom, being struck with invisibility, were shown through the senses symbolically to be being blinded according to their intellect. And those in the Kingdoms who were struck with invisibility [text corrupted: ῃαξατ ῃαξατ ῃαξατ ῃαξατ]. You do not say this without necessity, and you say that those who fall according to the truth through sophistical and plausible words fall into days of darkness and midday as if in night; but if the one standing for the truth exposes the thinness of their plausibility through proofs, they seem like the blind and the senseless, whom they are unable to withstand. They are also destroyed in the war, the struggle for the truth.

The symbols of these are the Egyptians, being led by Pharaoh and defeated by the Israelites by the help of God, and Goliath by David, and all those who were defeated by the servants of God according to the sensible. For these bring forth a sign that even the enemies of the wise according to the intellect are unable to stand against the truth advocated by them. But even more clearly is the example according to Moses, when he waged war against the Amalekites. For whenever the hands were lowered, a change occurred in the coming victory when they happened to be stretched upward toward God. From which it is shown, as the one with the high wisdom of the truth...
translator_notes: True OET; Pass A ≠ Pass B. Melito skipped; never Cyril Matthew densify.

title: Divine deliverance of the weak
english: Being unhindered and undefeated, he suffers 'false knowledge.' But he who turns downward toward the earth is blinded, and having been killed by ignorance, his intellect remains more inferior and more difficult.

'But the powerless one comes out from the hand of the powerful.' These things might be clearly indicated according to the form of the words, so that what is said might be: may the weak chance to find help, as if escaping the hands of the powerful. It is also possible to carry it forth from the narrative, so that it is thus: 'He who does great and unsearchable things, both glorious and wondrous, of which there is no number, he who gives rain upon the earth, who sends water upon those under heaven, who lifts up the lowly, who raises up those stumbling,' (Job 5:9) as it has been said, and the following. This one rescues all, even the powerless, from the hand of the powerful.

We have this in the Kings (1 Samuel 24), for Saul pursued David so fiercely that he had to hide in a cave, in which Saul was delighted. And what is the paradox? For being surrounded by enemies, he was saved by divine power, as if the enemy were given into his hand, even though by the virtue of non-retaliation (1 Samuel 24:10) he surpassed the slaughter against the opponent, not only by not striking down but also by teaching him to turn away from hardship. For having cut off 'the lobe of the ear' (1 Samuel 24:10) of him, he showed him that he was able even to cut off the head. Therefore, he instructs both: the care of God regarding his own servants, and his own non-retaliation, for which he calls upon the enemy to imitate him, teaching him that God rescues the powerless from the powerful and the oppressors.

'May there be hope for the powerless, and may the mouth of the unrighteous be stopped.' And the wording accords with the argument of Providence. If one is powerless, lacking in strength, let him not reject himself, let not every expectation be turned away; for hope is for the powerless. And the mouth of the unrighteous is also stopped when they swell with arrogance.
I will provide for the strength of the nations
translator_notes: True OET; Pass A ≠ Pass B. Melito skipped; never Cyril Matthew densify.

title: The Purpose of Suffering and Divine Providence
english: The sins are made manifest through the word, concerning heavenly things and not appearing through the senses. But hope, existing for those who are unable, is a reproof against the Novatians, who exclude repentance and cut off hopes. They ought to have been instructed even by Eliphaz, the one being rebuked, for there is hope of salvation with them.

'Let the mouth of the unrighteous be stopped' (Proverbs 10:14)—as it is said, 'all unrighteousness shall stop her mouth' (Proverbs 10:14), which is said instead of the unrighteous man. For often... If, indeed, Paul writes concerning love, the words are applied not to love itself but to the one possessing it. For he says, 'love does not wander, it is not puffed up' (1 Cor 13:5), and these things are spoken precisely concerning the one possessing it: 'love never fails' (1 Cor 13:8). Virtue does not fail, but the one possessing it.

Therefore, 'let the mouth of the unrighteous be stopped by unrighteousness,' that is, the unrighteous man, who is the devil, no longer having anything to say, just as Paul writes, saying, 'so that the one against you may be put to shame, having nothing to say concerning you' (1 Cor 16:11) instead of 'against us.' 'Blessed is the man whom the Lord reproves, and the instruction of the Almighty shall not offend' (Psalm 94:12). For He causes pain and again restores; He chastened, and His hands healed (Job 5:18). This is the most difficult thing in its delivery.

For it is said, 'and I will not visit their daughters when they whore, nor their virgins when they commit adultery' (Hosea 2:15). And observe that regarding the daughters, to whore is said, but regarding the virgins, to commit adultery. But also that which is said in Proverbs, 'Whom the Lord loves He disciplines, and scourges every son whom He receives' (Proverbs 3:12), subjects the mind to the same. And one of the saints, having this readiness and speaking boldly, offering words of repentance to God, said, 'I am ready for the lashes'; for I know that it happens profitably from You, just as one says to a wise physician, 'I am even ready for the incision, being confident in your skill.'

Therefore, still following the same principle, Job speaks in a certain way, as if toward a rebuke of a man (Job 16), as a type. For 'he causes pain and again restores' (Job 34:4). And regarding [the words], they are authoritative concerning God. Moses himself says from the beginning: 'I kill and I will make live, I strike and I myself will heal' (Deut 32:39).

For it is not according to the Manichaeans that one causes pain and another heals; for there is one who is being afflicted, who has permitted the induction of evils for the purpose of leading through providence, the demons driving [them]; for they... are able... they lead the things of affliction toward health: 'six times out of necessity you shall be delivered, but in the seventh no evil shall touch you' (Job 36:15). If one were to stand upon what is said and consider, as Eliphaz is not of the holy ones, how such words are spoken by him, which might even be spoken to holy ones.

It must be said toward this, that the wise according to God, and before the law and the inscribed teaching, said many things unwritten with wisdom, which someone later handed down in written form by divine supply. It is therefore probable that even the friends of Job, having a well-ordered understanding, remembered the words arranged by the holy ones. This is that which leads them to bring forward sensible words, even if in some respects they erred.

What the laid out verses then suggest is this: to whatever extent someone possesses a world having come about in six days, the injustices and tribulations enduring in it. For even if someone is holy, he has the necessity of the need from the body, from which he is delivered, having surpassed the world and having come to a seventh rest. This is made clear from: 'pain and sorrow and sighing fled away' (Job 3:11).

And according to this thought, he did not refuse to take the literal sense. For affliction does not touch the one who has surpassed the world, since even one having a way of being not lover of silver and being unrighteous, loss does not touch him, as it is sensibly understood to touch, as we previously noted, more than the word signifies; for in 'touching all' it signifies the approach and the touch itself, but in 'he who touches you as one touches his eye' the striking and the impulse.
translator_notes: True OET; Pass A ≠ Pass B. Melito skipped; never Cyril Matthew densify.

title: The Nourishment of the Word and Lending
english: It also shows an intention, even if the wrongdoer does not act it out through himself. It might also be understood thus: he who is still progressing, as if hastening toward the end through works and deeds, would become a kind of violent one in six necessities; for 'violent ones seize the kingdom' (Matt 11:12). But when he reaches perfection, he will no longer request a lack of progress through pain and sweat, being forced by violence toward perfection.

This, therefore, is shown symbolically in the Patriarch: Jacob first being called so because of 'fluttering' through the passions, and later Israel because of his leisurely delay with the passions again. Jesus also said this to his own disciples: 'You are no longer of this world' (John 15:19), having leaped over him.

And if anyone objects, as if not submitting to a theory raised against what was said by Eliphaz, he would be just to give his opinion and say, if he thinks he does not have sense in this way: that until the sixth tribulation God allows a man to be afflicted, but does not allow him to be afflicted the seventh, having the experience that as many men have entered into many trials; for this is not unlike. 'In famine he will save you from death, and in war he will release you from the hand of iron' (Job 5:19).

If anyone were to say, as if it were not contrary to think that he who considers the sufferer to suffer through sin is not unjust, that even one being admonished by the Lord, after the admonition, immediately becomes worthy of such things as being saved from death in famine and released from iron by God, that there is no contradiction to this; for many diligent men died in famine, and not all those destroyed in war are wicked, the word having its irrefutability according to its progression. For that which is said in the Psalms: 'I became younger; for I grew old and had not seen the righteous forsaken, nor his seed seeking bread. All day long he shows mercy and lends' (Ps 37:25-26), is true and necessary to be taken according to understanding; for even a righteous man does not need those who feed, being a soul full of the 'life-giving spirit.' But also his seed, being brought forth according to the divine generation, will not be subject to this deficiency of food; for the one becoming a diligent imitator of Christ, according to Paul saying, 'become imitators of me, just as I...' (1 Cor 11:1).

One who walks in the commandments and judgments of God has the food of Christ. He also shows mercy and lends, not by lending what is forbidden—for how could he?—since his silver he did not give with interest, but rather provides instruction to children, from which progress and profit come to those hearing and to the teacher.

Regarding those who are knowledgeable, Jesus hastens to not have 'a bronze belt' (Matt 10:8) nor to have anything at all, as he says boldly: 'Silver and gold I do not have' (Luke 6:35). He says, 'Do not turn away from him who asks to borrow from you' (Luke 6:35), as previously stated. The foolish one, therefore, being lent to, does not cut off the connection. For hearing many words leading to instruction, he brings nothing to work.

But also this: 'You will lend to many nations,' said in precedence: 'but you shall not lend' (Exod 22:25), not having history—for how could it be possible to cross hostile nations to charge interest?—but it has also been said concerning the Israelites lending: 'You shall not charge interest to your brother' (Exod 22:25), and if you deposit it, 'before the setting of the sun you shall restore it' (Exod 22:25), which shows them being in need. It has the thought that one having the divine wealth must instruct all who approach him, not coming into the state of him who needs.

For the righteous were famished and in war endured many tribulations, it is evident to the reader in the royal histories, of the sons of the prophets famishing and of Lazarus, and David having been in many circumstances, showing that they had spiritual food according to what is said: 'Open your eyes and be filled with bread,' and being found outside of temptation according to thought, they did not consent to undergo death of the soul or the bond of sin, becoming outside the threat, by which it is said, 'not a famine of bread nor thirst of water, but of hearing the word of the Lord' (Amos 8:11), drinking from the water which Jesus provides of the righteous, which also 'becomes in them a spring of water leaping into eternal life' (John 4:14). 'He will hide you from the scourge of the tongue, and you will not fear the evils coming' (Ps 54:5). Concerning the one being admonished by the Lord and as if having repented, he says these things again, following his own principle, not being of this nor this being necessary, as he says. For the righteous were often reproached, of whom Joseph is the prudent one in Egypt...
translator_notes: True OET; Pass A ≠ Pass B. Melito skipped; never Cyril Matthew densify.

title: The endurance of the righteous against slander
english: Sosan also testifies to incorruptibility, she who endured the lashes of slander from the 'lawless elders'. If, indeed, one thinks that not being slandered or reviled means that the 'tongue is hidden from the lash', the word does not possess truth in this way; for the one living according to God cannot be separated from virtue by slander or reviling, nor can he be shown to be guilty by the so-called lash of the tongue, being hidden from the fault of those who speak.

The same person does not even receive the expectation of evils, according to the blessed Paul, saying: 'Who shall separate us from the love of God? Tribulation, or distress, or persecution, or famine, or nakedness, or the sword?' (Romans 8:35). For he overcomes these things by the possession of virtue. Nor will such a person be hidden from the sophisms of false wisdom, which 'unravels the purposes of the many-scheming God' (the purpose of God being unraveled) from those who use it.

Regarding the saying: 'and you shall not fear the coming of evils', the prophetic word is equally capable of saying: 'your tribulation will come from afar' and that which is understood thus: the good is within us. For it is said: 'the kingdom of heaven is within you' (Luke 17:21). For we have a natural inclination toward the virtue which he has called 'kingdom'. But the penalty and the evil come from without, as does the shame of sin.

For man, having become 'in the image' (Genesis 1:26) of God, has within himself the seeds of the good. If he is diverted by evil, he encounters it without having received from God the impulse for this. 'The unrighteous and lawless shall deride you; from wild beasts do not fear. For wild beasts shall make peace with you.' It is clear that he speaks these things concerning the righteous one who has come through admonition, to be derided by the unrighteous and lawless, indicating that: having escaped the plots against him by them, he derides those who have plotted much against him. But this could not happen to the righteous; for the earnest man is not a mocker, but rather sympathetic, saying more like Paul: 'Great and unceasing is the pain in my heart' (Romans 9:2), which he said regarding the righteous. If someone were to take this derision in the same way, that the earnest man is said to deride those who attempt vainly, it is to show they are worthy of laughter. And 'from wild beasts do not fear' and the following...
the lover of beauty
translator_notes: True OET; Pass A ≠ Pass B. Melito skipped; never Cyril Matthew densify.

title: The House of the Virtuous
english: "It shall be to you like the all-herb of the field." For he was not dividing [life] as one who is thus devastated and ageless produces offspring; for this one was devouring worms and slugs. And what did he say, "the lifestyle of a tent"—is he not complaining about not having a tent at all, but having thrown it away?

Therefore, since the history is being forced toward sensible things, the mind must be cleverly guided, especially since we thought those who went before were not unsuitable for the kind of teaching; for they do not seem trivial. For on account of ignorance, Job is urged to bring a sacrifice to God for their sins (Job 42:8), and indeed even friends (Job 42:8-12) of such greatness (Job 42:8-12) and virtue (Job 42:8-12) follow (Job 42:8-12); to know that... one cause of the inductions exists, they were struck.

It is therefore said that: of the "wild beasts," as it was given that they "would be at peace with you," and the "house" of your mind "will be at peace," and "the lifestyle of your tent," which is the improvement in your progress, "will not complain." And in addition to these, "you will know," that in your good thoughts a "seed" multiplies, resulting in the generation of children and becoming [real]. Like "the all-herb of the field" because of the spark of virtue and increasing even more.

And in truth, we have in the divine letters, and regarding the house of the saints, the state, the conduct, the virtue, just as it is written concerning the midwives of the Hebrews: "because the midwives feared God, they made houses for themselves" (Exodus 1:17), which shows the virtue constructed by them from the fear of God. For they were not without dwellings before this. And what is said in Proverbs: "the houses of the lawless shall owe cleansing, but the houses of the righteous are received" (Proverbs 15:25). For these things are not spoken concerning sensible things, but concerning the dispositions in the mind, requiring the cleansing of the trivial ones, while the excellent ones are found to be received, the received one showing not...
It is not something chosen by a person, but something worthy of praise; for the good is something chosen even if no one chooses it, and it is acceptable even if no one accepts it.

And regarding the saying about 'the one fearing the Lord and desiring his commandments exceedingly' (Ps 112:3): 'wealth and glory in his house' is not spoken concerning a sensible house or glory; for many fearing God do not have either human glory or a wealthy house, like Elijah, like Elisha and those similar. Of the 'one being rich in good works' and 'in every word and in all knowledge' (1 Tim 6:18), as Paul writes, [he is] having wealth and glory in the house of the intellect and being adorned through all virtues in his way of life.

Furthermore, the Gospel clarifies such a house; for it says: 'whoever hears my words and does them is like a prudent man, who built his house upon the rock, and the rain descended, the winds blew, the rivers came, and the house was not shaken' (Matt 7:24-25), which is the state of the virtuous person of having turned the words of the Lord into works, who remains without want, not being harmed by any of the opposing energies. For upon 'the rock' [he has] 'Christ,' the one of such a kind has established his state and his choice. For to the one confessing him, it was said by him: 'You are Peter, and upon this rock I will build my church' (Matt 16:18); but to the one hearing the words as they happen and not connecting deeds to the words, [he is] 'a foolish man resembling one who built his house upon the sand' (Matt 7:26), which is the state upon the fluid things of life, things not receiving firm foundations.

Therefore, this one being unstable, he has a quick fall after a short trial being sent, whether through teaching from another or through some circumstance being led by an evil spirit. He who has a stable standing of the praiseworthy house will, according to Moses, be heard toward God. 'But you...'
translator_notes: True OET; Pass A ≠ Pass B. Melito skipped; never Cyril Matthew densify.

title: Seed and Offspring
english: "Let him stand with me." And concerning him the Savior says: "There are some standing here who shall never taste death" (Ps 116:9). Thus also Job had a house, which the wise man, "having built," established firmly "upon the rock" (Matt 7:24). Having this, even the disciples of Christ held an immovable stance, observing the life-saving words.

And "the house" of the intellect brings peace, being unmixed and unyielding, working the peace of virtue because it follows them; for nothing is discordant in the important matter.
