Concerning the virtues, the proverbial thing is spoken aptly: "Wise women built a house, but the foolish one dug it down with her hands" (Prov 14:1). For wickedness works a distortion of the buildings quickly.

One virtue toward the building of a house is not sufficient. For this reason it is said in the plural: "Women built a house." But one wickedness is sufficient for distortion. For it is said: if anyone performs all the righteous acts, but performs one lawlessness, all his righteousnesses are set aside. For they no longer stand, nor do they remain, upon one [wrong] entering.

And his own virtue happens to be "not even to complain about the conduct of his tent" (Ps 119:10). For it is necessary for one progressing, which is shown through the tent, not to stumble nor to sin; for it is possible, even while one is still progressing, that the one dwelling in the house is already bringing peace through perfection, from the progressing of the one having borne fruit and singing: "I will pass through a place of tent-dwelling until the house of God" (Ps 119:154), in which the one having fallen short of having arrived at the perfection of virtue is slow-moving and most certain.

This is shown from: "Everyone born of God does not commit sin" (1 John 3:9). And assigning the cause, he asserts: "because his seed remains in him," saying that [it] made him. For concerning such a thing it is also said in the Gospel: "No one is able to snatch [them] out of the hand of my Father" (John 10:28). And we did not say that the virtuous one is unshakeable, but that he is difficult to shake.

But by himself he would become outside the hand of God by falling away; for "they themselves" say "they pushed [him] out from your hand" (Matt 26:56), clearly having become unworthy of being guarded by the hand of God, which Judas himself experienced, going out from the covering hand of God. For he has not said...

No one will come out, but 'no one is able to snatch [them] from the hand of my Father' (John 10:28). He himself will reject those who previously tore themselves away. For it is said: 'God will strike them down, because they did not listen to him' (Ps 67:4), the one who guards, knowing that his seed is very much. For the earth of the diligent mind is good, receiving the seeds from the Word of the Brideway [the Bridegroom] familiarly and eagerly, or he himself sows the disciples through the Word given to him.

And the seed is often called a child: 'the seed of Abraham'—his children—not necessarily being both seed and child already. Regarding the Jews who cry out that they are the seed of Abraham, the Savior did not say: 'You lie,' but led forward: 'If you are children of Abraham, do the works of Abraham (John 8:39); for not all these [are] from Israel, the [descendants] of Israel. Nor is it that they are the seed of Abraham always a child.' He therefore says to them as not being children of Abraham: 'Do the desires of your father.' But those doing the desires of the devil, accepting him as father, are not children of Abraham. Blessed is the one becoming the seed of Abraham according to having the virtues of godliness and becoming a child, through being formed and not becoming dull, but bringing forth.

And there is when both the seed and the child are said in parallel, as is also set forth in the present. The intellect of the holy, which must be understood, brings forth offspring corresponding to the 'increase of the field' and a multitude exceeding in vital power, so that this 'man of the kingdom of heaven' (Matt 13:47) might thus 'become like' according to the Gospel, sowing in the field of his own heart, so that he might bear fruit 'a hundred, sixty, thirty' (Matt 13:8) at first, middle, and last, 'sowing in tears' (Ps 126:5), so that 'he may reap in joy' (Ps 126:6) and 'seeking the Lord, so that he may bring to him fruits of righteousness.' 'He will be released in a tomb like grain ripe being harvested in season, or like wheat of a threshing floor being gathered according to the hour.' Nothing of the existing things is without a proper end, even if it is taken by art. Nature and art both have an end and a purpose; for a vine is grown for the reasonable enjoyment of man, and a house is built by a craftsman having a purpose to complete a house for habitation. And so that not...
translator_notes: True OET; Pass A ≠ Pass B. Melito skipped; never Cyril Matthew densify.

title: The End of the Patient Man
english: Much is said: man was created so that he might live according to virtue. The Psalmist, seeing this, said: 'Lord, make me known my end and the number of my days, who it is, so that I may know what I lack' (Psalm 39:4), so that he might say such a thing in peace: 'For this purpose I have become, so that I might live according to virtue and participate in all of your wisdom, and I speak and act according to it.'

Since I see myself lacking much, which he says through moderation, 'make known to me my end' (Psalm 39:4), how much time shall I remain here, so that I may strive in it, replenishing my deficiencies? According to this thought, it is also said in Ecclesiastes: 'Do not become hard, lest you die in your own time' (Eccl 12:5), which indicates that: since you have become for the sake of bearing fruit virtue, do not neglect it, lest you depart incomplete. Which again David, praying, says: 'Do not bring me up in the midst of my days' (Psalm 39:13).

But Abraham also was said to be 'old and full of days' (Gen 25:8). And if we take this more simply, many of the many before him lived more years and were neither older nor full of days. Full of days is he who, having received the illuminations of the 'sun of righteousness,' is honored among those elders, concerning whom it is said: 'For old age is honorable, not by length of time, nor is it measured by the number of years, but it is much wisdom to men, and old age is a life unblemished.'

Since, therefore, 'Abraham believed God' (Gen 15:6) so that 'his faith was counted for righteousness' and he was 'full of days' and 'old,' it is fitting that 'having been nourished in good old age' he fell asleep. For that fullness of days is thus understood and is confirmed from others: 'Honor,' he says, 'your father and your mother, so that it may go well with you and you may be long-lived upon the earth which the Lord gives to you' (Exod 20:12).

And this is not contradictory; for many, having shown much honor toward parents, died early, and others, dishonoring mother and father, have become long-lived. But also in the Psalms it is said concerning 'him who dwells in the help of the Most High': 'With length of days I will satisfy him and show him my salvation' (Psalm 91:16), which indicates completion; for not even the staying here for more...

For they say he was 'seized', 'not by wickedness but by his understanding'. All these things are said to us to show that all things happening occur toward a certain end, and by many, but even more so by God. And Eliphaz, knowing this, being both respectful and wise, moved by the things set before his mind, speaks in this way: that having received the admonition gently and toward a return, he shall have a good and precious end, which is shown to him through: 'he shall be released in the grave like grain being harvested in its season' (Job 5:17).

The word follows for him in sequence from: 'Blessed is the man whom the Lord reproves' (Job 5:17), when he is also exhorted not to 'displease the Almighty's correction' (Job 5:18), as he is 'striking and chastising, six times being rescued from the necessities of famine and war, from the whip of the tongue and from hiding behind iron', from which it will happen to this one, to whom these things happen, not to fear the onset of evils and the following things. Upon all of which, he says, he shall receive a good end in due time and season, like grain being gathered in a threshing floor.

And it is blessed to be such a one, concerning whom the Savior says: 'The good seed are sons of the kingdom' (Luke 8:15). And concerning this: 'If the grain of wheat does not fall into the earth and die, it remains alone; but if it dies, it bears more fruit' (John 12:24). And the fruit of this grain is not sensible offspring, but men, 'sons of the kingdom'. And great is also not to hear: 'I will uproot you and transplant you from the dwelling and your root out of the living earth' (Jeremiah 23:9), but rather to be fulfilled in virtues like the grain that is fulfilled and harvested and gathered in season.

And the season and the hour lie parallel, as in: 'Keep this law according to the hours and seasons from day to day'. But the perfection of the spiritual soul is unmeasured. For 'going', they 'were going and weeping, lifting up their seeds' (Psalm 126:5), which shows the beginning of virtue through their labors and exercises. 'But coming, they shall arrive in joy, lifting up their sheaves' (Psalm 126:6), which signifies, as previously stated, the perfection. For this is shown by 'having been gathered together'. For the end, in reality, is certain. We learn this well from the Savior saying: 'Whose [grain] falls in his hand and...'
translator_notes: True OET; Pass A ≠ Pass B. Melito skipped; never Cyril Matthew densify.

title: Job's Magnanimity and the Nature of His Suffering
english: He cleanses his threshing floor and gathers the grain into a granary, and burns the chaff with a lime-fire. It is clear that these things are not spoken concerning sensible things; for chaff is not burned with a lime-fire, nor does he seem to take up threshing concerning a sensible woman—for man is not a threshing-woman—but rather the perfection and fullness, as we have said.

We have, most wisely, in the Song of Songs, something said concerning the bride, who is the church or the perfected soul: 'Your navel is like a rounded vessel; the swelling of your womb is like a fenced threshing-floor of lilies' (Song of Songs 4:2). And that the soul does not have this commonly called 'belly,' concerning which it is said: 'food for the belly and the belly for food' (1 Corinthians 6:13), but rather that one concerning which it is written: 'your law in the midst of my belly' (Psalm 119:11), and: 'from the fear of you in the belly we have endured pain and have given birth' (Isaiah 42:14).

And this same soul also has a 'navel' which is the middle of the intellect, which has become, according to the 'wine having been strained by wisdom,' the divine thoughts and having ascended super-eminently. And since these things were not able to be thought by men, they were strained with human words, so that in this way they might reach the 'swelling,' to receive the hearing of the naked, those unable to [hear] the things of wisdom.

And it is possible to show the non-human through the vessel, but also to say to the [human]: that you have an old and new scripture, which is the vessel, in the middle of your ruling principle. And you also have a 'belly' resembling a threshing-floor, 'fenced in lilies.' For since through the color of the lily there is whiteness without, but within it resembles a deathly color, it would perhaps show that the perfected soul becomes white according to the word, concerning which it was said: 'my sister is white' (Song of Songs 6:4), being killed from the deathfulness of asceticism.

'Behold, these things we have searched out, these are the things we have heard. But you, know yourself if you have done anything' (Job 28:24). The aforementioned is confirmed, that being wise and perhaps having heard from old saints who taught divinely without writing, he was led to say someone having a reason, of which we also find similar things in the divine letters and set them aside. For through 'we have searched out' his wisdom is demonstrated, and through 'we have heard'...

Unless someone says that he speaks of instruction as if it were experience and knowledge of things, he follows the same beginning and remains [with the idea] that he has suffered through sin, and he brought forward: 'But know yourself if you have done anything,' so that he might also through this be making it manifest that: [gap] what I said concerning those committing sin; for I do not think it just to be punished. But I do not know the [details] of each of the sins.

'But know yourself,' which is to say: having known, repent, which is again remaining as if he were concerning a sin. For he thought one cause for the inductions. 'And having understood, Job says: If indeed anyone were to set my anger in a yoke, and to lift my pains in a yoke together, and indeed it would be heavier than a sandbank.' Just as from all the other things, so also from the things set forth, the magnanimity of Job is shown, bearing the circumstances bravely and very manfully. For many, when they come into circumstantial and distressing [situations], they consider those who exhort and [gap] blame them as superfluous. But this one has prepared himself even for an answer [gap] of the circumstances [gap].

Therefore, he would say the things set forth against the things spoken by Eliphaz: 'But now toil has come upon you and has touched you, and you have hurried' (Job 2:10), to demonstrate at the same time that these things are not happening because of sins, and [to show] moderation, supposing himself to be wavering even though the inspired spirit of the writer testifies to him that he might be 'blameless.' Therefore he says: if anyone would desire to set our trespasses and the provoked anger in a yoke, he would find it heavier than our trespasses. For the saint knew that these things were not happening because of sins but because of a struggle, where in the following he declared: 'I know that I shall appear righteous' (Job 27:6). Therefore he strove to lead his friends into such knowledge.

And if even the 'setting' signifies the cessation, he perceived it. And let it be understood thus: a yoke is said to be lying upon the neck of suffering animals. He might be saying: if anyone would be willing to pull with me the yoke of sufferings, so as to silence me from them through fellowship. But look, lest this be unworthy of the saint to lead us up to the first response. And he took sandbank aside because of the...
translator_notes: True OET; Pass A ≠ Pass B. Melito skipped; never Cyril Matthew densify.

title: The Necessity of Feeling Toil
english: my words are worthless

Regarding my own [experience], and Paul says 'even unto the third heaven' (2 Cor 12:2), 'whether caught up in the body I do not know or out of the body I do not know' (2 Cor 12:2). For when men do not grant a leisure that is brief regarding external things, then indeed their [reward] is not moderately sprinkled.

Therefore, by declining this, he in a way instructs also his friends to keep their mindset on things above and to care little for external things while idling in contemplation. Consequently, the power guarding the saints also gives them a little perception of toils, so that in this way the granting of the crown may be reasonable.

'For does a wild donkey cry out for nothing, but seeking grain? Or does an ox cry out on the threshing floor having the foods? Will bread be eaten without salt? Or is there taste in empty words? For my soul cannot cease. For I see my food as the scent of a lion' (Job 6:5-6).' Regarding the seizure made upon him by this, as if presenting questions regarding the words spoken by Job, he himself says as if bringing forward inquiries so that from which he may answer and no longer be blamed for the one crying out because of external things, even though Job said nothing of avoidance.

He asks: 'What then? Does a wild donkey cry out for nothing, but seeking grain?' (Job 6:5), which is: does a wild donkey not leave a cry in vain, lacking food? But neither does the ox cry out on the threshing floor where the foods are lying. So, do not blame me, if I cry out according to your assumption because of the painful things of a nature being weak, so that he might lead him toward sympathy so that he is not blamed for the one grieving if he cries out; for it is not necessary for the saint to be unfeeling, even if he bears the afflictions patiently. For this is virtue, when someone, receiving the perception of external things, surpasses the painful things through God.

And the following: 'Will bread be eaten without salt' (Job 6:6), having been inserted by the blessed [one], and for this reason, if it were to produce ambiguity, it might according to our ability be such a thing: the benefit of the soul and...
translator_notes: True OET; Pass A ≠ Pass B. Melito skipped; never Cyril Matthew densify.

title: The Courageous Soul and Divine Discipline
english: The nourishment of this thing exists not without toil and tribulation. Similar to this is the saying: 'through many tribulations it is necessary for us to enter into the kingdom of the heavens' (Acts 14:22), so that the bread might signify benefit, and the salt the toil, without which it is impossible for virtue to be perfected. From the same reasoning is also: 'and if there is indeed tasting in empty words?'. Every word lacking practical action is vain and empty.

A demonstration of this is: 'for the kingdom of God is not in word, but in power' (Luke 17:21). It exists not in empty promises, but in the word, the things of salvation are active. Therefore, do not think that I carry forward empty words, nor you, O friends, strive for that. For because of this, since I have done nothing empty and vain to myself, 'my soul cannot cease' from the toil against the adversary; for my aim is not empty, but having the hope of salvation.

For if my grains are filled because of the difficult eating of the wound, my soul will not cease. For nothing 'will separate us from the love of Christ: tribulation, or distress, or persecution, or famine' (Romans 8:35) and the following. Let all things shine in Paul. And if he wishes to signify that the standing up of the devil against him impedes his virtue, it is customary for his grains to exist through the wound, consider this.

'For if [he] might grant, and my request might come, and the Lord might grant my hope, let the Lord begin to wound me, but let him not lift me up to the end' (Job 6:3, 7:17-18). He who asks to be wounded by himself, not returning his request to come, but aiming to be fully satisfied in his own right, prays; and this was the end of the perfection: to lift up or even to appear to friends, for their benefit, the cause of the toils, that they were struck for the sake of the struggle.

For in this way they would not only not sin against the just, but also receive divine zeal, hastening to imitate the patience and courage being perfected in the holy one, through which also he was saying: 'if [he] might grant'—instead of: 'would that the Lord might grant'—'and my request might come, and the Lord might grant my hope'. For he prays for both, so that he himself might receive the crown of the contest and those who follow might not think their patience to be in vain. And it is possible to see and to marvel at him, even in the most extreme toils.

He is manly, because first he does not lack the initial response to a friend, treating the troubles as a leisure; and again, just as a brave athlete says, he stands militantly against the one set against him, knowing that his being brought low has happened not without the cooperation of God, saying: 'Let the Lord begin to wound me, but let him not raise me to the end,' instead of saying: 'May he grant the escape from tribulations.' Similar to this is: 'And let us not be brought into temptation' (Matt 6:13), which is often interpreted instead of: 'May it happen that one does not fall to the deceivers.'

See also the divine assurance: that the thing hoped for in prayer comes, not to everyone knowing if they pray profitably, or only to the saints. Living according to the will of God, they receive 'the assurance of hope' (Heb 11:1). And that he is not speaking concerning the life here, in saying: 'but let him not raise me to the end,' it is clear from his having said: 'Death to a man is rest.'

Being a perceiver, therefore, the saint accepts the wound from God, receiving Him as the best teacher, not as a tormentor, but as one seeking a testing, just as the Psalmist says: 'Test me, O Lord, and try me' (Ps 26:2), and the proverbial saying: 'He disciplines every son whom he receives.' This happens so that he may not become a tormentor by not being sympathetic to the discipline. For the saint, having surrendered himself entirely to God, does not waive reproof, 'knowing that tribulation works patience, and patience, testing, and testing, hope; and hope does not disappoint' (Rom 5:3-5).

'Let my city be a tomb, upon which I was leaping atop the walls, I will not show mercy upon it.' He who has despised all human glories and polities and the like, considers all things 'refuse' because of the saving hope, 'reckoning' political glories as a 'tomb' when dying, like Paul who says: 'It is no longer I who live, but Christ lives in me' (Gal 2:20). For those who boast greatly upon these human glories, like those leaping upon walls, the weary ones spring upon them, even if not the saint. For it is evident that he has said these things addressing the human person. For it is moderate-minded, even if someone else were the blessed one, to be testified to be 'blameless' and 'righteous.' And even saying these things: that even as a well-fortified city...
translator_notes: True OET; Pass A ≠ Pass B. Melito skipped; never Cyril Matthew densify.

title: Divine Support and Patient Endurance
english: I happened to be suffering from wealth and glory, but for me these things have died, and I do not consider their loss to be heavy. Therefore, I do not spare these things. Having died to them, I do not possess any desire for them at all, from which I live a blessed life.

For it is good 'to die to sin' (Rom 6:2), so that we may live for God and not, like the 'squandering widow' (Luke 21:34), live only to be delivered unto the death of sin. 'For I have not spoken the holy words of my God.' Because of this, I consider all human things to have died to them, since I have not spoken false words concerning God, namely, because I have not stumbled in anything but am 'righteous'—this he says according to the one saying, 'I have no conscience against myself' (Ps 26:4)—or because the things spoken in testimony toward God he showed to be not false, as it is said concerning him: 'and he did not give foolishness to God' (Num 23:19).

For by the words of God, which testify to Him, his way is found to be in agreement with that which is in virtue. Therefore, he also speaks of God's virtuous deeds of himself according to the one saying, 'Not I, but the grace of God with me' (2 Cor 12:9). And it is also an indication of being disciplined by God that he says, 'For I have not spoken the holy words of my God.' Nothing appears less unformed from God than actively showing that: 'do not boast in your wisdom' (1 Cor 10:7). For he confesses all things to God.

For it is useful not to cast oneself upon oneself, which the divine word again exhorts: 'Let not the wise man boast in his wisdom, nor the strong in his strength, nor the rich in his riches, but let him who boasts boast in this, that he understands and knows the Lord' (Jer 9:23). We have examples in the Scriptures of the ungodly boasting and trusting in themselves: Goliath and Pharaoh, who did not long for what they hoped for, 'their pride being quenched.' And 'those claiming to be wise become fools' (1 Cor 3:19) according to the saying. But also concerning those boasting in wealth it is said: 'Do not fear when a man becomes rich and when the glory of his house increases, for he shall not take all by dying' (Prov 23:5). For either he will leave the same things himself, or the same things will leave him when change has occurred.
But the holy man, casting nothing upon himself, entrusts all to God. 'For what is my strength, that I endure? Or what is my time, that my soul is sustained? Is the strength of stones my strength?'

“Or are my fleshly parts made of bronze? Or did he not rely upon them? But help from me has ceased. Mercy failed me, but the Lord's oversight looked down upon me.” (Job 10:18). Being loving, he wants to instruct his friends, so that they do not wonder why he endures such a heavy burden of painful things, and to show them that, if not by a divine calculation, he would not have borne these things given human weakness—for by what strength, he asks, do I endure these things, or for what length of time will I be able to live enduring these? My strength is either of stone or my flesh is bronze, so that I do not feel the pain through them? —so that they do not despise patience by remaining unfeeling. For some even reason about the martyrs that they do not feel the pains, which would deny them virtue.

But he also wants them to grasp this with their mind, that he does not suffer because of sin, saying: “Did he not rely upon it?” (Job 13:15). And to this he adds, hinting at the forgiveness from God: “But help has ceased. Mercy failed me, but the Lord's oversight looked down upon me,” so that from these they may understand that the saint, being conscious of these things happening to himself, bears them bravely standing against the one questioning, having believed that even if the Lord pardoned him by forgiving the one who asked, he was encouraging him to endure. Such also the blessed David sings, saying: “Waiting, I waited for the Lord, and he attended to me.” (Psalm 40:1). And it is possible that he says these things in his rebuking outburst: “You think so, that both the help and the oversight of the Lord looked down upon me.” He himself knows that for the sake of testing, God delivered him, as “blessed is the man who endures temptation, for having been proven he will receive the crown of life, which he rejoiced in for those who love him.” (James 1:12). “My closest ones did not attend to me, like a mountain stream leaving or like a wave passing me by.” (Psalm 31:11). And this happened to him for testing; for the absence of friends in afflictions is no small pain. Enduring this tribulation, the holy David also sang: “They looked to the right and looked, and there was none recognizing me.” (Psalm 31:13). And if even the invisible powers of the saint through his virtue...
translator_notes: True OET; Pass A ≠ Pass B. Melito skipped; never Cyril Matthew densify.

title: Distinctions of Friendship
english: The brief passing of the trial shows that he was visited, for the mind rushes to the statement: 'the Lord's oversight found me too high' (Job 5:9). Just as the Lord of all, not hating, did not merely visit him, but did so to show the adversary that his evil cannot prevail against human virtue, so too might the divine powers—being worthy to know the will of God—allow the struggle to coincide with Job, so that his achievement might appear more brilliantly.

'Those who deceived me have now fallen upon me' (Job 6:15). Perhaps he reproaches them, saying: 'Unaware of the cause of these inductions, you dare to say such things which you did not say before.' It is also likely that many others despised him because of his suffering, and this was also the doing of the one who made the request. See that we have not surrendered the divine powers by allowing the trial to pass briefly just so his virtue might be known, but rather that other opposing powers were permitted to leap upon him and fight against him.

'Like snow or congealed crystal, as it was arranged that heat should come and it was not recognized what it was, so I too was left by all. I was lost and became a stranger' (Job 6:17). The phrase 'Like snow or congealed crystal, as it was arranged' is spoken hyperbolically, being rendered as: 'As snow or crystal was arranged.' The example is appropriate to the hyperbole of his change, making him utterly unknown, like snow or crystal being dissolved by heat and thus making the place where it was, unknown. And it is good to use such an example; just as snow and crystal make the place indistinguishable when dissolved by heat, so also a friend, appearing to be one, is revealed when trials arise, and what he hid before, he makes manifest.

When a distressing time is present and the forming of friends is tested, the saints have certainty, while those who love possess this condition of friendship, keeping it incorruptible both in ease and in adversity. And it is no wonder if they even extend love toward enemies, being peaceful with those who hate peace, according to what is said by the Lord through the prophet:

“Say, our brothers, to those who hate you, so that the name of the Lord might be glorified, but they themselves will be ashamed” (Matt 5:11). And once, since the discourse began concerning friendship, it followed to recognize the differences of friendship.

One is that which is beautiful in itself, which even the saints establish; another is because of utility, such as when someone has a friend of a physician because of this very thing. This friendship, even if it is not perfect, does not possess any human artificiality. Another is [friendship] except because of the pleasant, without which the friend is no longer a friend, and because of ambition, so that they might seem to the many to be friends, contributing nothing to the honor of those. But the one choosing only for utility, a friend is most uncertain; according to the fact that when the need is no longer present, he replaces [the friend], eliminating friendship according to this; he chooses the useful things before the pleasant things, which is also subject to reproach.

The discourse exhorts toward true friendship, saying: “Do not abandon your friend and a patrimonial friend.” “For the recent one is not like him.” I call the recent one “uncertain,” [whereas] the “ancient” or patrimonial one has stability, even if you receive him according to time; ... the one who has come through experience does not neglect the recent one; for he, truly knowing the hearts from experience, ... as he performs the judgment.

And the “I was lost and became a stranger” (Job 1:21) he says toward the lamentation of the many considering the loss of all, the taking away of the possessions and moneys of all, and that he encountered poverty. Therefore also he became a stranger, having been abandoned by all his own. “Behold the ways of the impious, the paths of the ungodly, who look upon [them]. And those trusting in cities and money shall owe shame” (Ps 73:18). I myself, he says, suffered these things, having fallen away from wealth and many children and glory and the other human things. And yet, I am not amazed or surprised by any of these. For even the saints, imposing [themselves] upon the nature of the indifferent, do not consider the taking away of these things to be a heavy burden, and they exhort others just as the blessed David, singing, “If wealth flows, do not add to your heart” (Ps 62:10). And again: “Do not trust in princes and in the sons of men, in whom there is no salvation” (Ps 146:3). Therefore, the saint, correcting them, spoke thus in his leisure.
translator_notes: True OET; Pass A ≠ Pass B. Melito skipped; never Cyril Matthew densify.

title: The Reward of Patience and Gentle Correction
english: He makes the Word say: 'Behold the paths of the Bold, the ways of the Sabeans who see' (Job 20:5), which is: seeing with intellect, so that his whole mind might be such; but I became a stranger and was stripped of all.

Understand the paths of the Bold, judge the ways of the Sabeans, even if they are well-off; we think with minds that, trusting in wealth and glory, they do not have right paths or ways. And he was saying these things submissively and to those who seemed like friends, that he who falls into such evils is carried away, saying: even if you are kings and will not fall into misfortune, but understand the paths of the Bold and the Sabeans—their paths [text gapped]—that trusting in human things, you are incurring shame.

If you would also take the interpretations of the names, this thought would occur, that the 'Bold' are those falling away, while the 'Sabeans' are those returning. Therefore, he exhorts those falling away from virtue, who have trusted even in wealth, to observe them, but he also exhorts to understand those returning to the nature of things, because it does not always remain in prosperity, but also frequently turns back.

Therefore, there is shame in trusting in money or in cities, saying 'cities' meaning the human glories and as if they were in safety. If those falling away were to be praised, he exhorts: understand, how there are also others leaving evils and not always prospering in human things.

If you would wish to learn that things receive much change, those enjoying [things] frequently lose many of which they were deprived; you would not have placed them as if they were permanent. For 'he who has trusted in wealth will fall, but he who grasps what is just will rise' (cf. Luke 16:25), just as Lazarus was carried into the bosom of Abraham (Luke 16:22), but the rich man is delivered to the torment having fallen upon it (Luke 16:23), who through arrogance overlooked Lazarus. For indeed the word observed that...

Regarding 'he was set at the gate' and that he was very rich, so that he might not have an excuse saying that they did not know him or did not possess sufficiency. And 'rising' is also well [used]. For just as the sown things, having undergone decay, later bloom, so he who is pressed by circumstances and endures will have the rising as a reward for his patience, 'shining like the sun in the kingdom of the Father' (Job 23:10).

For he was persuaded in the Lord according to the things said: 'Blessed is the man who trusts in the Lord' (Psalm 84:12); 'those who trust in the Lord are like Mount Zion' (Psalm 125:1)', and saying: 'I have trusted in the Lord', not 'in money or in human cities', but in the Divine Wealth and 'the city of the great King' (Psalm 127:1), whose 'foundations are in the holy mountains', calculating the words of the Lord as 'desirable things far above gold and precious stone'.

'Even you also have come to me compassionately.' And he who admonishes those who have fallen into false accusations with a gloomy countenance is not correcting them according to reason by being moved. For this is not the purpose, but rather to urge them toward manliness and to engage bravely. For to say: 'Why then did we sin?' is more heavy than to be light in toil.

For in truth, they approached him compassionately to rescue him from being tossed about concerning the cause of the indictment, and because they were trying to correct him by accusing one who was not submissive. 'So having seen my wound, you were afraid.' The saint is most pastoral and toward those who are not rightly disposed toward him, he approaches by correcting them from their own error and receiving from their own state the beginning of the exhortation; for every one who sins falls into gloom, and he who fell from sins suffered this, and you also be afraid, receiving fear from our wound. For it was clear to them that 'no one is clean from the filth of men'. And these things indeed the blessed one says as correcting regarding their error, but also useful toward...
translator_notes: True OET; Pass A ≠ Pass B. Melito skipped; never Cyril Matthew densify.

title: The Logic of Intercession
english: Sympathy and the prevention of the words being made hollow. 'For what did I ask? Do I depend on the strength from you, so that you might rescue me from the hand of enemies or from the hand of the powerful?' The irrationality of the rebuke, even while he himself corrects it, he says: if, when I am asking for myself, you say you are unable to carry the prayer for me because it is in sin, there was a reason. But since this has not happened, the charge against me is in vain.

And we have this same thing in the divine writings. For sometimes a prayer happens for those having an inclination toward repentance, but for those opposing, what happens has no reason. Immediately also, God says to the prophet: 'And you, do not pray for this people.' And he says he can proceed with the reasoning of not needing to bring a prayer to him, saying: 'Do you not see what these are doing? Their sons are gathering wood and their fathers are burning fire and the women are making hollows for the army of heaven,' they have introduced a common zeal through a common sin; therefore, do not pray for them.

It is necessary, therefore, if ever an embassy is sent to God by a holy person concerning someone, to run together for that one for whom the embassy is made. For if one acts contrary to the one interceding, he does something similar to what is said: 'One building and one tearing down. What more did they profit than labors?' Furthermore, it is as if the intercessor is shamed.

The Mosaic things testify to this; for when he had ascended to God, it was said to him concerning the people passing below: 'Hasten down; your people have sinned' (Exodus 32:31). And observe what has been said; for when he was being sent to begin for them and to lead and to legislate, God himself says from his own face: 'Go and bring out my people' (Exodus 3:10). For it was worthy of him to be a people. When he turned away from the sincere healing toward him, they are no longer God's but man's. For he says: 'Your people have sinned' (Exodus 32:31), and he is not being philanthropic by this. For having seen the people unworthy of himself, he did not reject them completely, but again through Moses he lets them go, bringing them back to the care concerning them by saying: 'your people,' so that he might thus intercede for them and again turn them back from error, which also happened. For he said, praying: 'If indeed...'
blot me out from your book
translator_notes: True OET; Pass A ≠ Pass B. Melito skipped; never Cyril Matthew densify.

title: Suffering for Discipline, Not Sin
english: To turn back toward virtue. 'For I will not endure even a single word from you.' This is courage; for many men, hearing words while in the midst of heavy burdens, often falter, so that they even weaken through them. But the holy man accepted neither the rebuke from friends nor the words regarding brevity, not at all receiving them as things capable of shaking him.

'Instead, you fall upon an orphan, but you strike at a friend.' Because of this, I do not accept the rebukes from you as being righteous, because just as you fall upon an orphan and a helpless person, not seeing that everyone is a helper, you also strike at a friend, not recognizing the duties of friendship. The saying is useful for not interfering in the misfortunes of others.

'But now, looking into your faces, I will not lie.' The saying is instructive for not bringing forward words of gossip concerning those who are absent, but for speaking what is necessary to one's face. For it has been said: 'Do not speak, nor listen easily to one gossiping.' And it is a matter of outspokenness to say: 'I will not lie,' just as Paul says: 'That I do not lie' (2 Cor 1:12).

'Sit down then, and let it not be unjust. And again, come together to the righteous.' These things are permissive and not harsh, teaching with leisure and attention, which is shown by the 'sit down,' and examining what is to be spoken. This is also said elsewhere: 'Before you examine, do not condemn.' And great is the command: 'Let it not be unjust.' For it is great not to act unjustly in speech, as it has been said: 'If anyone does not stumble in speech, he is able to bridle his whole body' (Jas 3:2).

'Again, come together to the righteous.' The 'again' is like their previous state, when he was teaching them to come together when he was not in a crisis, that they must not make their judgment out of the necessity of the afflicted, but looking toward the righteous. And he fulfills the promise reverently, saying: 'Looking into your faces, I will not lie,' advising them to occupy themselves with the pursuit of the righteous.

Since the friends thought that those in distress were as those who must encounter God concerning sin, as if this were the cause of their sufferings, he prays that he may make known to them why he set himself as a rod for himself, that it is through struggle and not through sin; for not everyone who encounters God suffers this because of sin. 'Am I a burden to you?' I think I am a burden.

It is upon me; for they weigh me down saying, 'You suffer because of sin.' And because of this, they impose a kind of burden upon me through me, as if punishing the innocent. But I say that you do not punish me, but you train me, even if they thoughtlessly consider that anyone receiving the trial unhappily suffers because of sin.

And why should I not make my iniquity a forgetfulness and a cleansing of sin? To seek those things according to Him is to teach friends and to reason, 'that,' even if I have sinned something, the good God, like the friends, overlooks the faults, provided they themselves did not suffer, so that from this they may understand that he suffers not because of sin, but through struggles. And these things lead them into understanding and are not a little of the righteous, as we have said, so that they may not observe him through his own goodness, but rather that cleansing for sin happens not through continuous punishment.

Now I shall depart to the earth, but I am no longer rising at dawn. He explains the disposition of those who do not correctly take this to mean: if these have taken me to be a sinner and suffering because of sin, they think that having me thus established with nothing after this, 'I have hoped most in this life alone,' and according to them, if I depart to the earth, I shall no longer be; and after days pass, I shall no longer be; for another age will not receive me at all according to them.

But it is a holy voice, upon which also the blessed one hoped, saying: 'I shall rise at dawn' (Ps 43:5), and again: 'Out of the night my spirit rises toward you, O God' (Ps 42:5), and: 'O God, my God, toward you I rise' (Ps 42:5); which also indicates the daily staying awake and the awakening from this age into the coming age. If anyone should say plausibly that: until I am in the shadows, I happen to be in night, but having risen and having become in the day, I am no longer in transitory things.

As we also previously noted, these things are not spoken of for a short time; for he would not have testified as righteous. But Baldad the Sachite, having supposed this, says: 'Until when will you speak these things? A spirit of many sorrows from your mouth (Job 7:9). Will the Lord not judge unjustly, or he who made all things trouble the righteous (Job 9:22)?' Being of the same grief as the one perishing, and he too—that because of sin the evil things certainly...
translator_notes: True OET; Pass A ≠ Pass B. Melito skipped; never Cyril Matthew densify.

title: The Restoration of Righteousness and the Nature of Purity
english: Regarding the words directed toward Job, it is being sent—and by sharing in the same cause as the former friend, he makes the subordinates act—it was necessary to consider that whatever is harmful falls not only through trivial things but also through significant ones; for they are indifferent. Furthermore, it was more necessary to realize that the righteous man is more wonderful when enduring afflictions and pains.

Thus, this one also rebukes the blessed [one], saying: 'Until when?'—saying only: 'Until when?'—'Do you not perceive the cause of the pains?' And he charges him with much talk, he who ought to have marveled more at him, because, as if forgetting the pains, he was making these words regarding doctrines, which the friends did not know, even while they were not imposing themselves upon investigation, although they were being driven by distress. Then, further confirming his opinion and presenting a reasoning to him as well, he says: 'Will not the Lord judge unjustly, or he who made all things trouble the righteous?' For there was a disturbance of justice according to their assumption, if being righteous he suffered. But they are ignorant of these things; for the concession made against him has happened for the sake of highlighting and for the purpose of courage.

'If your children have sinned against him, he sent [it] at the hand of their lawlessness' (Job 1:5). This one also holds the word together and carries himself along with the doctrines, saying: 'Even if you did not sin, but your children did, you would not have considered that one would punish another for another.' But this also he was merely striking at, because through his own sin lawlessness was sent at the hand of them, hinting at the fall through which his children were lost. And he makes a mention of a son, making the word from the best part; for Job also had daughters. It is therefore evident that the sinning of sons and having much benefit from Job, as also the daughters sinned, is clear.

And against him again, his opinion and these things are being criticized. 'But you rose up early to the Lord Almighty, praying: If you are pure and true, he will listen to your prayer and restore to you a way of righteousness' (Job 27:5). He says this while contending. For having said that 'he sent [it] at the hand of the lawlessness of your sons,' he says to him: 'You rose up early to the Lord; if you are pure, he will listen to your prayer.' For how [can he be] pure, concerning whom he was implying that through sin [he was...]

Does it follow? Most especially, that it brings [it]: 'and he shall restore to you a manner of righteousness' (Job 22:27), instead of: he will give to you as to one pure, restoring the pleasant things again. But we have 'the pure' signifying instead 'the upright', just as it has been said: 'blessed are the pure in heart' (Matt 5:8); for this reason it is said, because they do not have the impurity which is from evil; 'as it has been said' concerning the wicked: 'it is crushed through the impurity of the soul'; and again concerning something: 'its impurity toward its feet.' Such also are those whose 'feet run toward wickedness' (Prov 1:16).

But if righteousness is being restored to him, he does not have it now; and if he does not have it now, how is he pure? Or how does he waver, that he is pure, remaining [in doubt], because he is a sinner by falling in circumstances? And this opposition of theirs followed from having placed a beginning that errs, which follows every heresy. For saying to the one in wrongdoing: 'if you are pure and true, he will listen to your prayer and restore to you a manner of righteousness' (Job 22:27-28), he shows that it is possible for the good and true to fall into these things; which follows by necessity, that not everyone who is in circumstances is wicked and in sins; therefore your first things shall be few, and your last things unutterable (Job 8:7).

Again, both then and now he fights for his beginning; for as he follows, he receives [the understanding], that God restores the pleasant things to the pure after much suffering in many ways. For it seems through these things that he introduces the manner of the bringing in of painful things, which he did not previously set forth, through which he says 'his last things [shall be] unutterable' (Job 8:7), making it clear as if, having endured bravely—unless someone says that he says these things will happen to him after he has repented from the prayer toward God—but this 'not' does not allow the saying: 'if you are pure', even though the thing said: 'but you, rise up early toward the Lord, the Pantokrator' (Job 22:28) is for the purpose of contrast.

For 'inquire of the first generation, search out according to the lineage of the fathers' (Deut 32:7). He wishes to establish his own word from the former men or writings, which contained their lives. For nothing is to be considered as being both an image and letters, especially because of the saying: 'who would give that my words might be written down?' and the following: also laws existed, according to which these also were walking, the friends say. For tomorrow...
translator_notes: True OET; Pass A ≠ Pass B. Melito skipped; never Cyril Matthew densify.

title: The Nature of Life and Teaching
english: We are, and we do not know it, for our life upon the earth is a shadow. For it is necessary to hear intelligently the 'for we are dust' (Job 3:6), because he says this regarding human origin, especially since he says, 'for I inquired of the first generation' (Job 8:8). For it is necessary to hear wisely the things said about man, such as—so that I may speak from the Scriptures—many things have been said about David, that he 'was a red-haired one with beauty of eyes' (Psalm 36:3). But this we hear not concerning the soul, but concerning the body. But when he himself says 'the indefinite things', 'and the hidden things of my heart you have made known to me', concerning the soul we understand this. And therefore the 'dust' we hear to be not according to the soul, but according to the human [nature]. Thus also it is joined: 'for our life upon the earth is a shadow.' Therefore he speaks concerning the life upon the earth, that it turns out to be a shadow.

And once since the memory of this word has occurred, it is necessary for us to discuss it. Therefore it is said, the shadow, in relation to a prototype, just as it has been said: 'for having a shadow, the law of the things about to come' (Hebrews 10:1). And a shadow is also the accompaniment, and the approach is often called a shadow, just as it has been said similarly: 'the Holy Spirit will come upon you and the power of the Most High will overshadow you' (Luke 1:35). And 'shadow-sketching' is also said to be an indistinct image of impression before the manifest writing; it is therefore possible to take the human life to be a shadow according to what is suitable and productive for discourse. And it is also possible to be contrasted against a prototype; for just as the present age exists as a shadow toward the life that is to come, existing as vanity. And this life can also be called a shadow-sketch, since here indeed knowledge is 'in part' (1 Cor 13:12), and perfection will be in the coming age. And it can also be viewed as shadows, since we say that even the shadow of the bodies is an accompaniment; and behold, is this not made manifest in: 'Vanity of vanities, all things are vanity' (Eccl 1:2)? For not simply are the creatures of God vanity, but...

Just as vanity exists in things that are temporary and quickly changing compared to the eternal heavenly things. Life signifies many things, namely this living or the way of life; it also signifies possession, as it is said: 'whoever has the life of the world and sees his brother in need' (1 John 3:17). And money is said to be life, as it is said: 'if a man gives his life in love, they will render him nothing.' Do not these teach you and also announce and bring words out from the heart?

Wishing to believe these things from the older [traditions] as being more successful in matters, whereas those in his time did not succeed. Once, since the discourse is about teachers, let us say that it is a great praise to the teacher, if—whether he learned from those [before him], or read it himself, or learned from another—he sometimes himself establishes things not contrary, but in agreement. For just as no one would accept a land that gave back the sown seeds, so no one would accept, in his own land, only providing children and monks with what he heard, providing wonders, but rather, by producing other wonderful things through this, being able to bring forth what he learned through the power of tongue; for there are those unable to this, able to benefit only themselves and not others.

If you say that teaching and announcing can be different, consider how the one teaching brings proofs, while the one announcing contains a narrative of the clear things, from which the unclear things are known. That thoughts send out words from the heart, the Savior says from the opposite: 'for from the heart come out evil thoughts' (Matthew 15:19). And if you were to say that to bring words out means to transition into the works themselves, you would not be erring, as others hear from a parallel [passage] about bringing out and announcing. Does papyrus not flourish without water, or will a lotus be raised without drink? While still on the root, it will certainly not be harvested. Having said, that
translator_notes: True OET; Pass A ≠ Pass B. Melito skipped; never Cyril Matthew densify.

title: The Unstable House of the Wicked
english: The teaching of the ancients and the fathers is passed down to those who come later; he prepares it by way of a parable, saying: just as a papyrus without water does not flourish nor rise up as a reed unless it is watered, while it is still upon the earth—for it will likewise happen to it, even not to be harvested—so it is impossible, without receiving benefit in the mind from superior things, to bring forth useful fruit.

And he can also speak concerning human affairs, saying that just as these things are watered by water through providence, without which they would be thin and dried up, so also, if anyone falls into calamities and then again has a change from these, it has become such through providence. And if the things happening through men have even the appearance of a human root, they will not have substance without providence directing them.

Similar to this is what is well said by the Psalmist: 'Unless the Lord builds the house, they labor in vain who build it' (Psalm 127:1). Before drinking, every herb will be dried up (Job 14:7). This is said regarding the former [parable] concerning every herb. He says, therefore, that whether it be small or great, that which is in life is under providence, being dried up unless this providence watches over it. Thus, in all things, the end of those who forget the Lord will be so.

He says something glorious regarding a concept of unceasing steadfastness: that just as plants not watered by water are dried up, so human affairs happening outside of providence have no substance. If even this [author] is speaking at the end with a concept concerning the coming age, consider this: for it is not contrary that those who forget the Lord will encounter such an end according to the sensible, as those living prudently have said: 'And they slept in the rest of Hades.' But the hope of the ungodly will perish.

In reality, the hope of the ungodly is not concerning a subsisting thing. For hope is nothing other than, by nature, an expectation of good things. And he who fears expects, but not good things; for fear is an expectation of evils, while hope is of good things. Since, therefore, the ungodly do not expect subsisting things, their hope is destroyed; for as they remain, they use [things] for pleasures, and in this they have a vain hope. You have this in Proverbs, differing much in wording, but agreeing with what is now said: 'Ab...

When a righteous man dies, he does not regret (Job 27:15); for if the righteous man dies, he finds the things he expected and did not regret having labored for them. Here it is said: 'The hope of the ungodly perishes' (Proverbs 14:34), and in Isaiah: 'Hope to the godly' (Isaiah 57:19). But those 'hoping only in this life' and 'saying: Let us eat and drink,' have a vain and empty hope, stretching themselves toward this visible thing; but Paul says naturally: 'But the hope that is seen is not hope; for what one sees, what does he hope for?' (2 Corinthians 4:18). And his house shall be desolate.

Regarding this sensible thing, it is not entirely true. It is clear, however, that he who transforms the words of Jesus into works builds a dwelling; and this is the virtue, of which the one holding fast will never have this house desolate; for the righteous must remain in his own virtue; for 'his righteousness remains unto the age of ages.' Since evil is without substance, for this reason the wicked man is desolate, being always unstable and possessing nothing firm, because evil itself is a following-after; and if anyone says this also concerning the good, claiming that men acquire virtue by effort, but rather the good itself has happened. 'Therefore the house of the ungodly shall be desolate'; for clearly the truth dissolves the deception. And his tent shall fall away like a spider's web. The spider's web shows variety, constructed from a natural fabric, which is easily dissolved when someone touches it. Thus the works of the wicked and the construction of their way of life resemble a spider's web, not standing firm.

And in Isaiah it is said concerning the wicked who have conceived iniquity and spoken injustice: 'They weave a spider's web, for they conceive pain and bring forth iniquity' (Isaiah 59:5); and their practice is also described, saying: 'They have made wailing shields, and the one about to eat of their prey has crushed a viper and found a basilisk in it; their web shall not be a garment, but a spider's web they weave' (Isaiah 59:6). And see, that regarding their instability, the harmful thing also signifies through the shields. Even if there were a dove according to what is said: 'Who are these? Like clouds flying and like doves with their young' (Isaiah 56:6), it would have wailing, which, having been divided, provides living offspring because of nobility; but the...
translator_notes: True OET; Pass A ≠ Pass B. Melito skipped; never Cyril Matthew densify.

title: The Unholy Construction vs. The Spiritual House
english: Deceiving through evils, they produce unavengeable snakes, which are trampled by the holy according to the psalm saying concerning the perfect: 'Upon shield and basilisk you will step and trample lion and dragon' (Psalm 91:13). But these are not fabrics of garments covering the shame of sin, but of a useless and dissolvable web, which is also shown by the [saying]: 'They will not surround themselves from the works of their own hands'—the important one surrounding himself from the works of his own hands, as speaking boldly and thankfully saying: 'My soul will rejoice in the Lord; for he has clothed me with a garment of salvation' (Psalm 68:19), which is a garment Paul says to put on: 'Put on the bowels of mercy' (Psalm 68:2) and the following. And again: 'Put on the Lord Jesus Christ' (Romans 13:14). This garment is not a web; for it is incorruptible and therefore remains; but the [web] of the evils is unsubstantial; for it is wickedness. Therefore it has been said: 'His sin will be sought and will not be found through it;' for it resembles a web, dissolving; therefore also a tent, but it does not have a house like the one guarding the words of Jesus. If he should attempt to overspread his house, he will not stand.

For instance, the impious one—he who represents the deception of houses by craftiness and bad probability—this one, being convicted by the truth, will not stand, just as his deception cannot even have a standing. And when he is seized, he will not remain. For the thought of the evils, called a tent, is a falling, easily-destroyed thing, so that it has not even seemed to have happened at all. For it is moist under the sun, and from its rot his broom will come out. It is supposed that the life of the impious is something chaotic, as being dissolved by brief heat. And it should not be wondered at, if it is said to be 'moist under the sun'; for there are things that are dissolved under the sun like wax, since also under fire. Thus also the impious will be. For it has been said: 'As wax melts from the presence of fire, so the sinners shall perish from the presence of God' (Psalm 68:1). And being sifted by the 'sun'—not of 'righteousness', but that one, concerning whom it is said: 'The sun of the day shall not burn you' (Psalm 121:6)—it brings out a broom from wickedness and rot, becoming 'under it' the 'planting which the Father did not plant' (Matthew 13:25).
which also shall be uprooted. It lies upon a heap of stones, and in the midst of pebbles it shall live. This he says, because the impious one intends to be an anti-god and an anti-Christ.

For God indeed dwells in a temple and Christ dwells, according to what is said: 'Do you not know that you are a temple of God and the Spirit of God dwells in you?' (1 Cor 3:16), and again it is said: 'If anyone loves me, we will come and make a dwelling with him' (John 14:23). 'For we are the house of Christ, if we hold fast the boldness and the boast until the end' (2 Cor 3:6). A house is a composition of stones according to art, having union with others; such is virtue and purity and the very participation of the One.

But what is the scattering of stones and the mixing of pebbles? It is near to evil, which has no union but disorder. The impious, therefore, has his whole conduct in a house of evil, being scattered like stones being built up among those outside, which do not fit 'the building of the tower' according to the Shepherd. If he presses down, the place will deceive him.

Even if we submit the words, as many as are held firm, to the minds [of which the words spoken by the diligent are near], we should not be surprised. For he said: 'Inquire of the first generation, and search according to the race of the fathers' (Wisdom 10:18), as he himself learned from them; and do not let your thoughts be lost through not knowing, lest you fall into any misfortune.

The 'pressing down' is often taken in Scripture as that: 'Israel was trodden down, and became among the nations as a useless vessel' (Judges 5:23), that is, he is conquered. And again: 'In the rising up of men against us, would they have trodden us down while living?' (Ps 69:1). And again: 'That the mortal might be trodden down by life.'

It is said also concerning the sophists and those advocating the 'wisdoms of this age' and of its 'rulers': 'Their strong ones trod down those holding stones'; what kind of stone, the stone of Christ? 'For the stone was Christ.' Thus also 'Aaron's rod trod down the rods of the Egyptians who rejoiced' (Ex 7:12), being symbolically shown that the confession of the truth conquers the 'false names of knowledges.' If, therefore, he 'presses down' and begins to conquer, 'the place,' which he holds through 'the gathering of stones,' 'will deceive him,' [being] unsubstantial.
translator_notes: True OET; Pass A ≠ Pass B. Melito skipped; never Cyril Matthew densify.

title: The True Joy of the Righteous
english: Being according to what was said: 'and injustice lied against itself' (Job 21:13) because it lacks a secure foundation. By the lion starting from itself, having trampled the two legs and the lobe of the ear, the one who came for salvation scattered them, having corrected our wandering powers and our hearing. The place is often called instead of ranks and order: 'from where Judas passed over.' So also regarding the deceiver, who deceives the user without offering anything certain to him. Have you not seen such a destruction of the ungodly? And he brings as a witness all the things previously said concerning the ungodly, which he also named the destruction of the ungodly, because he does not remain upon those things on which he boasts, as these things fall away from him.

This is shown by: 'do not fear when a man becomes rich and when the glory of his house increases, for he will not take all things in dying, nor will the glory of his house descend with him' (Psalm 49:16-17). And whether poverty or prosperity alternate, they do nothing, for they are among the indifferent. But he who remains in wickedness until the end will have a great destruction. And from the earth he will sprout another; for the Lord will certainly not cast away the simple. It appears that even if the ungodly undergoes destruction, not all are lost; for there will be a diligent one sprouting anew. For God will not turn away from the simple, that is, He will not entirely exclude justice.

Here 'simple' means the one not having guile, not the well-disposed; for the name signifies both. For when he speaks concerning the heretics, saying, 'through fair speaking and blessing they deceive the hearts of the simple,' he means the well-disposed, those slow in understanding. And again: 'the simple and well-disposed clung to me,' which signifies the righteous, the 'simple believes every word' (Jeremiah 11:19) signifying the one who is uncontrolled and unable to discern the falsehood in the words, believing everything plausible. And he who says, 'but because of my simplicity, I received' signifies virtue. And every gift the ungodly will not receive. It is appropriate to the Lord, who does not cast away the simple, that not even one of the gifts of the ungodly be attached to him. 'For thanks are not good from the wages of a prostitute' (Proverbs 7:33), and 'the sinner sacrificing a calf to me as...

[The one] killing the dog. It is noteworthy, however, that 'all is a gift' is said instead of 'nothing is a gift' according to prophetic custom, just as when God says in the prophet: 'if a righteous man does one sin, all his righteousness shall not be remembered' (cf. Job 2:10), instead of 'not any'. And the mouth of the truthful shall be filled with laughter. Throughout the whole book, he remembers the truthful regarding the righteous. Thus also Job himself was testified at the beginning, that he was 'truthful, abstaining from an evil thing'.

And truly, he is the one who is truthful, who does not pretend or mimic virtue, who does not pretend temperance, but is temperate, the one 'pursuing the righteous thing righteously.' Therefore, God 'will fill the mouth of the truthful with laughter.' And from this it is to be imposed, lest even this one, having learned according to the 'inquiry of the first generation' concerning the coming age according to that which is said in the Gospel: 'blessed are those who weep now, for they shall laugh' (Luke 6:21), [be lost].

For laughter is twofold: the one being false, occurring with pleasure, which is followed by weeping; the other being the gift of the Spirit, being joy, which shall be given to those weeping now in the life to come. For 'blessed are those who weep now, for they shall laugh' (Luke 6:21), they have the harvest of this from afar because of virtue; the holy one, having received the experience of this from afar, as I said, said: 'You have turned my mourning into joy for me, you have torn my sackcloth and girded me with gladness' (Psalm 30:11).

The example of Lazarus is here, first weeping because of suffering, but resting in the bosom of Abraham; whereas the rich man, laughing through pleasure, wept while being tormented in Hades bitterly concerning that laughter spoken of. He honored [himself] by making himself a god in some way, just as others [make] the belly, concerning whom it is said: 'of whom God is the belly.' It is also said concerning laughter: 'the altars of laughter shall be removed, the sins of Israel' (Hosea 10:5). For the preoccupations regarding sufferings and pleasures are altars of laughter, remembering these sufferings of their own.

He who does great and unsearchable things, glorious and wonderful, of which there is no number. The great one does great things by necessity; it is not necessary for one doing great things to be great. For he does not turn back. Indeed, the disciples doing great things...
translator_notes: True OET; Pass A ≠ Pass B. Melito skipped; never Cyril Matthew densify.

title: The Inscrutability of Divine Providence and Anger
english: They had these things from the great God.

So that I may also use a human example, I say, that the grammarian writes grammatically; but not always every writer has it correctly from grammar, but also from luck and habit. It appears therefore according to greatness, that he who is great alone, by doing, does great things; and analogously also according to our power we contemplate God and receive the concept of God Himself.

And he said this so that the friends, those supposing a single cause of labors, might understand that he who does great and fearsome and deep judgments has them also unsearchable, which are also glorious, as to say filled with glory. Paul also writes something similar, saying: 'O depth of the riches and wisdom and knowledge of God; how unsearchable are his judgments and unsearchable are his ways; for who has known the mind of the Lord?' (Rom 11:33). And in the Psalms there is something near: 'Great are your judgments' (Ps 18:49). For who having understood heaven, sun, moon, stars, and the motions of these, will not marvel at the Creator? And if even you were to pass through into each thing even to the smallest of him, as that teaches: 'Go to the ant, you sluggard' (Prov 6:6) and the following, you will marvel at the wisdom of this God. If he surpasses me, I shall not see, and if he passes me by, I have not even known how.

The ungraspable nature of God's judgments is signified here; for for man, and more so by nature born, to grasp these things by private effort is impossible. This [is]... to him... this the holy [one]... came to the mind, so that from the inability to grasp the judgments of God they might understand and remember Him, and [understand] regarding the things happening to Him as not being accidental, and so that they might avoid supposing a single cause regarding the things happening. Whether therefore or whether therefore, he says, whether the Lord surpasses me or passes me by, so that he is even near to me, I am not able to know by...

of my mind regarding what becomes men. For someone wishing something might elude him, and surpassing him and passing by, will not sufficiently grasp it. And it is possible even to say, that if the things concerning the earth were to become near to me, I would be able to know according to our imposition; for how the economy of the heaven and those in it happens is unknown to me; if indeed I should come again to the lands, God passing by me and in some way training me among them, even so I am not self-sufficient in knowing.

If he removes [it], who will turn back? Or who will say to him: 'What have you done?'; for he himself has turned away in anger. To remove is possible in every matter upon which God works; for if he wished to dissolve human life, who can turn back his will? If to bring about painful things or to cease these, no one of those things happening from him can promise a hindrance, nor can anyone of strength say to him: 'What have you done?'; according to the apostolic word: 'Shall not the creature say to the creator: Why have you made me thus?' (Romans 9:20). ... let those speaking blasphemously to him say: 'What have you done?'; for not ... the word, but ... of him worthy of ... 'What have you done?'; for those calculating the bitter things for a short time, not knowing their purpose, speak blasphemously: 'What have you done?'; according to the fool saying in his own heart: 'There is no God.' And he also brings the reason for not being able to say anything to him: 'What have you done?'; asserting: 'For he himself has turned away in anger'; for by a judgment of anger he has made the turning away. But someone, recognizing this graciously, said: 'I will bear the anger of the Lord, because I have sinned against him' (Psalm 38:18). Therefore he turns away the worthy in anger; but the righteous one does not have the worth of anger, so he has not turned away the righteous. Even if the righteous one suffers, it is not by anger, but he undergoes a struggle. For look, if one is being disciplined as a combatant, and another is being struck, is not the same manner of wounds? Thus even painful things to the righteous and...
translator_notes: True OET; Pass A ≠ Pass B. Melito skipped; never Cyril Matthew densify.

title: The Nature of Prayer and Divine Judgment
english: When a bad thing happens, it did not occur in the same way; for one is under wrath, the bad one, I say, but the other did not, but rather turned away the wrath from the righteous, desiring to prove himself a victor, as the witnesses and Job himself. For he turned away the wrath being sent upon the bad ones by making his virtue manifest. And the cattle under heaven were scorched by him.

And according to the account of history this is true; for if he himself had not subjected them, these things would have been beyond doubt to men. And even in the other predatory beasts you will find this by passing through the reasoning. But also the evil spirits, the cattle named allegorically, he himself bent. For neither was human nature such that it would not be scorched by God without being so. And it is fitting that he also spoke of those under heaven, in order to make all things manifest, those in the air and in the earth and in the lower regions. For all things have been subjected: 'for the cattle was spread by knowledge' (Job 39:25).

And if God had not said so continually, not even to Job: 'the beginning of evil is the devil' (Job 1:6). For the opposing powers do not come by their own wicked intention. For they do not have authority to approach with evil and hardship, unless God permits it. But they hasten to cast evil by their own impulse. For so also, according to a private intention, 'into the heart of Judas' (Luke 22:3) those providing him with sufferings, they gather evils dwelling there.

If he obeys me, does he discern my words? He wishes to teach that not, if we pray for something, this does not always happen 'and' in agreement with our words for the discernment of God. 'For what we ought to pray for according to what is necessary, we do not know.' What therefore he says is such: that even if he obeys, he does not discern human words to approve them in this way, but his own judgment, being wise, will impose it upon us, being a lover of mankind and doing nothing unjustly. For if, O righteous one, he does not listen to me, I will entreat his judgment. He confirms what was said before, teaching that even if someone is perfect among men, the eye of God 'searches the things of the heart' (Romans 7:24) and perceives even the unseen. Such is what the apostle says: 'I know nothing about myself, but I am not acquitted by this; but the one who judges me is the Lord' (1 Cor 4:3); therefore the saint desires his judgment according to: 'refine the...'

"the kidneys and my heart," which no one in a state of sinning says. Still, regarding these things, he teaches them again not to grasp the secondary things for a single cause, by assuming a hypothesis: that if anyone is righteous and prays for pleasant things hypothetically, he will not certainly be heard; for even he requires the judgment of God.

There are some who have read the verse without a substantiation, that it is: "He will not listen to my righteousness" (Job 11:6). Understand then, that the repayment has a reason, because the one who spoke before, the friend, was saying: "But you rise up early to the Lord praying; if you are good and true, he will listen to the prayer of supplication" (Job 8:6), teaching him that God does not always give to us the words we ask, but those that are profitable; he says this hypothetically, that "for if you are righteous, he will not listen to me;" for thus the judgment triumphs.

He spoke hypothetically because even the holy one knows that the judgment must persuade him and not demand a solution from him unseasonably. Even if I call and he obeys, I do not believe that he has listened to me, lest he should turn me away through my ignorance. Since it was easy and convenient for Bildad to say to the blessed Job, as we also said before, the "but you rise up early" and the following, toward his own words spoken without distinction, teaching that the one praying will not certainly succeed, nor is it fitting to ask God for everything with "uncovering hands"; for he who sends up prayer rightly to God deserves to receive those things which are effective for him and suit the one bestowing.

For since the kind of good things is twofold—the first being the truly good, which are the virtues, and the second being the pleasant and customary good things—one must not ask God unseasonably for the customary things, but for the truly good; for God will judge whether we are being removed from hardships or being kept in them. And the diligent one asks for the truly good things, such as gifts, knowing intelligently that "to each is given the manifestation of the Spirit for the profit of the Spirit" (1 Cor 12:7). Often indeed some say: how... to pray... "a gift of healing" or something else, I say "a reason" of "knowledge" and the rest; but they say these things not knowing that these things happen profitably from God. For not all use well those things which exist. Toward these, then, of the friends, I say, he answers with a hypothesis, teaching again hypothetically how one must pray. For if, he says,
translator_notes: True OET; Pass A ≠ Pass B. Melito skipped; never Cyril Matthew densify.

title: Unit 14 rem mid
english: cloud
to rule lawlessly
translator_notes: True OET; Pass A ≠ Pass B. Melito skipped; never Cyril Matthew densify.

title: The Equality of Trials and the Distinction of Ends
english: These things apply to both kings and commoners. It seems he also stirs them up so that they do not think that they have been separated from their equals because of the duties they are surrounded by; for these things are common to the important and the trivial, to the free and the slave, to the commoner and the ruler, and quite simply to all.

But the things sent upon them because of triviality, he has made a separation for the sinners from all the righteous. For 'the death of the righteous is precious before the Lord' (Ps 116:15). And concerning the trivial, it is said: 'the death of sinners is bitter' (Prov 1:32). And the dissolution of the soul from the body is the same; but the trivial one receives punishment, because his death is shameful, while the important one receives promise and divine rewards; for 'the Lord takes' 'the gentle' (Ps 103:13). And to each of the righteous is a similar voice, by which they say: 'He who raises me from the gates of death' (Ps 18:4). Of what death, indeed, is this, or the one that consumes the soul from blessed life? For this one, having been raised from the gates of death, comes to the gates of blessed life beyond, bringing forth: 'that I may declare all your praises in the gates of the daughter of Zion' (Ps 78:7). These are indeed excellent deeds and entries into good works.

But the righteous are mocked and are delivered into the hands of the ungodly. The trivial ones, he says, truly experience in death what is shameful, but the righteous are mocked by the trivial ones doing this, when they see them being in distress. This is not a reproach of the righteous, but of those who mock, not knowing that they are being delivered into the hands of the ungodly; which he says he is making manifest, thus showing the cause of his own ill-treatment. For it was not fitting then to say, that because of a struggle I am delivered into the hands of the ungodly and such a trial is; for sometimes, as if being self-exalting, he gave space to the adversary to seize him. He will cover the faces of his judges. He shows the harshness of the ungodly by covering his faces to approach deceitfully to deceive. It is therefore said: 'Who shall uncover his face-covering, or who shall enter to fold his garment?' (Job 13:13). For when they change the faces through the same [means], they often approach someone deceitfully, baiting him into...
wolves in sheep's clothing
