english: According to the saying, "they shall build and I will turn back," says the Lord (Job 22:28). And concerning those having a bad building, it is said: "you destroy them and will not build them." Thus, if it is shut according to men, no one will open; for if God is not prospering a certain action, which someone pre-ordains, through whom words are known, who is able to open? He shut the escape from Pharaoh and the Egyptians, and an opening was not found. And in its entirety, many such things you will find.

For He closes against the useful, not allowing the enjoyment of human things, but to be in want; and toward what? Toward salvation, He brings the difficult things. And He closes in another way according to men, when He does not allow them to prosper in evils, and this happening properly toward God, not as the Pharisees did; for it was said to them: "you shut the kingdom of the heavens, you yourselves do not enter, nor do you allow those entering to enter" (Matt 23:13). And the kingdom of the heavens is shut when those who seem to be teachers, through whom they work evils, make certain imitators of themselves, so that neither they nor those imitating them may enter into the kingdom.

If, therefore, God also shuts to the one who has shut [it] because of his conduct, who will open to him? Likewise the water and that which hinders according to the sensible, according to what is said, "one part shall be shortened and a part, on which I will not wet, shall be dried," hinders, it dries the earth; and of this you have the example in the Kingdoms; for He is "the one raising clouds from the end of the earth, making lightning into rain" (Job 37:3). And according to His own authority, He touches the earth toward growth and toward destruction of those in it, as in the flood according to Noah (Gen 7).

But if you lead these up with understanding, you will find also the profit from them. With Him are power and strength, with Him are knowledge and understanding. The reasonable proof of each of those things happening from Him, the God, is that no one else would be able to do it, or Him, as He teaches, asserting: "with Him are power and strength." And so that no one may irrationally suppose that He makes God remain by power and strength alone, He brings: "with Him are knowledge and understanding." For even if someone is displeased with the things happening, saying, "why is this fertile and wealthy land again becoming a wasteland, while the needy remains without bread?", let him hear.

The phrase 'with him are knowledge and understanding.' For He himself, 'having arranged all things by weight and measure,' provides to each according to the words of His providence what He wills. The production or administration of existing things does not occur by chance, but the diversity of created things and the wisdom of administration have come from and stand in divine wisdom.

It must be noted that it is not said, as if God were a compounder, that 'strength and might are with him' and 'with him are knowledge and understanding'; for all these things the Son is, being simple and uncomposite. He leads away captive counselors, and he makes the judges of the earth err. And these are the works of providence; for by will and by judgment, captive counselors are led away and judges are displaced.

And if 'counselors' refers to those who blow great in the state, many of these are also found scattered in captivity; which is clear from the captivity of Israel, concerning which Jeremiah lamented over their city, saying: 'How sits the city once full of people, now as a widow full of nations; she who ruled among the lands has become a tributary' (Jeremiah 2:36). And if 'those who advise' signifies the name of counsel, then God leads away those who do this for evil. An example of this is Ahithophel, whose counsel and life were perverted.

For from this also one can understand the work of providence: that even those most wise among those advising, following the purpose of advising, fail in their outcomes, not as if they advised badly, but as if providence is testing them otherwise. So also rulers who have done all things by themselves fail; for the end belongs to God. By His own power He 'made judges err.' And if 'made err' signifies madness, this also happens to those using judgment in a way that is not required; for God displaces such people, proving them foolish. But 'made err' can also signify their displacement; for by the providence of the Word of God, 'judges are displaced' and kings are seated on thrones. Similar to this is 'through me kings reign' and 'the Lord establishes kings and removes them.' Often He gives these both in anger and according to...
translator_notes: True OET; Pass A ≠ Pass B. Melito skipped; never Cyril Matthew densify.

title: The Scattering of Counsel and the Pouring Out of Dishonor
english: The phrase 'I gave them a kingdom in my wrath' is used. Because things apart from God's judgment are hollow, He himself says, lamenting, 'They reigned and not through me; they began and did not make known to me' (Ps 2:2), through which, in wrath, such people are again released, the opportunity for reconciliation being provided again for a time.

For a throne is often taken to mean a kingdom, even if it is used instead of a teaching office, as is clear from 'The Lord King is established forever' (Ps 145:13), and again: 'Your throne, O God, is unto the ages of ages' (Ps 45:6), and even more: 'A throne of authority is prepared with righteousness' (Ps 89:14). But it is also said to the disciples: 'You also shall sit on twelve thrones judging the twelve tribes of Israel' (Matt 19:28). When it is said, 'The scribes sat upon the seat of Moses' (Luke 13:31), this seat is one of teaching. And he girded their loins with a belt. Unless he himself lives, the one being girded has no strength; therefore, it is God who is He and who governs all these things by His own providence. And the matter of the belt signifies as 'And rulers shall hold the earth through me.'

He sends them as captives. If he speaks of those not using the matter correctly, it shows that He spares not even them when the time calls. But if he means those using it according to what is necessary, God also sends even these many times, like those concerning Daniel and Jesus the son of Josadak, into captivity for the sake of the usefulness of another multitude; for how great was the thing they were doing, they were not worthy to undergo captivity. Consider, however, the greatness of them, that even having become captives and being in Babylon, they remained unshaken.

And if, then, we see the saints being sent into this life, let us reckon that it was not for their own sake, but they underwent this for the benefit of others. The apostle, alluding to this, writes: 'This attitude was among you which was also in Christ Jesus, who, existing in the form of God, did not consider being equal to God a thing to be grasped, but emptied himself, taking the form of a slave' (Phil 2:6-7). He destroyed the powerful ones of the earth. For it is by the judgment of this God that these also undergo destruction, just as Pharaoh and Nebuchadnezzar. And God destroyed the arch-evil devil; for it is said: 'But the angels who do not obey...'

He scatters the lips of the faithful. Some think that certain words are faithful and unanswerable, and God scatters these. Without fail, it is said concerning Ahithophel, the counselor of King Israel, who was previously a counselor to David and later to Absalom; for it was said of him that the counsel of Ahithophel was like the counsel of God, and this was being circulated about him as being unsearchable in his counsels. Without fail, David, to whom the unmanifest and the hidden things of wisdom were revealed, praying to God said, 'Scatter the counsel of Ahithophel' (2 Sam 15:31), and so it happened. He recognized the understanding of the elders.

And he recognized the understanding of the elders who have instead of many [opinions] prudence and the unceasing life instead of old age; for it was worthy of his knowledge. It is appropriate to hear 'recognized' in the sense of understanding; for he also recognizes the foolish and their counsels. But it is clear how he, recognizing those things—speaking of the elders according to Abraham—accepts them. Pouring out dishonor upon rulers, but humbling the lowly. For of him who 'appoints and removes' (1 Sam 2:7), it means to grant honors in the appointing, and to pour out dishonor in the removing; and to 'pour out' signifies doing this abundantly; for many times we have observed this, as in 'the love of God is poured out in our hearts' (Rom 5:5), instead of 'has been greatly given' according to what is said; 'a myrrh emptied out [is] your name,' which became 'a wonder in all the earth' (Ps 72:15) according to the Psalmist, before this sending out the fragrance only to Judah, and later reaching all, as it is said, 'You have magnified your holy name over all.' But it also serves as a demonstration of the grace being abundantly given, 'I will pour out from my spirit upon all flesh' (Joel 2:28). Therefore he says that there will be a pouring out of dishonor upon rulers according to justice, of those being humbled by God; for he himself makes the honored dishonorable, the poor rich, and the weak strong, according to him who 'raises the poor from the earth and lifts the needy from the ash heap' (1 Sam 2:8). But if you take the lowly according to opinion and choice, he humbled them by 'making [them] into highness.'
translator_notes: True OET; Pass A ≠ Pass B. Melito skipped; never Cyril Matthew densify.

title: The Shadow of Death and Divine Wandering
english: He prevents a perceived destruction by making things appear insignificant, according to the principle of 'treating non-existent things as if they were existing.' Thus he says: 'Humble yourselves therefore under the mighty hand of God, so that he may exalt you in due time' (1 Peter 5:6). And again: 'The Lord opposes the proud, but gives grace to the humble' (James 4:6). For he brings those who have perfected the virtue of humility into the kingdom of heaven; for he is the one about whom it is said: 'And he will save the poor in spirit' (Matthew 5:3). He reveals deep things out of darkness.

Having said this, he will proceed regarding creation and providence, and regarding foreknowledge and his unchangeable nature, as well as knowing the things being done in secret. Similar to this is what is said by David: 'Lord, you have tested me and known me; you knew my seat and my rising; you understood all my thoughts from afar' (Psalm 139:2). For it is not that when I reason, you come to know my thoughts, but rather you exist as a foreknower of things, and so also of thoughts. 'Where shall I go from your spirit, or from your face where shall I flee? If I ascend to heaven, you are there; if I descend to Hades, you are there; if I take up the wings of my dawn and dwell at the limits of the sea, even there your hand will guide and your right hand will hold me fast' (Psalm 139:7-10).

But even beyond these things, he says something else in the 'I said: therefore darkness shall overpower me,' instead of 'hide me.' But even this, teaching again that the knowledge of God cannot be prevented, he says: 'The darkness shall not be darkness from you, and night shall be enlightened as the day' (Psalm 18:11). For to men, indeed, the night makes a difference from the day, but to you, O Lord, even these things are enlightened, instead of 'they become manifest'; which is also what the apostle makes manifest, saying: 'all things are naked and laid bare to the eyes of him' (Hebrews 4:13). And in Daniel it is said: 'knowing all things in the darkness, and the light is with him' (Daniel 2:22), which is our Savior, who 'enlightens every man' (John 1:9). Therefore, everything is manifest to him... and the deeds of men, those happening in secret and in darkness, he makes manifest when it is necessary. And he is also able to reveal the obscure parts of words, according to 'he will understand a parable and a dark saying' (Matthew 13:35), through enlightenment.

Having become mine in thought, he led the shadow of death into light. Now he calls the shadow of death the wickedness which is hidden and operating with deceit toward someone, as if to call the shadow of death himself. For often those operating are signified by the name of the virtue, just as the righteous is called righteousness in 'that we might become the righteousness of God in Him' (2 Cor 5:21). And the apostle, regarding those having love, indicated it by the name of love, saying: 'Love is patient, does not boast, is not rude, does not think of evil, believes all things' (1 Cor 13:4). He does not speak these things concerning the virtue, but concerning the one having the love.

Then again he selects: 'Love never fails' (1 Cor 13:8); and it is not a great thing that a virtue 'does not fail'—it is not its nature—but he speaks concerning the one established in this; for as much as anyone has of it, he is not to be lost. Therefore, if he says 'to lead the shadow of death into light', he does not mean the wickedness, but he speaks of the one operating it, according to 'for you were once darkness, but now light in the Lord' (Eph 5:8). For when they were darkness, existing in ignorance, they happened to be a shadow of death. But when he enlightened them having known them, then he led them out from the shadow of death, so that it might be said concerning them: 'as luminaries in the world' (Phil 2:15), who 'having put away the lie', which is 'darkness', 'speak the truth', which is what is light.

He is wandering nations and destroying them. Wandering is a homonym. For deception is also called wandering, and lawlessness is called wandering, according to that which is said: 'and they became wanderers among the nations' (Acts 13:41). But God does not wander in an unwholesome way in doing this, but is pulling them away from wickedness. And if he also says that 'to deliver to a reprobate mind' is wandering (2 Thess 2:11), he does not do this in an unwholesome way, as it is heard from the Lord saying: 'Behold, I will send him a delusion' (2 Thess 2:11), which is: because he turns toward evils, while caring for his salvation, God turns him away, instead of the soul prospering in evils. He turns him toward a useful wandering placed for him. In the same manner, it is said that he destroys the wicked, either by subjecting them to punishment or by destroying their vice through a turning back. Thus, God either destroys the nations by punishing them or by destroying their wickedness. So also 'to seek and...
translator_notes: True OET; Pass A ≠ Pass B. Melito skipped; never Cyril Matthew densify.

title: The distinction between medical help and malicious criticism
english: To save the lost who have come. Overthrowing nations and guiding them. Those who exercise foresight and say that God governs all things, a difference is brought forth; for some say that God governs in general, but not in particulars; and we also say this.

They also use such an example: the market-regulator, they say, exercises foresight for the city, making the crops abundant, but he does not carry out the other administration for the people of the city. And they say about a creator, that he creates the kinds of beings, but not the particulars. We also say this, hearing 'for you made me' (Ps 139:13) and 'your hands formed me and made me' (Ps 139:15) and 'before you formed me in the womb I knew you' (Jer 1:5), which they interpret regarding the manner of forming, stumbling upon this or that.

The 'overthrowing' therefore signifies this; for this is the word also applied to those inscribed in the constitution. What he says is that through the providence of God all things go well and in order, and even regarding the particulars, he does this; for this is most clearly shown from 'guiding them'. 'But not, but I will speak to the Lord, and I will contend against him, if he pleases' (Job 13:3). Having accused them as being mistaken, he says 'I will speak to the Lord', showing his own self-confidence. And 'I will contend against him' is instead of 'I will demonstrate my own position, if he wishes according to the hypothesis; for I know that he himself knows the cause of the harm'.

Similar to this is 'Do I now persuade men or God?' (Job 13:15) and 'The one who judges me is the Lord' (Job 19:25). It is not small, but perfect, and as God testified in the beginning 'righteous and blameless' (Gen 2:4), so to say 'I will speak to the Lord' and 'I will contend against him, if he pleases' is perfect. For apart from his will to do such a thing, which is not lawful. And you are all unjust physicians and healers of evils. An unjust physician is according to...

The readily available other aids are brought to those suffering, according to what is useful. This happens in two ways: either from the physician's abundance of resources or from ill-will. These ones who were rebuking Job said to him, more out of ignorance than out of malice, 'You suffer because of sins,' thinking they were bringing words of consolation; they were therefore unjust because they were ignorant of the cause. As for 'all are physicians of evils,' this might be said regarding those who think highly of themselves, as if they were able to heal what is happening to others by chance.

May you be struck deaf, and may it result for you in wisdom. He prays that they might have knowledge of the seasons, when it is necessary to speak and when it is necessary to be silent, having recognized that they stumble; for this shall be to them a beginning and a precursor of wisdom. For if they would learn that it is also possible to be afflicted in a different way in order that the present virtue might be revealed, wisdom shall be to them.

[Textual gaps] ... as it is said in Proverbs: 'To a fool asking for wisdom, wisdom shall be reckoned.' For when anyone recognizes that there is need of students and of a teacher who enlightens, it shall result to him in wisdom. Just as he who is able to speak about wisdom and to teach is wise and a teacher, so also he who is able to ask what ought to be asked is in part wise. He called him 'foolish' not as being entirely lacking, but as having something lacking. Similar to 'may you be struck deaf' is 'the season to be silent'—and 'the season to speak.' 'Hear the rebuke of my mouth, and pay attention to the judgment of my lips.' He says mouth and lips instead of the word. But the holy one rebukes as holy and judges as becomes Him; he uses rebuke and judgment skillfully and legally; for the righteous does not have an untimely rebuke, nor does he do this falsely, but having judged. 'For the mouth of the righteous shall meditate on wisdom, and his tongue shall speak judgment. The law of God is in his heart, and...
translator_notes: True OET; Pass A ≠ Pass B. Melito skipped; never Cyril Matthew densify.

title: The Judge's Impartiality and the Conscience
english: "His steps will not be made to slip." (Prov 4:26). For the law of God is in the heart of the righteous; he meditates on wisdom and his steps are not made to slip, which are "the walking powers of the soul." Such a thing also the saying of Proverbs means, "the judgments of the thoughts of the righteous" (Prov 20:27). And when such thoughts exist, the word follows to be like this: "for the good man brings forth good out of the good treasure of the heart" (Luke 6:45). Whether you speak not in the presence of the Lord, and speak deceit toward him, or whether you shrink back? From their own conscience he begins to teach them by reproof, that whatever they bring forth, seeing God, they speak; but he also announces to them the deceit as being brought forth in his presence for the sake of correction, so that they might cease from such a disposition, since they have the Lord watching over them. And therefore he prevents their audacity, because just as they shrank back from a man, hiding deceit and speaking against him, [so they do to God].

The words are useful against those who lie and use deceit, concerning which also David says: "of those speaking peace with their neighbors, but evil in their hearts" (Ps 55:21). But you yourselves become judges. It is well, if it searches you out. If anyone says: "How is it that he just said 'you are unjust doctors' (Matt 23:27) and 'whether you speak not in the presence of the Lord, and speak deceit toward him'" and now says: "but you yourselves become judges"? To this it must be said: that each of those sinning, being enticed by pleasure, does not perceive the eye of the God who watches. But if a righteous and wise man, or even another such, is called, the conscience of the sinner leads him to the realization that God sees the inward thoughts of each, striking him into perception. This is therefore what the saint does, saying: "but you yourselves become judges. It is well, if it searches you out." For those being conscious of a slip do not wish to be searched out even by a righteous man, how much less by God; for of the saints it is such, according to David saying: "refine my reins and my heart" (Ps 51:10). For if, doing all things, you are placed before him, nothing less will convict you. Even if the...

“Having done all things that must be done, you shall be added to him”—instead of “you shall make yourselves his own”—“you shall again be subject to reproof through ignorances.” This indeed the blessed apostle was saying: “I do not consider myself my own conscience, but not in this have I been justified” (cf. 1 Cor 4:4). For it enters into me to overlook something of the ignorances, and I have not been justified because of that. And as far as I think I have no conscience against myself, I think I am without responsibility. But it is not my judgment that shows me having been justified, but the judgment of God.

The blessed David also confirms this, saying: “Who will understand trespasses? From my secret parts cleanse me” (Ps 51:2). For in truth, someone recognizes sins, but trespasses, which in a certain way are unintentional, someone hardly understands. “And if therefore,” he says, “you do all things toward purity, from the unintentional things, as from God judging, you shall have the reproof.” Through which also the Lord said to his own disciples: “When you have done all things, say: we are unprofitable slaves, what we ought to do, we have done” (Luke 17:10).

And if even in secret you should admire faces, whether not his agitation will trouble you, and fear will fall upon you from him? The best judge of matters is the examiner; he does not look toward the faces of those being judged. For if those being judged were rich or rulers or others possessing superior value, he does not look toward their face, but toward the actions, which he judges. This also is carried forward in the Catholic Epistle: “admiring faces for the sake of advantage” (Jas 2:9), and it is clear that the flatterers are justifying the ungodly because of gifts and removing the justice of the just. But God, standing as protector, does not will thus, but lays down law: “according to the great and the small you will judge, you will not receive a face,” clearly of the rich, and “you will not have mercy on the poor in judgment” (Deut 10:17). And it is said elsewhere: “justly let the just pursue the just.”

For it is not necessary to add to the rich, nor should the poor, pitying his need, overlook the just. And it becomes the work of a righteous judge, just as it is handed down in the history concerning David, so that after the judgments and outcomes of matters, if it should happen that the poor is there, or one who has ignored the just, or one acting unjustly, the rich man is exhorted so that he might show philanthropy toward him. And the righteousness of the judge will be more ready for this.
translator_notes: True OET; Pass A ≠ Pass B. Melito skipped; never Cyril Matthew densify.

title: The Purpose of Sin's Ashes and the Body's Nature
english: Accepting. Thus indeed it is said concerning David: 'doing judgment and justice' (Ps 72:2). ... Job ... 'if you also marvel at faces in secret' (Job 27:19); for every bribetaker does not accept the things of those providing from the visible, but in secret, often also in a disguised manner, according to that, he wishes to come together. And he brings fear, saying that if someone dares to hide the thing of partiality by craft, but God, being angry through the onslaught against the sinners, will shake them, instead of 'he will let the passion be provided to them.'

He says the onslaught with the impulse of passion is like the movement of the swirling waters according to the dawnings, so that what he says briefly is such: 'do you bring his movement, if he is indignant?' Similar to this is what is brought in Zechariah, said to the sinners: 'the Lord shall go in the whirlwind of his wrath' (Zech 9:4). And the whirlwind of wrath signifies the anger because of their sins, for he himself is ... The 'shall go' might perhaps be similar to that said in Genesis concerning Adam, that he heard God walking just as he was sinning (Gen 3:8); through this he receives a sensation of the departure of God because he no longer has anything luminous in himself. For those lengthening themselves from God hear: 'the Lord is far from the ungodly' (Ps 144:5), not in place of this being said, but in distancing the one being good and the one being bad from Him. And these things are because of the 'shall go in the whirlwind.'

Let us return to the beginning, to those 'marveling at faces in secret,' whom also the anger of God according to a whirlwind will shake, as it was given; and upon them also fear falls from God, and this is for benefit, so that they may know that a threat is brought against them as sinners. And of this fear, which I say according to the threat, is another by which it is said: 'the fear of the Lord surpassed all' (Ps 112:7), which is primarily reverence. For there is no other fear of God or heightened respect, through which those having it become lacking; 'for there is no deficiency to those fearing him' (Ps 115:11). But the passive fear follows the sinners. For another of this kind is said to be sent upon sinners for punishment; observe...

Otherwise, it signifies nothing else through the name of fear or the avoidance of wrath. This is not a passion of God; for it is said, 'I sent away the wrath' (Ps 106:42/implied); a passion is not sent away. But your boasting shall pass away like ashes. The word shows the state after the wrath of those sinning, being brought to nothing in the revelation occurring through the wrath, the conceit of those judging secretly being consumed.

Since ashes signify worthlessness, it is to be learned from one of the twelve prophets saying, 'And you shall trample down the lawless and they shall be as ashes under your feet' (cf. Zephaniah/Prophetic imagery). For ashes are something burning that has lost its own power. Indeed, a threat regarding burning is brought in Deuteronomy, as through the fruits being hindered because the land has lost its own power. And it is for some benefit that sins are burned up; just as thorns and thistles, being burned, do not bring a little harm, so also the sins—even if they are burned according to what is said, 'the lawlessness shall be burned like fire and shall be consumed by fire like dry stubble' (Matt 13:40)—they no longer defile the soul, but are called out toward repentance according to what is said in the Gospel: 'If the powers that happened in you had occurred in Tyre and Sidon, long ago, sitting in sackcloth and ashes, they would have repented' (Matt 11:21).

For if anyone receives in his mind the salvation-fire, about which the Savior said, 'I came to cast fire upon the earth, and what do I want, if it is already kindled' (Luke 12:49), he burns up the former sins; and sitting, instead of 'having ceased from sinning,' he is turned toward repentance, choosing a somewhat severe and rigorous life. But the body is clay. Man is composed of soul and body. And there is a time when the body is led away as a slave by the soul and, in a certain way, is no longer being treated as clay, but being a servant to the soul along with reason and with the mind acting.

But when someone cares for nothing of his salvation, his soul, turning toward wickedness and serving the flesh, doing such things as do not differ from an irrational animal, he shows that his body is clay, as nothing helping from the soul's movements. For the body is something distinct from the soul, as the Savior himself taught, saying:
translator_notes: True OET; Pass A ≠ Pass B. Melito skipped; never Cyril Matthew densify.

title: The Metaphor of Teeth and the Soul
english: “Do not fear those who kill the body, but are not able to kill the soul.” Since they are able to kill the body of a man, but not the soul, it is clear that the same essence is not of soul and body. Therefore, when the soul is hindered from its own and natural impulses, then the man appears as a body of clay, not because the soul is changing into a body, but because its actions are no longer heavenly, but bodily; just as Paul calls “those walking according to the flesh” (1 Cor 3:3) and “according to man” men, saying they have human qualities and not divine energy.

For it is said by the blessed Paul to all those who have devoted themselves to the bodily and because of this are being human in mind: “For where is strife among you, are you not carnal and walking according to man?” (1 Cor 3:3). But when “walking upon the earth they have their citizenship in heaven” (Phil 3:20) and “bear the image of the heavenly” (2 Cor 4:4), they are not a body of clay. “You have made me deaf, so that I may speak and rest my spirit.” He says this, urging them to recognize those coming against them, shifting the cause to the saying “and rest my spirit,” instructing that if they might chance to be corrected from the state of being divided, his spirit—which he had rightfully been angry against their iniquity, not passionably, but as the law is laid down to be angry against sinners—would rest.

And the name of deafness signifies silence, as in “I was deaf and I did not open my mouth, because you are the one who made me” (Ps 31:9). For he says that not speaking is deafness. And again: “When the sinner stood against me, I was deaf and I was humbled, and he was silent from good things.” For when the sinner, who is the devil, having persuaded the soul to sin before it, reproaching it as “an enemy existing and an avenger,” then the soul, feeling shame, receives silence as deafness. Therefore he says, “hold your peace,” so that through the same, instruction might be born in them. Taking up my flesh for those who travel, he in a way gives them a respite. Since he himself had previously accused them as being “accusers of evils”—for they were not calling [to prayer] as they ought, but rather were stirring up grief and the...
Regarding what is being asked of him, he says: 'I take up my flesh to the teeth,' I am no longer angry against you, but against myself. Let the name of the flesh be thus smoothed over.

For often, when someone wishes to report a crushing having happened to himself, he remembers the flesh according to what is said: 'when those doing evil to me approach to eat my flesh,' (Job 2:10) instead of 'to harm me'; for it was not his flesh they were eating under the skin, but they were distressing him. Similar to this is the 'so that while living they would devour us,' which shows the aggressive action of those who force.

One might say: 'I take up my flesh to the teeth. Thus I nourish my teeth. And just as food being taken up to the teeth is thinned and its usefulness is shown, so also, nourishing my teeth and receiving the increase of benefit from the harms of these, I proceed.' But if he shows endurance through saying 'having taken up the flesh to the teeth' instead of 'not caring for the harm,' consider this.

I will place my soul in hand, if the powerful one should strike me, since he has also lifted [the hand]. In agreement with the 'having taken up my flesh to the teeth,' one should also strike upon the 'I will place my soul in hand,' so that he is saying: 'and I also despise my own soul, being subject to the one striking me and having already been subjected to this, in order to benefit you in some way,' thereby declaring the God who has consented with the one asking him. 'I am therefore ready to be given over to death.'

But if he says this regarding the change that is about to be, it is worthy of the one understanding to observe: 'since he has also lifted' does not contradict, calling God good because he rescues from those who afflict; 'I will indeed speak and convict against him,' and this will result for me in salvation. In all things, his zeal is to instruct the friends concerning the cause of the oppressors, so that he might win them over not to think against him.

For he reckoned this as salvation, to know this and the account of the providence concerning this, which he wished to make manifest by saying 'and I will convict'; for often the conviction signifies the proof, just as Paul says: 'all things being convicted are made manifest by the light,' (Eph 5:13) and again 'faith is of the things hoped for.' (Heb 11:1)
translator_notes: True OET; Pass A ≠ Pass B. Melito skipped; never Cyril Matthew densify.

title: The Purpose of Divine Discipline
english: He uses 'subsistence, the demonstration of things unseen' instead of 'proof.' For no deceit will enter against Him. Desiring to present its truthfulness and its reverence, he says: 'What I say, I speak as one seeing God. For it is not possible for any deception to occur to God, as to let deceit enter before Him.' This, however, could be understood in two ways according to the similar parallel, which is thus essentially evangelical: 'And the light shines in the darkness, and the darkness did not overcome it' (John 1:5). For that which is overshadowing is released by the presence of the light, or whatever approaches as a deception near the light is turned away; when the deception is released, it does not grasp at all. For all those who deceive and scheme are ignorant in their zeal; for the beauty of the truth they shall not grasp. Thus, deceit does not approach the spring of truth because those using it do not dare to bring it to itself. And in another way, there is no deceit in God; for it is not His nature to be in Him. 'For God is faithful, and there is no injustice in Him' (1 Cor 4:3). And again: 'If we are faithless, He remains faithful' (2 Tim 2:13). For He is unshakeable and unchangeable.

Hear, hear my words; for I announce them to you as you are listening. The word repeats, so that He might call them firmly to listen. For it is possible for the hearing to be struck by the voice without having heard, because of not paying attention with the mind. Therefore, the Savior, awakening those listening so that they might listen truly, said: 'He who has ears to hear, let him hear' (Matt 13:9). And again, to others not paying attention, He says: 'Neither His voice have you heard, nor His appearance have you seen' (John 12:38), and interpreting how it proceeds: 'Nor do you have His word remaining in you,' which happened if they were listening truly. Thus also the blessed Job, desiring to prepare their hearing, said the 'Hear'; for as He says, 'since you have been prepared, I am pleased to speak,' desiring them to become wise listeners: 'an ear...'

But the desire of a wise man is to listen. 'Behold, I am near to my judgment' (Job 42:6). This is the beginning of instruction for them, and now it is being cast down as a discipline, because he has been judged to suffer not because of sin, but because of a struggle, so as to know the time according to which the judgment will end. I know that I shall be revealed as righteous.

For who is the one to be judged by me, saying, 'That I will now deafen and exclude [him]'? He does not say this out of arrogance, but to discipline them so that they may not have any impression concerning him other than the truth. For when someone speaks well of himself without intending to do this, when another is determined concerning him to do otherwise. For if someone has a certain service at hand to fulfill for those in need, and if he slanders it as if it were being struck away, we would not blame in a defense one saying, 'I am providing all our things to those in need,' if he had not said this previously.

In this way, do not blame Job for self-love, but because of the stated reason he says these things and says them with pure boldness: 'Who is he that will be judged by me so that I may deafen,' instead of 'I will be silent' (Job 7:25), 'and exclude,' instead of 'I will cease speaking.' It will be necessary for me to die: 'Then from your face I will hide; withhold your hand from me, and let your fear not terrify me' (Job 13:24).

The ambiguity of the things foretold would be smoothed out by him saying, 'If as the friends say, it will be necessary for me to do this, showing it as trivial, "from your face I will hide"; but if as I say, "withhold your hand from me and let your fear not terrify me".' 'For every one who sins, working unworthily, is hidden from the face of God,' just as Adam was hidden from the face of God. Contrary to this is being hidden by God according to what is said: 'You will hide them in the secrecy of your face from the disturbance of men' (Psalm 32:3). This too covers the earnest one with God's protection, so that he may not fall by human disturbances. But the secrecy of the face...
translator_notes: True OET; Pass A ≠ Pass B. Melito skipped; never Cyril Matthew densify.

title: Job's perception of God's hiddenness and the friends' judgment
english: The divine mysteries would be distinguished from what is manifest. For it is not possible to see God in secret through the works of providence and the created things, but in the manifest. It has been said: 'because the known of God is manifest in them; for God has revealed himself to them. For his invisible things, understood from the creation of the world through the works, are seen' (Rom 1:20). Therefore, to be hidden by God is salvation, but to be hidden according to Adam is useless, which he says does not happen because of the non-existence of sin: 'withhold your hand from me' (Job 13:14) and the following, 'that these may be instructed, that they may not suffer this because of sin (Job 13:15). For the friends did not intend anything other than that he suffers because of sin (Job 13:15). Then you will call, and I will answer you; or you will speak, and I will give you a reply (Job 36:23).' Through many things he makes known his boldness toward God, so that in this he might lead them into the true knowledge of what is happening concerning him. And this is a proof of him being righteous.

And you have this also concerning the priest Moses, being made worthy to speak to him in 'Moses spoke and God answered him with a voice' (Exod 3:9). But the answer occurring toward God should not be thought to be a bare voice, but a divine energy, through which he speaks pleasantly toward God. 'How many are my sins and my lawlessness? Teach me, what they are' (Ps 51:5). Again through them he says such things, so that they may learn that the one having sin and lawlessness has not known God. And he himself, having said 'I know that I shall appear righteous' to the friends, speaks reverently toward God saying, 'Teach me, how many are my sins' (Ps 51:5). Similar to this is 'I know nothing about myself, but I am not justified by this; the one judging me is the Lord' (1 Cor 4:3). And it is good also to learn mistakes, so that from these we may turn away.

'Why do you hide from me, and consider me your adversary?' (Job 13:22) And this is toward their misunderstanding; for God dwelling in him was not hidden from him, but because of them thinking this, these things were said. 'For these think that you are against me, supposing that I suffer because of sin (Job 13:23).' Or, like a leaf moved by the wind, or like grass carried by the spirit, you have opposed me.

Regarding me, the whole of the understanding would be thus: 'Why do you hide me, supposing me to be against you, like a leaf moved by the wind and grass carried by the spirit?' This turns out to be characteristic of a changeable manner and fickleness, according to that which is said by the Savior concerning John: 'Why did you go into the wilderness to see? A reed shaken by the wind?' (Matt 3:7)—instead of 'something easily dismissed and falling by chance.' These things, as previously said, Job says toward the dispute of the friends.

‘That you have recorded evils against me, and you have left for me the sins of youth.’ It is clear that he speaks toward their assumption; for now he says 'evils' regarding the afflictions. For the friends, supposing that he suffers through sin, he himself joined to 'you have recorded evils against me' the 'you have left for me the sins of youth,' meaning that 'from which my friends, running against me, judge me to be suffering through sin, they have the following following: to suppose that the sins of youth have been left around me now.'

'You put my foot in mire.' He does not say these things according to his own will, but toward the one supposing that every one being afflicted undergoes this. Being smoothed out, it would be thus: 'The power of my walking, by which I act rightly, was understood differently by them as being of my sinning, and because of this, by participating in tribulations, you placed [it] in mire.' For he himself acted in a certain way, giving it out to the one asking, from which it happened that his foot was placed in mire, being prevented by them, as it is said, from sins, not wanting their the progress of the righteous, which is the ability to perceive correctly.

For since you are accustomed to the Scripture and to those things established from opinion to say that the one acting speaks as if from God because of the agreement, it will be clear to you from 'God handed them over to sufferings of dishonor' (Rom 1:28) and 'to a reprobate mind' (Rom 1:28) and 'the desires of their hearts' (Rom 1:28). If even through the total affliction he could no longer perform for himself the things toward the needs or the requirements or other things—as he also has said—'but my door stands open to everyone coming'—he was saying this, realize, which he did not ignore because it had happened to him through struggle. For many such things God does because of the benefit, as from...
translator_notes: True OET; Pass A ≠ Pass B. Melito skipped; never Cyril Matthew densify.

title: The brevity of life and the purpose of suffering
english: It is to be learned concerning his people, whom God led through the wilderness usefully for three days, so that they might not adopt a hasty return to Egypt. And understand, lest even the communion toward the body be seen as a burden and becoming a secret thing through economy, this being said as the extreme purity is not being completed.

And this again is for some reason; for not us, and not God are to be blamed. 'You have guarded all my works' (Ps 32:8). The blessed one knows what was said by David, being holy, that God does not observe all the iniquities of the birds, but training them again, through which reason they suffer—that is, through struggle—the one preceding has said as, having guarded all his works, and thus leading him to the 90, so that from this they might understand that the greatness of so many leadings is not because of sin, but because of struggle and a goal of manliness.

The 'you have guarded' here is not instead of 'you kept,' but 'you will have observed.' And if even he says of his own 'sins of youth' and provides the 'you have guarded all my works' as having sinned, it is not to be wondered at; for all the saints, for the sake of moderation and of good-mindedness, offer such voices, just as the men in the furnace and the blessed David saying: 'Do not remember the sins of my youth and my ignorances' (Ps 103:3). 'You have reached to the roots of my feet.' Instead of 'you have made all that is concerning me so exact as the roots, that is, both the reasons and the beginnings of my practical progressions, to observe so that you might lead me to punishments.' And this again he says according to their assumption.

That which grows old is equal to an ascetic or like a garment of coarse linen. 'Of those,' he says, 'you remembered the sins that have grown old like an ascetic.' But an ascetic having grown old is inactive toward the need for which he was prepared; for he does not hold the liquids being poured in. So also the sins of youth have grown old and, like a garment of coarse linen, no longer provide the need. But sins grow old when they are worn away by virtue; for when being practiced they are always made young, even if the one practicing them is long-lived, he himself being called newer from the character of the one making things new. But a mortal, born of woman, is short-lived and full of wrath. He wills for them...

He presents the cause of his suffering by joining together the weight of the temptation and human life; for having examined that 'you have laid the sins of my youth upon me' (Ps 38:5) and 'all my works you have guarded' (Ps 38:5), as if you had sent so many to me, he brings forward as a supporting argument for the matter not being so, 'but man born of woman is short-lived and full of wrath' (Ps 88:5). Because of the hardship of life, he would not have brought such punishment upon the short-lived and full of wrath, unless he had encountered it for the sake of a struggle. For if the goodness of God and the brevity of men's lives had coincided, these things would not still have been reckoned as having happened because of sin.

But consider, lest he also have such a mind; the one who has not become God through virtue, but remains in the human condition, he is in wrath and is short-lived in a certain way, 'in this life alone, hoping.' But the one believing in the Savior so as to become God, he is not subject to punishment through wrath, even if he is afflicted, the affliction being called wrath in another way. He says therefore, 'if I also lived according to man, observe, so that from this you may judge, that I fell through wrath.' Or, just as a flower bloomed and fell away, and a shadow that will not stand. These things are to be joined with those before them.

That for the passing man, like a flower and a shadow, such evils were brought upon him, it is not according to the present [context] because of sins. 'For if he observes iniquities, Lord, Lord, who shall stand? But with you is the atonement' (Ps 143:2). So it was to be understood by the friends, that not because of mistakes, but as is foretold, because he was set before the goal of manliness, these things happened to him. And these things, first, according to a first thought.

But according to a second, it would be said thus: as a flower falls, 'he who walks according to the flesh' (Gal 5:25), and as a shadow, resembling an accompaniment and doing nothing previously. For since the shadow is received instead of the unsubstantial, it is shown by 'my days pass away like a shadow' (Ps 144:4). Will I not also make a point of this, and that you made this to enter into judgment before you? In agreement with the former response, someone might be, joining these things thus: 'if even the one born of woman is short-lived and filled with toil, so as to resemble one fallen like a flower and a shadow that flees quickly,'
translator_notes: True OET; Pass A ≠ Pass B. Melito skipped; never Cyril Matthew densify.

title: The Measure of Life and Divine Providence
english: But indeed I have composed a discourse of this, not bypassing it so as to let it enter into judgment before you. A proof of this would be what is said toward God: 'My people, what have I done to you?' (Exodus 32:9) and again, 'Behold, I am being judged against you.' For God, bringing in such a care concerning men, would not have demanded justice from man so unyieldingly and absolutely, as his friends suspected him of punishing.

These things he brings forward as a defense, so that he does not suffer otherwise than for it to appear just according to: 'Do I suppose I have dealt with you differently, so that you should appear righteous?' (Job 13:15) For who is clean from filth? Not even one, even if his life on the earth be but one day, and his months be numbered before you. And he joined these things together so that they might understand that he does not suffer because of sin. For if it were so, no one would be without trouble, even if he lived for a short time.

And these things [are for] how the friends might be instructed in the cause; for if an objection were to be said against what was spoken of him, he said this, saying something standing in place: 'For even if you are short-lived and passing like a shadow (Psalm 103:15) and falling like a flower, it does not prevent you from suffering because of sin.' To which he most directly said: 'For who is clean from filth? But no one,' so that it was necessary for all, as has already been said, to suffer. And filth and sin, someone else might say, signify the same thing, with the one saying the filth of sin as something lesser of the other.

You have concerning filth and sin in Isaiah thus: 'The Lord will wash away the filth of the sons and the daughters of Zion, and will cleanse the blood from their midst' (Isaiah 1:16), the blood signifying sin there, the unclean thing, and the filth the unintentional [acts], which the Savior, having come, cleansed by himself. For because blood often signifies sin, it is said toward the ancient evil devil: 'In whatever way a garment stained with blood is not to be clean, in the same way you will not be clean.' For he did not happen to be stained with blood, but it is clear that the blood signifies to him the 'sin unto death.' Therefore, the one having a fault capable of being washed has filth, but the one [is] as if unrepentant, like the one 'having blasphemed against the Holy Spirit' (Matthew 12:31) and the like, is not under filth, but sin, and the one transgressing the commandments with [the intent] of knowing.

And 'neither is the life of the one on earth even a single day' can be interpreted in two ways. There is the one being born now who has the sin of Adam by succession, who is the one beginning to judge things by the word, when he also fulfills the word of man. Nor will such a person be purified in a day, because ignorance remains for the one who has also begun now to distinguish the false from the good, even if he lives for a day, even if he lives for a numbered number of months.

The worthless one is 'blotted out from the book of the living' (Ps 69:28) and is not numbered by God, but the diligent one is numbered by Him. 'If, therefore, he assumes such a thing,' he says, 'even this one has not been kept from filth' (Job 7:10). Similar to this is 'I have no conscience against myself, but I am not justified by this' and 'Cleanse me from my secret sins' (Ps 51:2). For he has habituated himself to a time and will not exceed it.

The providence concerning man is made clear here, not as if it remains in life as it happens and as it pleases, but from the judgment of God, not exceeding the time appointed by Him. And these things are not to be said as being held by fate, but as the will of God, 'having appointed each thing by limits and measures.' And if he speaks allegorically that the one being led by God in a certain way does not exceed his duties because virtue is measured, consider this.

Depart from Him, so that he may be at rest and find the life well-pleasing like the laborer. Since God is present to him through providences, the 'depart' has been said instead of 'cease your anger.' For approaching God is different: that by participation and that by anger. For they suppose that he suffers through the sins of friends, and having spoken so harshly of those things passing away—that 'man is short-lived' (Job 14:2), 'like a falling flower' (Job 14:2), 'like a shadow' (Job 14:2), and as if 'God makes his word'—showing them that he is not brought low through sin, he says 'depart from Him.'

For if he imposes such a multitude of afflictions upon him, man has no opportunity for repentance. He instructs them, therefore, that they do not understand this sensibly, through 'depart from Him, so that he may be at rest.' For he is not able to bring about an opportunity or to find the life well-pleasing after so many circumstances—so that he may give as a wage to the worker. Otherwise, he alludes differently: if he suffered through sin, it would be sufficient.
translator_notes: True OET; Pass A ≠ Pass B. Melito skipped; never Cyril Matthew densify.

title: The Purpose of Reproof and the Metaphor of the Tree
english: The reproofs were intended so that from this stillness might come, and that he might work the remainder like a hired laborer. But these things are said again to them as it becomes manifest that God gives tolerance for the sake of repentance, as Paul says: 'Or do you despise his tolerance and patience, not knowing that the goodness of God leads you to repentance?' (Rom 2:4). For it is said that to be still—meaning to cease from evil and to take up virtue—is clearly shown by the words, 'You sinned, be still,' and by 'The earth feared and he was still when God arose to judgment.' For men, having grasped the notion that God is judge, were still from sinning.

For there is hope in a tree; if it is cut off, even so its shoot shall sprout again and its branch shall by no means fail. Through many things he demonstrates that he did not endure the pains because of worthlessness, as the meaning of the word becomes clear: 'Let this be so by hypothesis: the lashings have been sufficient as it is the time to depart.' For neither are the things of repentance rejected, nor does God, as if the will were unchangeable, punish without measure. For there is a fitness in the souls, even if a great pouring out of punishments occurs; therefore, repentance can come to pass.

And he calls the man a tree, as is also said in many places of the Scriptures: 'Already the axe lies at the root of the trees; every tree not producing a good fruit is cut down and is thrown into the fire' (Matt 3:10). And again: 'Either make the tree good and its fruits good, or make the tree rotten and its fruits rotten' (Luke 6:43). Having set this aside once, we shall not leave it unexamined. For the Savior does not command that one should become a rotten tree or bring forth rotten fruit, but that the state of each one be manifest through their actions, and not to prefer the hypocrisy of this. And there is also another way to understand this: the Jews were saying concerning the Savior: 'By Beelzebub, the ruler of the demons, he casts out...'
from the scent of water
translator_notes: True OET; Pass A ≠ Pass B. Melito skipped; never Cyril Matthew densify.

title: The Freedom of the Savior in Hades
english: so that from this there might come rest

He was excessively liberated, from the more excellent staying and guarding in Hades—not according to punishments, but regarding the guarding... being hidden there, 'until the wrath passes' (Rom 13:10), as it is being said of God to remember him, in order to say more clearly that he would rather receive the time of his resurrection in Hades than undergo so many pains.

For indeed, he who truly experiences in Hades according to each one, the righteous man lives better during the time before the coming of Christ, since he is about to be liberated from the clamorous and sickly body to enjoy the incorruptible. For the Savior, according to the human, was not subject to being in Hades, even if it happened there through others. For it has been said of himself: 'I became as a helpless man among the dead, yet free' (Acts 2:24). And indeed, angels lead the holy ones, but the wicked ones, the shadows. But the Savior, being free, did not need angels, being master of them and being ministered to and led by them. For he said: 'No one takes my soul from me, but I lay it down myself' (John 10:18).

But also in the Song of Songs, through symbols, he says he is smelling the myrrh of death, showing himself free: 'I will go my own way to the mountain of myrrh' (Song 1:4). And also 'there is no man of the nations with me' (Song 1:5) shows his unattached state according to the human. Instead of this, another interprets 'I alone shall drink the wine-cup.' But also, when Peter says: 'I will lay down my soul for you,' he rebukes him, saying: 'You will lay down your soul for me? Before the cock crows, you will deny me three times' (Matt 26:34).

Because the holy ones are led by light-bringing angels and the wicked ones by dark demons, it has been said: 'O fool, in this night take your soul from you,' implying they are punished. And concerning Lazarus it is said: 'It happened when the poor man died, he was carried by the angels to Abraham's bosom' (Luke 16:22), clearly by good angels. For if a man dies, he will live having completed the days of his life. Not unsuitably, being persuaded and knowing concerning the resurrection of the dead, he places the more excellent deliverance from the painful life here, that it is more beautiful 'to be dissolved and to be with Christ' (Phil 1:23), saying: 'for if...'
translator_notes: True OET; Pass A ≠ Pass B. Melito skipped; never Cyril Matthew densify.

title: Resurrection as a New Birth
english: "If a man dies, he shall live having completed the days of his life" (Job 14:14), from which a doctrine concerning resurrection is presented and a judgment of each life in this life, not occurring randomly or by chance when death happens. And even if "having completed the days of his life" can signify the days before the resurrection, consider also that which the eternal life shall receive: "I will wait, until I become again."

In the same sequence of words, and the opinions of those previously arguing against him, are placed alongside the true ones, so that while they lie parallel, we may see which are being dismantled and which are being constructed. For he was saying, regarding their erroneous opinion: "but a man having fallen asleep shall not rise" and "a man having ended his life has gone, and a fallen mortal is no longer." For the nature of man did not have it as they thought, that having possessed subsistence until the present life, having cast off this life, he is no longer, just like the irrational animals.

For the souls of irrational animals are scattered with their bodies, and therefore they are destroyed. But since the [nature] of man is not scattered, nor is he destroyed; for he is immortal. And since the friends did not depart, as it happens through painful struggle just as it happened to him the blessed one, considering that he suffers because of sin, opposing their opinion, he says the calculation that to bear the painful things is to become again. "I will wait," for he says, "until I become again," signifying the resurrection, which those saying [he is] being destroyed do not accept, [some] placing the nature of [the soul]... but the "I will wait, until I become again" [is part] of "if a man dies, he shall live having completed the days of his life."

Possessing this presupposition, the blessed Paul also wrote: "if in this life we hope only, we are more to be pitied than all men" (1 Cor 15:19) and "if I have fought as a wild beast against men in Ephesus, what is my profit, if the dead are not raised?" (1 Cor 15:32) Thus, not setting aside the opinion of the friends, that it is through virtue to suffer, the [saying] "but a man having fallen asleep shall not rise" was said...

But 'I will respond to you when you call again' stands in opposition to the opinion of those who mock: 'Let us eat and drink, for tomorrow we die' (Isa 22:13). The phrase 'until I become again' must be explained in this way: resurrection is a kind of birth. For this reason, 're-birth' is spoken in relation to the Savior. For the former birth, having a different manner, consisted by the change of matter, either as dust in the first maker, or as the side as in the Eve of the seeds as in those born, or by a virgin turning something of herself into the salvific womb, such being the change. Thus also of the resurrection, whether it is a transfer into the dust of the body, or into something else according to these changes, the rising body is raised incorruptible. It is, therefore, a birth.

Then 'you will call, and I will respond to you.' Wishing to show that not only the body is raised, but also the soul possessing the thoughts concerning God, he says, 'you will call, and I will respond to you.' For to listen to God calling is proper to a rational being. 'Do not cast away the works of your hands' (Ps 31:5). Having taught concerning the resurrection of the whole human and the immortality of the soul, he instructs his friends so as not to consider him judged as insignificant by God. 'You have enumerated my faults to me, and you will not pass over any of my sins' (Ps 32:5). Teaching an unerasable knowledge of him, through these things he also in a certain way instructs his friends who are at odds, that through sin he suffers, how he must repent and not be arrogant regarding the purity existing within him, for the sake of moderation toward himself and toward them, raising them to repentance by saying these things. 'I will note if I have passed by unintentionally' (Ps 51:6). As if speaking to them again, he says these things while they are at odds, as if he were undergoing these things as a sinner, and by moderation and for their instruction, so that they might imitate him being so pure and bringing forth words of repentance. 'You have sealed my iniquities in a bag' (Ps 51:6). That is to say: 'You have included in them both the quality and the number.' And it is necessary to perceive these things also, similar to the former. And besides, a falling mountain will fall. Believing in the cause of all things, that he will complete the contest.
translator_notes: True OET; Pass A ≠ Pass B. Melito skipped; never Cyril Matthew densify.

title: Divine Rejection and the Sinner's Delusion
english: Having crushed the one who requested the mountain called here, he says to them that 'he will weaken so as to fall from the expectation which he expected, trying to see me.' For indeed all request, as it is foretold, but they do not know that the purpose of the opponent will fall away. And the rock will be made old from its place. Even if the opponent thinks himself to be the rock, 'it will be made old'—instead of 'a stumbling block shall be seen'—signifying the appearance of correctness.

And the rock is mentioned because it sends out the impression as unshakeable, and because Christ is being formed and is an imitator of the true rock, concerning which it was said: 'And the rock was Christ' (1 Cor 10:4). And he calls the state here a place, according to which the virtuous man wishes to see. Since the place is also called a step, it is said in the Acts: 'Master, Knower of hearts, reveal one to take the place of this ministry from which Judas passed' (Acts 1:20).

And even after saying that 'you sealed my iniquities in a bag' (Ps 69:6) and how regarding his own sin he had brought forward the previously set forth things, he applied 'but the mountain falling shall fall, and the rock shall be made old from its place' (Job 14:10) to show that 'even if a mountain arises through pride or through hardness, its condemnation shall be,' having perceived this. Waters smoothed the stones, and waters overwhelmed the depths of the earth's soil; and did you destroy the endurance of man? He confirms through these things the previously spoken, that repentance is powerful.

For through 'waters smoothed the stones' (Job 14:11), he demonstrates that the one beginning to repent, persisting in this, according to the water which removes the excess from the stone, frees himself from the superfluities of sin, as if no longer having the roughness from it, and just as lying in the depths of soils, he works the flood of sin. 'If these things have this manner, do not recognize the endurance of man, nor say that this is destroyed when it has worn him down and gone to an end.' He moves the word toward God. For after saying that repentance is possible and that one must not lose hope in man, he brings the 'having worn him down and gone to an end' as an instruction, that unless God is a co-worker, the things of endurance are in vain. 'If...

For unless the Lord builds the house, they labor in vain who build it (Ps 127:1). God does not push away the worthy person, but the one positioned in such a way, saying: 'Depart from me, workers of iniquity, I never knew you' (Matt 7:23). He turns His face away and drives them out.

It is said: 'The face of the Lord is against those doing evil' (Ps 2:5); and again the saints pray: 'Let your face shine and we shall be saved' (Ps 67:1); and in others: 'May His face shine upon you and give you peace' (Num 6:25). Therefore, if the sinner, through God's great patience, remains unfeeling toward his failings, not thinking himself to be God, but desiring to remain hidden, saying: 'Darkness covers me from every side and the walls, who sees me?', God says: 'I am a God drawing near and not a God far off. Shall anyone hide in secret and I shall not see him? Do I not fill heaven and earth? says the Lord' (Jer 23:24).

Having turned His face from the sinner, He sends him away, instead of 'showing him to be a stranger to Himself,' according to: 'God will drive them away because they did not listen to Him, and they shall be wanderers among the nations' (Deut 32:28) and: 'Like wounded women cast down sleeping in a grave, of whom you no longer remembered, and they themselves were driven from your hand' (Isa 57:1). And though many of His sons became [so], he did not know; even if a few became [so], he does not know.

Understand, lest these things reveal the ungraspable nature of God's judgments. Rather, his flesh grieved and his soul mourned. This shows that as the wrath against the sinner moves according to the secret words of providence, the one falling into it suffers and mourns, but is ignorant of the words of the handing over. These things are instructional, so as not to say to friends that they know that one suffers through sin.

For the one who does not endure suffers and is consumed when he falls into calamities, but the brave man, even if he is stung by hardships, bears them courageously toward the goal, looking away (Heb 12:2). For only the one who seeks nothing good or useful suffers if he is afflicted. But the virtuous man, like a crowned athlete, does not regard the hardships because of the expectation of the crown. Having understood, Eliphaz the Temanite says: Whether the wise man will give an answer of the understanding of the spirit? And this one of the same...
translator_notes: True OET; Pass A ≠ Pass B. Melito skipped; never Cyril Matthew densify.

title: The Error of Judging Job by Sin
english: Existing in a state of delusion and thinking that he suffers through sin, he begins his words by asserting that it is wise to answer with understanding, implying that Job does not answer with understanding. This one, then, is a fool, and he is striking at the holy man regarding his lack of understanding. And he filled his belly with toil by reproving with words that are not to be used, and in words that have no profit. As it has been said, he begins foolishly; for he says that it is wise of the wise to answer sensibly, but 'he filled his belly with toil by reproving with words that are not to be used,' instead of [saying] 'from the pains, which he had in his heart and is unable to restrain, he brings forth words that are not to be used, and words in which there is no profit,' scattering his words as if they were useless and futile things sent forth. 'Will you not also cease from fear?' The preceding things are confirmed; for he reproves him as one who has not had fear, and it is clear that he also, by subjecting God, [claims] that because he has not had fear, but has suffered these things through sins, and that one not having fear uses such words. For they thought him bold, not knowing his virtue, supposing that having renounced fear, he says these things. 'Have you completed such words before the Lord?' Perhaps because of the easy availability of the words, which he brought forth purely from the one having conscience, he says these things, which this [accuser] considers as blasphemy, assuming the false beginning that he suffers through sin. 'You are guilty of the words of your mouth.' He dialogues with him with boldness as if he were bringing forth words against one who is not righteous. And he also thinks that he reproves him from his own words, asserting that 'you shall be reproved by words from yourself' (Job 11:6). You did not even distinguish the words of the mighty. Consider whether he says 'the mighty' to mean those who excel in understanding, either at the same time or before, as it is said in the things mentioned before: 'For he inquired of the first generation, and searched out the generations of the fathers' (Job 8:8), so that what he says might be such a thing: 'not through judgment...'
The text cuts off mid-sentence at the end of the provided Greek.

[The purpose is] the words of the wise, so that through them your words and your whole life are regulated. For it is often said that they rebuke you as if you were suffering because of sins. They say, 'Let your own mouth convict you and not I; let your lips testify against you.' They bring these things forward out of audacity, for they did not have the power to rebuke him in such a way. They bring this forward in reference to the initial dispute.

For what? Did you not first come from men, or did you come upon the earth before the dusts? They want to present to him that 'you do not differ from other men, nor do you exist outside of their nature so as to have grasped more than the others,' in order that they might present themselves as having reached the truth, for which he suffers a cause. And those who bring in the soul by associating it with the body take advantage of this—the Hierarchs and the Soldiers and the like—saying, 'if not before the dusts'—instead of 'before the earth' (for he named the whole from a part)—'but upon the dusts,' from which they will think to draw the soul to be scattered with the body, while others overturn this, saying the pivot of understanding is a moist thing, which does not suit a soul but a body.

Or have you heard a divine arrangement, yet wisdom has come to you? Proposing the unsearchable nature of judgments from this, he thinks he is wandering into not knowing, that he suffers through something other than sin, being held by this. For he himself was not one having heard a divine arrangement or having wisdom come to him, so as to have a dispute concerning the Holy One as one suffering through sin. For what do you know that we do not know, or what do you understand that we do not? (Job 28:23). He makes it common to all men, as if he were ignorant of the greatness of his virtue, and from this, as it is foretold, he is apparently overturning the idea of himself being righteous; which it was necessary that he, even while ignorant, should not pre-judge the judgment and be persuaded that he is bowed down as a sinner. And even an elder and an old man among us, heavier than your father's days. 'If even...
translator_notes: True OET; Pass A ≠ Pass B. Melito skipped; never Cyril Matthew densify.

title: The Greatness and Inconstancy of Man
english: "an elder," he says, "you are, and an old one among us, becoming more weighty than even your father"—instead of "more venerable"—"knowing more than we do." And he says these things from an arrogant authority. We have "weighty" instead of "old man" written in the Royal Histories; for the purpose of showing that Eli was an old man, the text says, "and the man was weighty." This also signifies honor and abundance, as if he were saying, "I will confess to you, Lord, in a great congregation, in a weighty people, I will praise you," instead of "in honor and in abundance."

"A few of your sins have been scourged." He says this meaning: "You have sinned and because of this you undergo lashes. But since, enduring this, you add injustice to God, your sin has become more weighty." And he says these things not with understanding; for he did not know the matter as it was, so that he was speaking falsely. And there are various ways of being false. For there is a way of having lied that is not [maliciously] lying; for often we hold an opinion about something as being such and we say it, having the intention of speaking the truth, yet that which is reported is false by its own nature, but it is not said by one who is lying. And there is also the case of one who, not knowing anything at all, brings forth a false word out of arrogance, which is what happened to him.

But there are others who lie in a different way, as one who has knowledge. "You have spoken with great excess" (Job 32:2). "What did your heart dare, or what did your eyes lift up?" (Job 31:24). And they held these opinions about him, both hearing [of his sins] and because of his words of boldness. Since the blessed one brought forth words from purity, they thought this was an excess of arrogance, in vain and without understanding. "That you have broken a heart before the Lord, and have brought forth from your mouth such words." They thought [his] boldness, which exceeds [all] from purity, was anger, which happened to them from their own corrupt nature, since they had subjected themselves to blasphemy, regarding the reasonable and as it is naturally yielded, the freedom of his words, as blasphemy.

For what mortal is there that will be blameless, or that, as he is to come, will be a righteous offspring of a woman? It is a characteristic of those who do not possess virtue to consider this undertaking difficult and to place it as if no one possessed it, just as the one before says, stumbling because of the body's [nature] as it is likely [to be] weak.

If he had observed according to the soul and according to the intellect, he contemplated the greatness of human nature, which the hymnographer teaches on both sides, saying: 'What is man, that you take thought of him? Man is made like vanity' (Psalm 8:4), which he has said regarding the weakness of the body as comparing it to divine things. But instructing on greatness, he says again: 'You made him a little less than the angels, you crowned him with glory and honor' (Psalm 8:5). And again he says another saying, 'a great man' and 'a precious man, merciful,' which is not according to being born, but according to being in essence receptive of justice in the composition.

He does not believe according to the saints. Similar to this is the 'if he does not believe according to his children, he thought something crooked concerning his angels.' Thus, there he says the angels are the saints, presenting that 'if even angels are corruptible, how can a man be blameless?' It should be noted that to believe often signifies the certain, as it is said: 'All his commandments are faithful' (Psalm 146:5). And he interprets their faithfulness saying: 'established unto the age of ages.' And again: 'the word is faithful and worthy of all acceptance.' And again: 'God is faithful and there is no injustice.' For God is not faithful from participating in faith, but from having certainty. And heaven is not pure before him.

Just as even the stars will not be compared to God's light, being without any darkness, and the heaven itself is not pure, not at all, but rather in addition to God. And it is possible to call these ones who 'left the heavenly dwelling' heaven here, whom he said 'his children, concerning whom he does not believe.' For God himself says in Isaiah from his own person: 'My sword is drunken in heaven' (Isaiah 34:5). And the sword signifies punishment, as it is said: 'My sword shall eat blood of wounds, and my arrows shall be drunken with blood' (Isaiah 34:6). Thus, among the angels who have fallen, he says the sword becomes drunken, bringing punishment called heavens. Therefore, this heaven is not pure before him. And a man, being detested and unclean, drinks an equal measure of injustice. Even if a heaven happens to be earthly through transgression, he is made like a man no longer worthy to be an angel, because the drink leads to injustice; for he carries unmeasurably the...
translator_notes: True OET; Pass A ≠ Pass B. Melito skipped; never Cyril Matthew densify.

title: The Fragility of Life and the Suddenness of Destruction
english: for evil is an episode

You hold [it], since you are not righteous, to whom the earth was given along with those like him, and no foreigner approaches. Thus, how he said this has been made clear. The Lord, commanding his own disciples, says: 'Do not worry about tomorrow' (Matt 6:34). And it is a command, so that 'we should throw all anxiety upon the Lord' (1 Pet 5:7). And if he also says that life is 'in care,' and that years are a numbered amount given to a ruler, then his fear is in his ears. This he says, that even if someone is a ruler and acts insolently, let him know that he has a numbered number of years.

Power does not make him long-lived; for time is measured for men by God toward His own judgment. Therefore, even if the ruler acts arrogantly, his life and his years turn out to be few, and he always has fear in his ears because of the uncertainty of the manner [of death]. Such a person has a fearful nature. For when he is in care regarding life, he reveres even death. But the diligent one, knowing that it is better 'to depart and be with Christ' (Phil 1:23), is hopeful, not being such as the wicked, but one who fears; for it has been said that 'the impious flees when no one pursues' (Prov 28:1).

When it seems to him that he is already at peace, his destruction will come. Even if someone exists in great prosperity, like the one saying in the Gospel: 'I will pull down my barns and build greater, and I will say to my soul: Soul, you have many good things, eat, drink, rejoice' (Luke 12:18-19); but the Lord says to him: 'Fool, this very night they will demand your soul from you; and what you have prepared, to whom will it belong?' (Luke 12:20). For when it seemed to him to be at peace in wealth, his destruction came.

These things, then, the divine word presents. It seems that he says these things, stumbling according to this, from the mishearings of the wise, because he was applying these to Job. Let him not believe that one turns away from darkness. The phrase 'when it seems to him to be at peace, his destruction will come' is similar to 'when they say: It is peace and security' (1 Thess 5:3). He says, 'Then, sudden destruction stands upon them just like the pangs of a woman in labor.' For he has already been committed into hands of iron, and has been arranged into pits of gypsum (Job 15:22b–23a). For the one sinning has hoarded for himself punishments, which [will come] through iron and gypsum.
translator_notes: True OET; Pass A ≠ Pass B. Melito skipped; never Cyril Matthew densify.

title: The Uninhabited Houses of the Soul
